tools.name: get_current_user
tools.description: Get your current user profile, admin status and whether you need to create an organization. The Profile fields are `display_name`, `title` (job role), `company` and, once verified in the console, `phone` / `phone_country` / `phone_verified_at` (null until then). `update_profile` changes the first three.

A brand-new account can be refused with 403 `turnstile_failed` when sign-up bot checks are on: they run in the browser, so the user signs up once at https://console.selfhost.dev and then signs in here. A 403 `account_restricted` on sign-up means the network it comes from is barred.

tools.name: update_profile
tools.description:
Update the signed-in person's Profile: `display_name` (2-60 characters), `title` (their job role) and `company` (each at most 60). Send only what changes; an empty `title` or `company` removes it, an empty name is refused. The same Profile the console's Settings show and the name is what teammates see in member lists and the activity log.

The mobile number is NOT settable here: it is verified by a code Firebase texts to the phone, a browser step with a reCAPTCHA, so point the user at the console's Profile page for it.

title.description: Job role, e.g. Backend engineer; empty string removes it

company.description: Company name; empty string removes it

tools.name: list_organizations
tools.description: List all organizations you belong to

tools.name: create_organization
tools.description:
Create a new organization (limit: 1 per user). You become the owner and receive 5 invite credits.

THIS NOW REQUIRES A VERIFIED EMAIL ADDRESS. Organization creation is the one capability gated on it and the refusal is a 422 carrying `code: "email_verification_required"` - not a 402 and not a field error. It means exactly what it says: the user must open the verification email and click the link, then retry. Relay that rather than treating it as a bug or retrying in a loop and note the check reads the live Firebase state, so a retry right after clicking through succeeds without re-login.

Everything else - projects, instances, databases - already requires an organization, so this is the only place the gate can bite.

tools.name: get_organization
tools.description: Get details of an organization (defaults to your active org)

tools.name: update_organization
tools.description: Update an organization's name or description (requires owner or admin role). The default instance IAM role is set by Selfhost.dev staff only.

tools.name: delete_organization
tools.description: DESTRUCTIVE: Delete an organization (requires owner or admin role). Refused while it still has database instances or project servers: delete those first (`delete_instance`, `delete_project`). With none left it soft-deletes the org with its memberships and DNS records. You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.name: list_members
tools.description:
List members of an organization with their roles. Each row carries the user pid (as `id`), email, name, `last_active_at`, `joined_at` and `role`.

`role` is a SLUG, not a pid: one of `owner`, `admin`, `billing`, `manager`, `member`. `update_member_role` takes the slug too, so you can pass what you read here straight through.

The ladder, highest first: `owner` Owner (priority 100) - Full control, including billing and deleting the org; `admin` Admin (priority 80) - Manages members, settings, projects, instances and alerts; reads billing; `billing` Billing (priority 60) - Billing and payment management; `manager` Manager (priority 40) - Operates resources without member or billing control; `member` Member (priority 20) - Day-to-day access, no administrative control.

tools.name: remove_member
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: Remove a member from an organization. They lose access immediately.

AUTHORITY: an owner may manage everyone. An admin may only manage STRICTLY BELOW their own priority - never a peer admin and never grant a role at or above their own. You can never change your OWN role (self-demotion would lock you out, self-promotion would be an escalation); an owner stepping down has to be demoted by another owner. The last owner cannot be demoted or removed. The same strict-priority rule applies here as to `update_member_role`, deliberately - otherwise an admin blocked from demoting a peer could just remove them instead. Removing YOURSELF (leaving the org) is allowed.

If the intent is to reduce someone's access rather than end it, `update_member_role` is the tool - offer that first.

You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

user_id.description: The member's user pid - the `id` field from `list_members`

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.description:
Invite a user to your organization by email, at a role you choose.

Pass `role` as a slug - `owner`, `admin`, `billing`, `manager`, `member` - and this resolves it to the pid the API wants. (`role_pid` is still accepted for a role this tool does not know about, but you should not normally need it.)

The ladder: `owner` Owner (priority 100) - Full control, including billing and deleting the org; `admin` Admin (priority 80) - Manages members, settings, projects, instances and alerts; reads billing; `billing` Billing (priority 60) - Billing and payment management; `manager` Manager (priority 40) - Operates resources without member or billing control; `member` Member (priority 20) - Day-to-day access, no administrative control.

You can never change your OWN role (self-demotion would lock you out, self-promotion would be an escalation); an owner stepping down has to be demoted by another owner. The last owner cannot be demoted or removed.

Requires `members:invite`. The invitee gets an email with a token; the membership does not exist until they accept, so they will not show in `list_members` yet - track them with `list_org_invitations`.

tools.name: update_member_role
tools.description:
Change an existing member's role. This is the only way to promote or demote someone after they have joined - inviting them again does not do it.

Pass `role` as a slug: `owner`, `admin`, `billing`, `manager`, `member`. The ladder, highest first: `owner` Owner (priority 100) - Full control, including billing and deleting the org; `admin` Admin (priority 80) - Manages members, settings, projects, instances and alerts; reads billing; `billing` Billing (priority 60) - Billing and payment management; `manager` Manager (priority 40) - Operates resources without member or billing control; `member` Member (priority 20) - Day-to-day access, no administrative control.

You can never change your OWN role (self-demotion would lock you out, self-promotion would be an escalation); an owner stepping down has to be demoted by another owner. The last owner cannot be demoted or removed.

`user_id` is the member's USER pid - the `id` field from `list_members`, not their membership or email.

A 422 here is almost always one of the authority rules above rather than a fault: read the message back to the user instead of retrying. Confirm the change with them first - a demotion can remove someone's access to billing or to every instance in the org.

tools.name: list_activity_logs
tools.description:
List an organization's activity log (its audit trail), newest first: who did what to which resource, when and from where (`action`, `subject_type`, `target_type`, `metadata`, `user_name`, `actor_type`, `ip_address`, `instance_pid`, `created_at`). Every member sees the organization's visible actions plus their own private ones.

Paged: `limit` 1-100 a page (default 20) and `page`; the reply's `pagination` gives `total_records`, `total_pages` and `next_page` (null on the last page). Up to 0.12.1 this tool sent no parameters and dropped the paging block, so it only ever saw the newest 20.

`instance_pid` narrows it to one managed database's events (the console's per-database Activity tab); an unknown pid is an empty page, not an error. Project servers have their own feed in `list_project_activities`.

tools.name: accept_invitation
tools.description:
Join an organization the signed-in user was invited to: the console's "Join" in its organization menu. The invitation is listed by `get_my_memberships` as an entry with a pending `invitation`; pass that invitation's `access_token`. (The invitation email only links to the console; it carries no token.)

The signed-in email must be the address the invitation was sent to ("Email does not match invitation" otherwise) and it must be verified: an unverified address is refused with `email_verification_required` until the user clicks the verification email. An expired or already used invitation answers "Invalid or expired invitation": ask the inviter for a new one. On success the reply names the organization and role; then `select_organization` to work in it.

token.description: The pending invitation's access_token, from get_my_memberships

tools.name: list_credentials
tools.description:
List cloud credentials for an organization. Credential secrets are never returned.

Each credential has: id (PID), name, cloud_provider (e.g. "aws"), auth_method, status ("active"/"inactive"), is_platform_managed (bool), is_default (bool).

When selecting credentials for instance creation:
- Filter by cloud_provider matching the user's chosen provider (e.g. "aws")
- Only use credentials with status "active"
- is_platform_managed=true → Selfhost.dev's cloud account (no VPC needed)
- is_platform_managed=false → user's own cloud account (BYOC - VPC required, use list_vpcs)
- Present the user with a choice between platform-managed and their own credentials

tools.description: Add a cloud credential to an organization (requires owner or admin). Auth methods: access_key (provide AWS keys), iam_role or platform_managed.

tools.name: update_credential
tools.description: Update a cloud credential's name, description or keys (requires owner or admin). Cannot modify platform-managed credentials. cloud_provider and auth_method are immutable. ROTATING KEYS: new keys are re-applied to the running Kafka and ClickHouse instances that use them and the reply's message names those and any instance that needs reconfiguring by hand; relay it.

tools.name: delete_credential
tools.description: DESTRUCTIVE: Delete a cloud credential (requires owner or admin). Cannot delete platform-managed credentials and refused while any LIVE instance uses it: the refusal names those instances (and lists their pids in its data), so move or delete them first. You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.name: get_byoc_required_iam_policy
tools.description:
The IAM policy a bring-your-own-cloud (BYOC) AWS account needs, as a ready-to-attach policy document: what the console offers when linking an account, so the user attaches it once instead of discovering missing permissions one failed create at a time.

With no engine it returns the whole catalog. Pass `db_type` (and `managed_vpc` / `table_topics` where they apply) to get only what that engine's create needs. The reply has `policy` (the JSON document), `groups` (what each permission group is for) and `link_time_groups` (what linking itself checks). Then `verify_credential_permissions` confirms a linked key has it. Needs an Owner or Admin.

db_type.description: Scope the policy to one engine's create

managed_vpc.description: With db_type: the platform creates the VPC

tools.name: get_byoc_cloudformation_template
tools.description:
The CloudFormation template that sets up a BYOC AWS account in one stack, the console's download: it creates the IAM user, its policies and an access key, stores the key pair in AWS Secrets Manager and outputs `BYOCAccessKeyId` and `BYOCCredentialsSecretArn` (never the secret itself). Each download carries a fresh random ExternalId. Returns the YAML text.

Hand it to the user to deploy in THEIR AWS account (CloudFormation console or `aws cloudformation deploy --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM`); then they read the secret from Secrets Manager and link the key with `add_credential`. Do not deploy it yourself with their keys unless they ask. Needs an Owner or Admin.

tools.name: verify_credential_permissions
tools.description:
Re-check a linked BYOC AWS credential against the IAM permissions the platform needs, for a user who has just fixed their policy. By default it checks what linking needs; pass `db_type` to pre-check exactly what that engine's create needs before trying it.

Answers: all present (`missing_actions: []`); 422 `AWS_IAM_PERMISSIONS_MISSING` with the `missing_actions` to add (`get_byoc_required_iam_policy` has the full document); 422 `AWS_KEYS_REJECTED` when AWS refuses the keys themselves; 502 `AWS_UNREACHABLE`; 503 `AWS_PERMISSIONS_CHECK_UNAVAILABLE` when AWS would not let the check run, which is NOT a clean result: retry rather than reporting the permissions as fine. Access-key credentials only; needs an Owner or Admin.

db_type.description: Check what this engine's create needs

tools.name: estimate_instance_cost
tools.description:
Estimate the monthly cost of a database instance BEFORE creating it using the Selfhost.dev pricing API.
Call this to present accurate cost to the user for approval before calling create_instance.

Returns an itemized breakdown of compute, storage and add-ons. Prices are ALL-IN: the
platform margin is folded into each line rather than billed separately, matching the
console and the website - so quote these numbers to the user as-is and never add a
platform fee on top.

PASS type_of_dbms WHENEVER YOU KNOW THE ENGINE. Two engines provision nodes the pricing
endpoint cannot see and this tool only adds them when it knows the engine:
- clickhouse with replica_count=1 gets a dedicated keeper-only node (t4g.small + 20 GB)
  holding the Raft quorum. At 2+ replicas the quorum is embedded and there is no extra node.
- opensearch with replica_count >= 1 gets 3 dedicated cluster-manager nodes on top of the
  data nodes, each inheriting the data nodes' storage size. replica_count=1 is 5 machines,
  not 2, so leaving the engine out understates that cluster by three whole nodes.

The engine also sets the margin: it is sent as `db_type` and the endpoint prices through the
same billing path as the real charge, so each engine estimates at its own margin (ClickHouse's is
higher than the others'). Up to 0.12.1 this tool never sent the engine, so ClickHouse estimates
came out about 10% low; that caveat is gone once type_of_dbms is passed.

KAFKA: a three-broker HA cluster is replica_count=2. Kafka keeps its topic data in S3 and that
object storage and its requests bill on usage, OUTSIDE this estimate: say so beside the figure.
`schema_registry: true` prices the endpoint broker with the Schema Registry beside it and is
refused below 8 GiB and 2 vCPUs, exactly as create_instance refuses it.

THIS IS AWS ONLY. It cannot price a PaaS project server - those are Hetzner machines on a
different margin entirely. Use `list_server_types`, which returns real per-location prices.

iops.description: Provisioned IOPS (for gp3/io1/io2). Defaults to storage type baseline if omitted.

throughput_mbps.description: Throughput in MB/s (for gp3). Defaults to storage type baseline if omitted.

type_of_dbms.description: Engine being priced. ALWAYS PASS IT: it sets the engine's margin (sent as db_type), clickhouse at replica_count=1 adds a billed Keeper node and opensearch at replica_count>=1 adds 3 billed cluster-manager nodes, both invisible to the pricing endpoint. kafka adds a note that its S3 storage bills on usage, outside the estimate.

schema_registry.description: kafka only: include the Schema Registry beside the endpoint broker (needs 8 GiB and 2 vCPUs)

tools.name: create_instance
tools.description:
Create a new database instance on AWS. This is the core AWS provisioning tool.

RECOMMENDED FLOW (follow this before calling create_instance):
1. Ask the user: host on Selfhost.dev's cloud (platform-managed) or their own AWS account (BYOC)?
2. Call list_credentials - filter results by cloud_provider "aws" AND status "active".
   - Platform-managed: pick credential where is_platform_managed=true
   - BYOC: pick credential where is_platform_managed=false. If none exist, user must add_credential first.
3. If BYOC: call list_vpcs with the credential's id and chosen region - only present VPCs from the "public" group. vpc_id is REQUIRED for BYOC.
4. If platform-managed: vpc_id is NOT needed (skip VPC selection entirely).
5. Call estimate_instance_cost to show the user the estimated monthly cost before deploying.
6. Only call create_instance after the user confirms the cost is acceptable.

IMPORTANT:
- The password is NOT in the create response (it never was, whatever older versions of this tool
  printed): Owners and Admins read it with get_instance_credentials (each read is audited). Call it
  once the user wants to connect.
- NETWORK ACCESS: a database created WITHOUT allowed_cidr_ranges is reachable only from inside its
  VPC (backend #4102 / #4294, 2026-10-28; before that it opened to the whole internet). To connect
  from the user's machine or an app outside AWS, pass that address range, e.g.
  ["203.0.113.7/32"]. ["0.0.0.0/0"] opens it to everyone (the password is still required). Ask the
  user where they will connect from; ranges can be changed later with update_instance.
  `network_scope` on the instance says where its DNS name resolves: `public` or `vpc`.
  Each entry is a CIDR string ("203.0.113.7/32", opened on the engine's default port) or {cidr, port?, name?, description?}. A port must be one of the engine's client ports: its default port or postgres 6432, mysql 6033, redis 6380, clickhouse 9000/9090/9440/8443, opensearch 5601, kafka 8081/8083; any other port is a 422 (backend #4708). At most 58 ranges and fewer when a pooler, TLS ports or co-located services are on, because every range becomes one security-group rule per opened port and a group holds 60: about 29 with one pooler or one extra port, 19 for Kafka with the Schema Registry, 14 for ClickHouse with CHProxy and TLS. The 422 names the maximum for that configuration. Turning on a pooler, TLS, Dashboards or the Schema Registry later is refused the same way when the existing ranges would overflow: trim the ranges first.
- Storage IOPS/throughput requirements depend on storage type:
  gp3: iops required (3000-80000), throughput required (125-1000 MB/s)
  io1/io2: iops required (100+), throughput NOT used
  gp2/st1/sc1: iops and throughput NOT used

CLICKHOUSE SPECIFICS (they differ from the other engines - read before creating one):
- Minimum 4 GiB RAM. Smaller instance types are rejected; find eligible sizes with
  get_instance_types_for_region using min_memory=4.
- Replication is a Keeper/Raft quorum, not streaming replication, so multi_az REQUIRES
  replica_count >= 1 and the count changes the node topology:
    replica_count=1 → primary + 1 replica + a dedicated Keeper node (t4g.small, 20 GB)
                      that holds the quorum. That third node is billed - price it with
                      estimate_instance_cost using type_of_dbms="clickhouse".
    replica_count=2+ → primary + N replicas, quorum embedded on the data nodes, no extra node.
  2 is the recommended default and is what gets used if you enable multi_az without a count.
- Connect over HTTP on 8123 (native TCP on 9000) as user `admin`. Multi-AZ clusters
  expose the distributed cluster `selfhost_cluster`.
- Use 8123 as the port on allowed_cidr_ranges entries, not 5432/3306.
- Version: 26.8 LTS, the only one the platform supports. It is pinned at create and
  CANNOT be changed later - moving versions means a new instance plus a restore or migration into it.

OPENSEARCH SPECIFICS (a search/analytics engine, not a relational database - read before creating one):
- Minimum 4 GiB RAM: the JVM heap takes 50% of available memory. Find eligible sizes with
  get_instance_types_for_region using min_memory=4.
- HA IS A CLUSTER TOPOLOGY, AND `replica_count` BUYS FAR MORE MACHINES THAN IT LOOKS:
    replica_count=0 → 1 node (one all-in-one node; dev / non-HA only)
    replica_count=1 → 5 NODES: 3 dedicated cluster-manager nodes + 2 data nodes  ← HA minimum
    replica_count=2 → 6 nodes: 3 managers + 3 data
    replica_count=N → N+4 nodes
  Going from no HA to HA is a 1 → 5 node jump, not 1 → 2, because a quorum needs an odd
  number of managers and two would be split-brain-prone. ALL of those nodes bill. Price it
  with estimate_instance_cost using type_of_dbms="opensearch" and the real replica_count and
  quote that number before creating - this is the single most expensive surprise on the
  platform if you skip it.
- multi_az REQUIRES replica_count >= 1 and unlike every other engine it CANNOT BE TOGGLED
  LATER in either direction. Enabling afterwards would build a 2-manager set with 0-replica
  indices; disabling would terminate nodes with no shard drain. Decide HA at create or plan on
  creating a new cluster and restoring into it.
- manager_instance_type sets the three managers' size (default t4g.medium). Same 4 GiB floor -
  managers carry no indexing or search load, so they can be smaller than the data nodes, but
  not smaller than that. They inherit the endpoint node's storage size.
- ALWAYS HTTPS ON 9200, never plaintext. Use 9200 on allowed_cidr_ranges entries. Transport
  port 9300 is node-to-node only and is never customer-facing.
- TLS CAVEAT WORTH STATING UP FRONT: certs are per-cluster and CA-signed and the node cert's
  SAN covers the private IP rather than the public DNS name - so strict hostname verification
  against the endpoint fails even with the CA trusted. Tell users to trust the CA with relaxed
  hostname checking or connect from inside the VPC. `curl -k` for a quick start. The cluster
  CA is not downloadable through the API yet.
- No named databases (like redis) - do not ask for or display a database name.
- Vector search is BUILT IN (the k-NN plugin ships with the engine), so an embeddings workload
  needs no extension here - that is a postgres/pgvector concern.
- dashboards_enabled turns on the OpenSearch Dashboards UI on port 5601. It needs 4 GiB minimum
  (8 GiB recommended) because it runs alongside the JVM on the endpoint node and it can be
  turned on or off later with set_opensearch_dashboards. It never blocks readiness.
- Version: 3.8 or 2.19; 3.8 is sent by default, matching the console.

KAFKA SPECIFICS (Managed Kafka, implemented by AutoMQ: Kafka-compatible brokers that keep topic data in S3):
- Minimum 4 GiB RAM. Version 3.9.1 only (default 3.9.1).
- HA IS A FIXED 3-BROKER CLUSTER: multi_az=true builds 3 combined broker+controller nodes, one per
  availability zone, all billed; there is no other replica count. Without multi_az it is one broker.
- Clients connect on 9092 with SASL/SCRAM-SHA-256 as the instance's username (default admin) and
  password. Give clients EVERY broker as bootstrap.servers: get_instance and get_instance_credentials return
  `bootstrap_servers` (one host:port per live broker, the endpoint first) once the brokers are up. Use 9092 as the port on allowed_cidr_ranges entries.
- tls_enabled: chosen at create and never changeable afterwards. Omitted, the backend turns client TLS
  on (since 2026-10-28); the certificate is issued a few minutes after the broker starts, so clients
  connect with SASL_PLAINTEXT first and SASL_SSL once it lands. false keeps SASL_PLAINTEXT, where SCRAM
  protects the password but messages cross the network unencrypted.
- schema_registry: an optional Schema Registry (Apicurio, Confluent-compatible, port 8081, signing in
  with the cluster's Kafka user). It runs its own JVM on the endpoint broker, so that machine needs
  8 GiB and 2 vCPUs. Its certificate comes from the broker machine's own CA, so serializers that
  verify certificates (the Confluent Java and Python ones included) refuse it until they trust that CA.
- NO EBS BACKUPS: topic data lives in S3, so a disk snapshot cannot restore it. backup_enabled and a
  snapshot_id restore are refused for Kafka. The S3 object storage and requests bill on usage.
- The password cannot contain , [ ] " or \ (Kafka's credential tools parse them).
- The machine size is the one you create it on: Kafka has no instance-type resize yet (storage only).
- No PITR, no pooling, no config tuning and no extensions on Kafka.

ENGINE-SPECIFIC FOLLOW-UPS (route to the right tools per engine after creating):
- Connection pooling: PgBouncer for postgres, ProxySQL for mysql, CHProxy for clickhouse, none for redis, opensearch or kafka.
- Performance tuning: the pg-config tools for postgres, the mysql-config tools for mysql; none for redis, clickhouse or opensearch.
- PITR applies to postgres and mysql only - not redis, not clickhouse, not opensearch (there is no
  WAL-G equivalent, so opensearch durability is EBS volume snapshots and whole-volume restores only).
- database-users applies to postgres, mysql, clickhouse and opensearch - not redis.
- postgresql_config and `extensions` are postgres-only.
- db_version is fixed for the life of the instance on every engine. There is no in-place version
  upgrade anywhere on the platform any more (selfhost#2580 withdrew the ClickHouse one).

POSTGRES EXTENSIONS - pass `extensions: [...]` (an ARRAY of catalog names, not booleans):
- TimescaleDB is `timescaledb`, pgvector is `pgvector` (or its SQL alias `vector`). The old
  `timescaledb_enabled` / `vector_enabled` flags were REMOVED backend-side and are now
  IGNORED rather than rejected - sending them provisions an instance with no extensions at all.
- Call `list_postgres_extension_catalog` with the `db_version` you are about to use to see
  what is on offer; compatibility is per entry (`pg_textsearch` needs PostgreSQL 17 or 18).
  Do not work from a memorised list.
- Extensions chosen here are installed during provisioning, so the ones that need a PostgreSQL
  restart cost nothing extra at create - there is no restart to warn about on this path.
- Readiness accounts for them: the instance is not marked ready while any requested extension
  is missing. Any of them can be added later with `enable_instance_extensions`, but NONE can
  ever be removed, so ask the user before adding to the list.

throughput.description: Throughput in MB/s (required for gp3 only)

db_version.description: Database version. postgres: 18, 17, 16 (default 18). mysql: 8.4, 8.0 (default 8.0, the stable release). redis: 7.2, 7.0 (default 7.2). clickhouse: 26.8 (default 26.8, the LTS and the only supported version). opensearch: 3.8, 2.19 (default 3.8). Omitting this sends the default explicitly - the backend's own fallback is the oldest major it still supports.

username.description: Database username (default: admin). Redis ignores this (auth is a single requirepass/password); it applies to postgres, mysql, clickhouse and opensearch. On clickhouse the customer user is `admin` - the built-in `default` user is platform-internal and not usable. On opensearch the customer user holds `all_access` and the internal `admin` superuser is never surfaced.

custom_password.description: Database password (8-128 printable ASCII chars; on kafka none of , [ ] " \). Auto-generated if omitted.

cloud_credential_id.description: Credential PID from list_credentials. Use is_platform_managed=true credential for Selfhost.dev's cloud or is_platform_managed=false for BYOC. Always ask the user which they prefer.

vpc_id.description: VPC ID - REQUIRED when using BYOC credentials (is_platform_managed=false). Use list_vpcs and only pick from the 'public' group. Not needed for platform-managed.

multi_az.description: Enable multi-AZ replication (default: false). Required for any replica_count on clickhouse and opensearch. On opensearch it is PERMANENT - the only engine where HA cannot be toggled after create. On kafka it means the fixed three-broker cluster.

replica_count.description: Replicas to provision alongside the primary when multi_az is on. postgres/mysql/redis: 1 or 2. clickhouse: 1-5, default 2 (1 adds a billed Keeper node). opensearch: buys DATA nodes and silently adds 3 billed manager nodes on top - 1 means 5 machines. kafka: always 2 (three brokers); leave it out. See the engine notes.

manager_instance_type.description: opensearch only: size of the 3 dedicated cluster-manager nodes when replica_count >= 1 (default t4g.medium, 4 GiB floor). They carry no search load, so they can be smaller than the data nodes.

dashboards_enabled.description: opensearch only: install the OpenSearch Dashboards UI on port 5601. Needs 4 GiB RAM minimum (8 recommended) since it shares the endpoint node with the JVM. Can be changed later with set_opensearch_dashboards.

confirm_node_count.description: opensearch only: required acknowledgement that replica_count >= 1 provisions 3 extra billed cluster-manager nodes. Omit it first to be told the real machine count, then set true once the user has seen the price.

data_durability.description: postgres only: how long a COMMIT waits for a standby. `async` = local ack (RPO > 0). `preferred` = wait when standbys are healthy, degrade when not (never blocks). `required` = RPO 0 and BLOCKS WRITES when it cannot be held. Defaults to `preferred` with multi_az, `async` without.

sync_number.description: postgres only: how many standbys must ack a commit (default 1). Cannot exceed replica_count.

no_auto_failover_ack.description: postgres only: required when data_durability=`required` with exactly 1 replica - that topology has NO automated failover and this is the explicit acceptance of it.

anyOf.description: A CIDR such as 203.0.113.7/32, opened on the engine's default client port

port.description: One of the engine's client ports (see the description); anything else is a 422

allowed_cidr_ranges.description: Who may connect: CIDR strings ("203.0.113.7/32") or {cidr, port} objects, at most 58 and fewer with poolers or TLS ports (see the description). OMITTED, the database is reachable only from inside its VPC: pass the user's address range to connect from outside AWS or 0.0.0.0/0 to open it to everyone. A custom db_port is not an allowed rule port at create.

snapshot_id.description: Restore from a backup snapshot ID

extensions.description: PostgreSQL extensions to install during provisioning, by catalog name, e.g. ["pgvector", "pg_stat_statements"]. postgres only. Read `list_postgres_extension_catalog` first - names are validated server-side and an incompatible one is a 422. None can be removed later.

postgresql_config.description: PostgreSQL parameter overrides (use preview_pg_config to see available params)

iam_role_arn.description: IAM role ARN for the EC2 instance

db_port.description: Database port (default 5432 postgres, 3306 mysql, 6379 redis, 8123 clickhouse HTTP, 9092 kafka)

tls_enabled.description: kafka only, create-time only: client TLS. Omitted, the backend turns it on (the certificate lands a few minutes after the broker starts); false keeps SASL_PLAINTEXT. Postgres TLS is set_postgres_tls instead.

schema_registry.description: kafka only: add the Schema Registry (Apicurio, port 8081) on the endpoint broker. Needs 8 GiB RAM and 2 vCPUs on that machine.

tools.name: list_instances
tools.description:
List all database instances for an organization, grouped by `group_id` (master + replicas).

POLL `ready`, NOT `status`. Each instance carries a server-computed `ready` boolean, a `ha_ready` for the group and a `readiness_detail` hash explaining a false. That exists precisely so a caller stops guessing across `status`, `internal_status`, `provisioning_state` and replica health - a `running` instance is NOT necessarily usable. Answer "is my database up?" from `ready`.

`ha_ready` is the one to check before telling a user their cluster is highly available: it is true only when the master is ready AND every live replica's replication link is healthy, so it goes false on a quietly degraded cluster whose master still looks fine.

`deprecated_at` on an instance means its machine type is being retired. It keeps working, but flag it - a user planning capacity should know before the deadline rather than after.

tools.name: get_instance
tools.description:
Get detailed information about a specific database instance, including its latest metrics.

READINESS IS ONE FIELD. `ready` is computed server-side and is the field to trust: for a master or single node it means running, provisioning complete, no error and the agent healthy; for a replica it means running, complete and the replication LINK healthy (a small lag is fine - only a broken link blocks readiness). `readiness_detail` says which of those failed. Do not reassemble this from `status` and `internal_status`; a `running` instance can be unusable.

`ha_ready` covers the whole group: master ready and every alive HA replica link-healthy.

If an instance has been provisioning for more than about 15 minutes it is considered STUCK rather than slow - say so instead of advising the user to keep waiting.

NOT EVERY NODE IN A GROUP IS A DATABASE. Two fields say which is which and reading them avoids pointing a user at a node that cannot do what they asked:
- `clickhouse_node_role` - `keeper_only` marks the Raft arbiter. It runs clickhouse-keeper, not clickhouse-server, so it holds no table data: no query stats, no data backup, no scaling policy. It is not a node to connect to, but it IS a node on the bill.
- `opensearch_node_role` - which role this node carries in the cluster. Only the node with `opensearch_endpoint: true` is the client-facing 9200/DNS target; manager-only nodes serve no traffic and carry no data.

A HOT STANDBY IS A READABLE REPLICA, NOT A WRITE TARGET and it also cannot be scaled or reconfigured directly - those operations belong to its primary and the backend refuses them on a replica, naming the primary. When a user asks to change something on a node that turns out to be a replica, act on the primary instead of relaying a confusing refusal.

`deprecated_at`, when set, marks the machine type as scheduled for retirement. Worth surfacing unprompted.

instance_id.description: AWS EC2 instance ID (alternative to pid)

snapshot_id.description: Snapshot ID (to get original instance context for restore)

tools.name: get_instance_credentials
tools.description:
Read a managed database's master credentials: `username`, `password`, `database_name` (where the engine has one), `host` and `port`, enough for a connection string.

For Kafka the reply also carries `bootstrap_servers`: one host:port per live broker, the endpoint first. Give clients all of them.

The password used to be shown once at create and never again; since backend #3404 (2026-10-08) an Owner or Admin of the organization can read it here at any time. Any other role gets a 403 `data_access_required` (the permission is `cloud_instances:credentials` and platform staff never hold it). At most 30 reads a minute; never cached; each read is recorded in the organization's activity log as `credentials_viewed`, without the secret.

This is the bootstrap admin, which reads and writes all data. For an app, prefer a dedicated user with the database-users tools.

tools.name: get_instance_metrics
tools.description:
Read historical metrics for managed database instances - the same agent-heartbeat series the console graphs.

Use this to answer "how is my database doing?", to size a change before making it or to sanity-check an alert rule (a rule on a metric that never appears here will never fire).

Returns a per-instance, per-metric summary (latest / min / max / avg + sample count) by default. Set raw=true only when you genuinely need every sample - a busy instance produces hundreds of frames per day and they will flood the context.

Metric sets (same names alert rules use):
- system: cpu_percent, memory_percent, disk_usage_percent, load_avg_1/5/15, swap_usage_percent, cpu_io_wait_percent
- network: recv_bytes_per_sec, sent_bytes_per_sec
- storage: disk_used_percent, disk_free_bytes, inodes_used_percent, read/write_io_per_second, ... reported PER MOUNT POINT and keyed `storage[/mount]` in the summary. Read the engine's data volume (e.g. `storage[/selfhostdev/postgresql]`), not `storage[/]` or `storage[/boot]` - a full /boot says nothing about database capacity.
- <engine>.database: postgresql.database | mysql.database | redis.database | clickhouse.database | opensearch.database - the engine's own counters. `create_alert_rule` carries the complete per-engine allow-list; these are the same names.
- pgbouncer.stats appears once pooling is enabled. It is READABLE here but NOT alertable - the alert-rule catalog has no such metric_type, so a rule on it is rejected.

On a replicated instance `active_replica_count` is the one to watch for a quietly-degraded cluster: it drops without the instance's own status changing. Ratio metrics (`cache_hit_ratio`, `innodb_buffer_pool_hit_ratio`, `mark_cache_hit_ratio`) are already on a 0-100 scale - do not multiply them by 100.

An empty result usually means the agent has not reported in that window (a stopped instance or one still provisioning), not that the instance is idle.

instance_pid.description: Limit to one instance (awsinst_...). Omit for every instance in the org.

start_date.description: Inclusive start date, YYYY-MM-DD (default: yesterday). The window covers whole days.

metric_type.description: Only return this metric set. Cheaper than filtering client-side.

raw.description: Return every heartbeat frame instead of the summary. Verbose - use a narrow window and a single instance.

tools.name: update_instance
tools.description: Update an instance's configuration. Some changes are synchronous (db_port, backup, CIDR ranges), others are async (instance_type, multi_az, storage). Cannot update replicas - update the master instead. Cannot change db_version on any engine: the platform withdrew the in-place ClickHouse upgrade in selfhost#2580, so a version change is now a new instance plus a restore or migration into it. Cannot toggle multi_az on OpenSearch - its HA is a cluster topology chosen at create. Not handled here either: enabling postgres extensions (see the extension tools) or the OpenSearch Dashboards UI (set_opensearch_dashboards).

instance_type.description: New EC2 instance type (triggers async resize)

multi_az.description: Enable/disable multi-AZ (triggers async operation). NOT AVAILABLE ON OPENSEARCH in either direction - its HA is a cluster topology fixed at create. Refused on a Duplicate (a fork or a point-in-time restore: `multi_az_unsupported`) and on a Duplicate with Auto sync on (`auto_sync_enabled`: turn it off with set_duplicate_auto_sync first).

anyOf.description: A CIDR such as 203.0.113.7/32, opened on the engine's default client port

port.description: One of the engine's client ports (see the description); anything else is a 422

allowed_cidr_ranges.description: REPLACES the allowed sources. CIDR strings or {cidr, port}; a port must be one of the engine's client ports or the instance's own port. The security group is changed first and the ranges are saved only if that worked. Each entry is a CIDR string ("203.0.113.7/32", opened on the engine's default port) or {cidr, port?, name?, description?}. A port must be one of the engine's client ports: its default port or postgres 6432, mysql 6033, redis 6380, clickhouse 9000/9090/9440/8443, opensearch 5601, kafka 8081/8083; any other port is a 422 (backend #4708). At most 58 ranges and fewer when a pooler, TLS ports or co-located services are on, because every range becomes one security-group rule per opened port and a group holds 60: about 29 with one pooler or one extra port, 19 for Kafka with the Schema Registry, 14 for ClickHouse with CHProxy and TLS. The 422 names the maximum for that configuration. Turning on a pooler, TLS, Dashboards or the Schema Registry later is refused the same way when the existing ranges would overflow: trim the ranges first.

tools.name: set_postgres_durability
tools.description:
Change a PostgreSQL group's HA durability mode - how long a COMMIT waits for a standby to flush the WAL before the primary acks it. This is the RPO dial.

THE THREE MODES and the only difference that matters is what happens when no standby is healthy:
- `async` - the primary acks locally. Fastest and RPO > 0: commits can be lost if the primary dies before a standby has them.
- `preferred` - waits while standbys are healthy and DEGRADES to no-wait when none are. It never blocks writes, which is exactly why it cannot be described as zero-data-loss.
- `required` - RPO 0, honestly implemented: dead standby names stay in the wait set, so when the SLA cannot be held **THE PRIMARY STOPS ACCEPTING WRITES** rather than acking data no survivor holds. Availability is traded for durability, deliberately.

ONLY `required` WHILE `sla_held` IS TRUE MAY BE CALLED ZERO DATA LOSS. Read `sla_held` and `degraded` from the response before telling a user their data is safe: `required` with `sla_held: false` means writes are being refused right now and `preferred` with `degraded: true` means it is silently acking locally.

RULES THE BACKEND ENFORCES:
- PostgreSQL only and on the MASTER only - replicas follow the group mode (a 422 names the primary).
- THIS MUST BE SENT ALONE. Durability changes cannot ride along with any other instance update, so do not try to combine it with `update_instance`.
- Moving TO `preferred` or `required` needs standbys actually streaming; without them the move is refused ("no streaming standbys to wait on"). Moving to `async` is always allowed - it is the honest escape hatch from a stalled `required` primary.
- `sync_number` cannot exceed the group's HA standby count.
- `required` with exactly one standby needs `no_auto_failover_ack` - see below.

IF A PRIMARY IS STALLED because `required` cannot be held, the unwedge is moving to `preferred` (which starts shrinking the wait set) or `async` (which removes the wait). That is the answer to "my writes are hanging" on a `required` cluster and it is worth offering immediately rather than diagnosing further.

instance_id.description: The MASTER instance's PID - not a replica

data_durability.description: Target mode. Omit to keep the current one and change only sync_number.

sync_number.description: How many standbys must ack (default 1). Cannot exceed the group's HA standby count.

no_auto_failover_ack.description: Required for `required` with exactly 1 standby: that topology has no automated failover.

confirm.description: Must be true. Moving to `required` can block writes; moving to `async` gives up zero-data-loss.

tools.name: get_opensearch_dashboards
tools.description:
Read the OpenSearch Dashboards state for an instance - the opt-in Kibana-style UI on port 5601.

Returns `dashboards_enabled`, `dashboards_status` (`disabled` | `installing` | `running` | `degraded` | `failed`), `dashboards_url`, the instance's `memory_gb` and two RAM verdicts: `dashboards_supported` (>= 4 GiB, the hard floor) and `dashboards_recommended` (>= 8 GiB). Check `dashboards_supported` BEFORE offering to enable it - below the floor the enable is rejected outright.

DASHBOARDS FAILING DOES NOT MEAN THE CLUSTER IS UNHEALTHY. It is co-located on the endpoint node as a Node.js process next to the JVM and it is deliberately fail-soft and outside provisioning and readiness: the instance is ready when port 9200 is, whatever Dashboards is doing. Report a `failed` or `degraded` state as a separate, non-blocking fact, never as a broken database.

422 on any non-OpenSearch instance.

instance_id.description: Instance PID (e.g. awsinst_xxx). Must be the cluster's endpoint node.

tools.name: set_opensearch_dashboards
tools.description:
Turn the OpenSearch Dashboards UI on or off on an existing cluster (port 5601). Unlike most of this engine's shape, this one IS a day-2 toggle in both directions.

Call `get_opensearch_dashboards` first and check `dashboards_supported`: the endpoint node needs 4 GiB RAM to enable at all (8 GiB recommended, since Dashboards is a Node.js process sharing the box with the OpenSearch JVM). Below the floor this is a 422.

Other requirements the backend enforces: OpenSearch only, the cluster's ENDPOINT node only (not a manager or a non-endpoint data node), status `running` or `provisioned` and a registered agent to enable.

Enabling also opens 5601 on the security group. Poll `get_opensearch_dashboards` for `installing` → `running`; a `failed` outcome leaves the cluster itself healthy and serving on 9200.

instance_id.description: Instance PID of the cluster's endpoint node

enabled.description: true installs and starts Dashboards; false stops it and closes the port.

confirm.description: Must be true. Enabling adds a process competing with the JVM for memory on the endpoint node and opens another port; disabling takes the UI away from anyone using it.

tools.name: stop_instance
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: Stop one or more running database instances. Databases become unavailable. A replica cannot be stopped on its own - stop the master and the group goes with it.

STOPPING DOES NOT STOP THE BILL and this is the most common wrong assumption to correct. Compute stops accruing, but everything that still physically exists keeps being charged: the EBS volumes, snapshots and S3-backed storage including PITR WAL. A stopped instance is cheaper, not free. If the user's goal is to stop paying, the answer is `delete_instance` (and deleting snapshots separately) - say so rather than letting them believe a stop achieved it.

A final charge is issued at the moment of the stop, closing the window since the last billing run, so the next invoice includes usage right up to the transition.

You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.name: start_instance
tools.description:
Start one or more stopped database instances. A replica cannot be started on its own.

Compute resumes billing from the moment it starts. If the wallet is empty this can fail on the balance gate - check `get_wallet_balance` first when a start is refused rather than retrying.

tools.name: reboot_instance
tools.description: DESTRUCTIVE: Reboot one or more database instances. This will cause brief downtime. Cannot reboot replicas independently. You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.name: delete_instance
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: Delete one or more database instances. This action is irreversible.
Delete protection must be disabled first. Master deletion must include all replicas.

A final charge is issued at deletion for usage since the last billing run, so a small charge after deleting is correct, not a bug.

WHAT SURVIVES THE DELETE AND KEEPS BILLING: snapshots and other backup storage are separate resources and are NOT removed with the instance. If the user is deleting in order to stop paying, check `list_snapshots` and `list_backups` too - otherwise they will delete the database and keep the storage bill.

You MUST set confirm=true to proceed. Before calling this tool, always ask the user to confirm they want to delete these specific instances.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.name: fork_instance
tools.description:
Fork (clone) an existing database instance into a new instance, a "Duplicate" in the console. Cannot fork replicas or deleted instances. A fork is always a single node, even of a multi-AZ source (the reply carries a `topology_note` then). The password is not in the reply: Owners and Admins read it with get_instance_credentials.

A fork is built in its SOURCE's AWS account: `cloud_credential_id` may only name a credential in that same account (422 otherwise), so leave it out unless the user has a reason. A PostgreSQL 14 or 15 source can no longer be forked (#4924 dropped those versions): the 422 names the supported ones. A PostgreSQL Duplicate can later be refreshed from its source in place with `start_duplicate_sync` or on a schedule with `set_duplicate_auto_sync`.

cloud_credential_id.description: Credential PID; defaults to the source's. Must be in the source's AWS account.

tools.name: refresh_instance_group
tools.description: Refresh instance data for a group (master + replicas). Use this to get updated status after async operations.

tools.name: preview_pg_config
tools.description: Preview calculated PostgreSQL configuration defaults for an instance type and region. Use this to see what values will be auto-calculated before creating or tuning an instance.

tools.name: get_pg_config
tools.description: Get the current PostgreSQL configuration for a running instance, showing calculated defaults, overrides and effective values.

tools.name: update_pg_config
tools.description: Update PostgreSQL configuration parameters on a running instance. Set a value to null to revert to the calculated default. shared_buffers and max_connections require a restart. Changes auto-sync to replicas.

shared_buffers.description: Shared memory for caching (e.g. '256MB'). Set null to revert to default.

effective_cache_size.description: Planner estimate of OS cache (e.g. '768MB'). Set null to revert.

random_page_cost.description: Cost of non-sequential page fetch (e.g. 1.1). Set null to revert.

work_mem.description: Memory per sort/hash operation (e.g. '4MB'). Set null to revert.

maintenance_work_mem.description: Memory for maintenance ops (e.g. '64MB'). Set null to revert.

max_connections.description: Max concurrent connections (e.g. 100). Set null to revert. Requires restart.

tools.name: list_backups
tools.description:
List backups for an organization. Triggers a sync with AWS to refresh snapshot sizes.

Covers both families - read `backup_type` on each row to tell them apart (`aws_backup_job` = disk snapshot, `clickhouse_native` = ClickHouse data backup). A data-backup row additionally carries `options.backup_name`, `options.s3_bucket`, `options.scheduled` (true when a schedule took it), `options.backup_policy_pid`, a measured `size_bytes`, `error_message` on failure and `options.last_restore` (`in_progress` | `completed` | `failed`) once it has been restored from.

There is no single-backup GET: to follow a run or a restore to completion, call this again. A backup's own `status` stays `completed` whatever a later restore does - only `options.last_restore` moves.

tools.name: create_backup
tools.description:
Take a backup of a database instance now. Cannot back up a replica.

TWO TYPES, pick the one that matches what the user asked for:
- `aws_backup_job` - a DISK SNAPSHOT via AWS Backup. Any engine. Needs `options: {backup_vault_name, backup_plan_id}`. Restored by creating a new instance from the resulting `snapshot_id`, not by `restore_backup`.
- `clickhouse_native` - a DATA BACKUP: `BACKUP ALL` of every database, streamed to a dedicated offsite S3 bucket. ClickHouse DATA nodes only (a keeper-only node holds no table data). No `options` required - the backend resolves and provisions the bucket. This is the only type `restore_backup` accepts.

`s3_file_backup` was removed: the backend now 422s it and tells you to use `clickhouse_native`. Do not try it.

EXPECT THESE REFUSALS on `clickhouse_native`, all 422 and all worth explaining rather than retrying blindly: the instance is not running; a restore is in progress; a backup is already in flight (one per instance, a hard lock). A 503 means the backup bucket could not be provisioned - that one IS retryable and leaves no doomed record.

Returns the run in `in_progress`. Poll `list_backups` for the terminal state.

COSTS MONEY: snapshot storage is metered per GB-month against your credit wallet (SKU `ebs_snapshot_storage`; see `list_skus` for the rate) and keeps billing until the snapshot is deleted. A 402 here means the wallet is empty - top up with `create_topup`.

backup_type.description: `aws_backup_job` = disk snapshot (any engine); `clickhouse_native` = ClickHouse data backup to offsite S3

options.description: aws_backup_job needs {backup_vault_name, backup_plan_id}. clickhouse_native needs nothing - leave this unset.

tools.name: restore_backup
tools.description:
Restore a ClickHouse DATA backup (`clickhouse_native`) back into a running ClickHouse instance. This is the only restore path here - a DISK SNAPSHOT is not restored with this tool, you create a new instance from its `snapshot_id` instead.

THE RESTORE IS ADDITIVE. It MERGES the backup's tables into the target and never drops anything already there. It is not "roll back to this point": a row written after the backup was taken survives the restore. Say that to the user before running it, because "restore" usually means the opposite.

By default it restores into the instance the backup came from. Pass `target_instance_id` to restore into a DIFFERENT running ClickHouse data node - that is how you clone a dataset between instances. Pass `databases` to narrow the scope; names must be plain identifiers or the backend 422s.

While it runs the TARGET instance sits in status `restoring` (cleared on success and on failure alike). Refusals, all 422: the backup is not `clickhouse_native`, is deleted or is not `completed`; it has no offsite S3 copy so there is nothing to read; the target is not ClickHouse, is not running or is already restoring; or a backup is in flight on the target (running BACKUP ALL and RESTORE ALL together would capture a dataset mid-mutation and mark it completed).

A FAILED FULL RESTORE BLOCKS THE NEXT ONE into the same target, deliberately: a half-restored dataset merged into again is unrecoverable guesswork. The 422 says so and there are two honest ways forward - clean up the half-restored state and pass `restore_cleanup_confirmed: true` or restore into a FRESH target instead. Do not set that flag on the user's behalf without them confirming the cleanup actually happened. A scoped `databases` retry is exempt, because it replays a narrow scope rather than the whole dataset.

Follow it with `list_backups` and read `options.last_restore` - the backup's own `status` stays `completed` regardless of how the restore ends and it records which `retry_path` was taken.

target_instance_id.description: Restore into this instance instead of the one the backup was taken from. Must be a RUNNING ClickHouse data node.

databases.description: Restore only these databases. Plain identifiers only. Omit to restore everything in the backup.

restore_cleanup_confirmed.description: Required to RETRY a full restore into a target whose previous full restore FAILED - it confirms the half-restored state was cleaned up. Not needed for a first attempt or a scoped `databases` retry.

confirm.description: Must be true. Confirm the user understands the restore MERGES into the target and does not roll it back.

tools.name: delete_backup
tools.description: DESTRUCTIVE: Delete a backup. Removes the AWS snapshot if present and soft-deletes the backup record. This cannot be undone. You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

tools.name: list_backup_policies
tools.description:
List backup schedules for an organization. Optionally filter by instance.

TWO KINDS come back in the same list and you must read `details.policy_type` to tell them apart:
- absent / anything else = a DLM DISK-SNAPSHOT policy (block-level EBS snapshots, any engine).
- `clickhouse_native` = a ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule (`BACKUP ALL` to offsite S3).

An instance can have BOTH at once and they are independent. Do not present a native row as the instance's snapshot policy or vice versa - the console had a bug where one shadowed the other and users read the wrong retention.

Each row carries `schedule_interval` + `schedule_unit` + `retain_rule_count` and a `state` of `ENABLED` or `DISABLED` (that is the paused flag).

tools.name: create_backup_policy
tools.description:
Create a DLM policy for automated DISK SNAPSHOTS (block-level EBS). Any engine.

For a ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule use `create_data_backup_schedule` instead - it is a different resource with different required fields and this tool cannot make one.

If the instance is ClickHouse, note a temporary backend coupling: saving the disk-snapshot policy currently also rewrites and re-enables the instance's data-backup schedule. Warn the user if they have both.

COSTS MONEY: snapshot storage is metered per GB-month against your credit wallet (SKU `ebs_snapshot_storage`; see `list_skus` for the rate) and keeps billing until the snapshot is deleted. A 402 here means the wallet is empty - top up with `create_topup`. A schedule multiplies that: the policy holds `retain_rule_count` snapshots per volume at once, so the standing cost is roughly retention x volume size.

tools.name: create_data_backup_schedule
tools.description:
Create a recurring ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule: a `BACKUP ALL` of every database, streamed to a dedicated offsite S3 bucket, on a cadence you set. ClickHouse only. This is the scheduled counterpart of `create_backup` with `backup_type: "clickhouse_native"`.

Not the same thing as `create_backup_policy`, which schedules block-level DISK SNAPSHOTS. An instance can carry one of each.

ONE PER INSTANCE. A second create returns 422 naming the existing schedule - update or delete that one instead.

Retention is `retain_rule_count` runs kept, pruned oldest-first. Send integers, never numeric strings: the backend rejects a non-integer and the reason it is strict is that a string would cast to 0 and 0 means "every run" for the interval and "never prune" for the retention.

A 503 means the offsite bucket could not be provisioned. That is retryable and leaves nothing behind.

RESTORE DRILLS (`drill_interval` + `drill_unit`) PROVE THE BACKUP ACTUALLY COMES BACK and they are the only thing here that does. On the cadence you set, the platform provisions a SCRATCH single-node instance, restores the newest completed backup into it, compares post-restore row counts against the recorded baseline and tears the scratch down on every exit path. The verdict lands on the backup's `options.restore_drill` as `passed` or `failed`.

THEY COST MONEY WHILE THEY RUN: a scratch instance is a real billed instance for the length of a restore plus verification (timeout 24h). Say so when offering drills - a weekly drill on a large dataset is not free. Omit both fields for no drills, which is the default.

COSTS MONEY: snapshot storage is metered per GB-month against your credit wallet (SKU `ebs_snapshot_storage`; see `list_skus` for the rate) and keeps billing until the snapshot is deleted. A 402 here means the wallet is empty - top up with `create_topup`. Here the metered cost is S3 storage for the retained backups, not EBS.

cloud_instance_pid.description: The ClickHouse instance to back up. Must be a data node - a keeper-only node holds no table data.

schedule_interval.description: How often, as a positive integer paired with schedule_unit (e.g. 1 + DAYS = daily)

retain_rule_count.description: How many completed backups to keep. Older ones are pruned.

drill_interval.description: Restore-drill cadence, paired with drill_unit. 0 or omitted = no drills. A drill provisions a real (billed) scratch instance to verify the backup restores.

region.description: Defaults to the instance's own region - normally omit this

tools.name: update_backup_policy
tools.description:
Update a backup schedule. Works on BOTH kinds - the backend routes on the policy's own type, so pass the pid and the fields you want changed.

PAUSE AND RESUME is `state`: `DISABLED` pauses the schedule and KEEPS everything it has already taken; `ENABLED` resumes it. Prefer this over deleting whenever the user says "stop backups for now" - deleting a data-backup schedule destroys its runs (see `delete_backup_policy`).

On a ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule (`details.policy_type == "clickhouse_native"`) only `state`, `schedule_interval`, `schedule_unit` and `retain_rule_count` apply; the DLM-only fields are ignored. Send integers, not numeric strings or the backend 422s.

On a DISK-SNAPSHOT (DLM) policy the same top-level `schedule_interval`, `schedule_unit` and `retain_rule_count` now apply too (to every schedule in the policy; before backend 4eec1e872 they were silently ignored there) and `policy_details` may be PARTIAL: what it leaves out is completed from the live policy. Numbers must be integers above 0 and the unit HOURS, DAYS or WEEKS. Shortening retention is checked against the object-storage restore window and is refused with a 422 if the retained snapshots would outlive it.

state.description: DISABLED pauses the schedule and keeps existing backups; ENABLED resumes it

drill_interval.description: ClickHouse data-backup policies only: restore-drill cadence with drill_unit. 0 turns drills off. A drill provisions a real billed scratch instance to verify the backup restores.

drill_unit.description: ClickHouse data-backup policies only: unit for drill_interval

policy_details.description: Disk-snapshot policies only: AWS DLM policy details; a partial structure is completed from the live policy. Prefer the top-level schedule fields for interval and retention.

tools.name: delete_backup_policy
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: Delete a backup schedule. Works on both kinds and WHAT IT DESTROYS DIFFERS:

- DISK-SNAPSHOT (DLM) policy: removes the policy from AWS and stops future snapshots. Snapshots already taken survive.
- ClickHouse DATA-BACKUP schedule (`details.policy_type == "clickhouse_native"`): also DELETES every backup that schedule took - the S3 folders, the rows and the dedicated bucket once nothing else references it. Manual backups of the same instance are untouched. This is a deliberate backend decision, not a bug.

So on a data-backup schedule this is not "stop backing up", it is "stop backing up AND throw away the scheduled history". If the user only wants to stop, call `update_backup_policy` with `state: "DISABLED"` instead - that pauses and keeps everything. OFFER THAT FIRST.

Either way, if this was the last active policy on the instance, `backup_enabled` is turned off.

You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Ask the user for explicit confirmation before setting this.

THE METRIC ALLOW-LIST. `metric_name` must appear under the `metric_type` you pass or the rule is rejected:

- system: cpu_percent, cpu_io_wait_percent, memory_percent, swap_usage_percent, disk_usage_percent, load_avg_1, load_avg_5, load_avg_15
- network: recv_bytes_per_sec, sent_bytes_per_sec
- storage: disk_free_bytes, disk_free_percent, disk_total_bytes, disk_used_bytes, disk_used_percent, inodes_free, inodes_total, inodes_used, inodes_used_percent, read_bytes_per_second, read_io_per_second, read_utilization_percent, read_write_bytes_per_second, total_utilization_percent, write_bytes_per_second, write_io_per_second, write_utilization_percent
- postgresql.database: blocks_read_per_second, cache_hit_ratio, committed_tx_per_second, connections_total, max_connections, replication_lag_seconds, active_replica_count, transactions_per_second, timescaledb_hypertable_count, timescaledb_chunk_count, timescaledb_compressed_chunk_count, timescaledb_compression_ratio, timescaledb_total_size_bytes
- mysql.database: connections_total, max_connections, connections_aborted, threads_running, queries_per_second, slow_queries_per_second, replication_lag_seconds, active_replica_count, innodb_buffer_pool_hit_ratio, innodb_row_lock_waits_per_second, tmp_disk_tables_per_second, select_full_scans_per_second
- redis.database: used_memory, connected_clients, evicted_keys, expired_keys, keyspace_hits, keyspace_misses, instantaneous_ops_per_sec, rdb_changes_since_last_save, rdb_last_save_time, replication_lag_seconds, connected_slaves, blocked_clients
- clickhouse.database: query_count, queries_per_second, select_queries_per_second, insert_queries_per_second, failed_queries_per_second, inserted_rows_per_second, selected_rows_per_second, memory_usage, background_merges_count, replication_delay, replication_lag_seconds, active_replica_count, disk_used_bytes, connections_count, connections_total, broken_parts_count, mark_cache_hit_ratio, parts_active, keeper_connected, total_replicas, active_replicas, queue_size, future_parts, is_session_expired, lost_replicas, noquorum_detached_parts
- opensearch.database: cluster_status, active_shards, relocating_shards, initializing_shards, unassigned_shards, active_primary_shards, number_of_nodes, jvm_heap_used_percent, cpu_percent, disk_used_percent, indexing_rate, search_rate, replication_lag_seconds

Match metric_type to the instance's ENGINE. A rule using postgresql.database metrics never fires on a ClickHouse instance - it is accepted and then silently never evaluates, which is worse than an error, so check the engine with `get_instance` first if you are unsure.

Metrics that exist but never arrive are the other silent failure. The five `timescaledb_*` names are absent from heartbeats until TimescaleDB is actually installed and `active_replica_count` only means something on a replicated instance. A rule on a metric the instance does not report does not error - it just never fires. `get_instance_metrics` shows what an instance is really sending; if a name is missing there, a rule on it is dead.

Two engine-specific traps worth knowing:
- ClickHouse reports replication health as `replication_delay` (seconds behind the quorum). `replication_lag_seconds` also exists but `replication_delay` is the one the platform's own sync logic reads.
- Ratio metrics are already percentages on the 0-100 scale - `cache_hit_ratio`, `innodb_buffer_pool_hit_ratio` and `mark_cache_hit_ratio` alike. Set a threshold like 95, not 0.95. (`timescaledb_compression_ratio` is the exception: it is a multiplier, so 3.5 means 3.5x.) Redis has no ready-made ratio - compute it from `keyspace_hits` and `keyspace_misses`.

`storage` rules REQUIRE `mount_point` and it must name a real mount on the instance (`/`, `/boot` or the engine's data volume - they are reported separately and a rule on the wrong one watches the wrong disk).

tools.name: list_database_users
tools.description:
List DBMS-level users on an instance. Returns each user's id, username, role, status (`active` | `pending` | `deleting` | `failed`), target database, connection limit, password expiry metadata and `password_rotation_enabled`. Postgres, MySQL, ClickHouse and OpenSearch (not Redis).

Read `password_rotation_enabled` alongside the expiry when a user asks about credentials: `false` means the credential will be LOCKED at expiry (warned by email first), `true` means it will be silently rotated and a webhook fired. A credential nearing expiry with the wrong setting for how it is consumed is the failure worth flagging without being asked.

A `failed` user whose error mentions enforcement sync means a lock half-applied; `rotate_database_user_password` recovers it.

tools.name: create_database_user
tools.description:
Create a DBMS-level user on an instance. Postgres, MySQL, ClickHouse and OpenSearch - NOT supported for Redis (Redis uses a single shared requirepass; the backend returns "Database user management not supported for redis"). Username 1-31 chars, letters/digits/underscores only. Password 8-128 printable chars; on OpenSearch also at most 100 characters, strong (the backend scores it with zxcvbn and refuses a weak one) and not resembling the username, so generate a long random one there. Role determines DB privileges: read_only (SELECT), read_write (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), admin (broader DDL). Target database scopes the grant to one DB; leave empty for cluster-level access - and omit it entirely on OpenSearch, which has no named-database concept.

ON OPENSEARCH the role maps onto a security-plugin role (read_only → `readall`, read_write → a custom `selfhost_read_write`, admin → `all_access`) and six usernames the plugin owns are rejected here before the request goes out: admin, kibanaserver, kibanaro, logstash, readall, snapshotrestore. Only `admin` is in the backend's own reserved list, so the other five would otherwise pass validation and then fail at agent sync as `status: failed`.

PASSWORD LIFETIME: every user's password expires after 90 days and what happens then depends on `password_rotation_enabled`:

- `false` (THE DEFAULT) - the user gets reminder emails at 14, 3 and 1 days out. At expiry the credential is ROTATED TO A PASSWORD NOBODY IS TOLD and locked, so it stops working until someone calls `rotate_database_user_password`. Right for a human who logs in and can act on a warning; wrong for an app, because the app just breaks.
- `true` - no emails and no lock. At expiry the password rotates automatically and a `database_user.password_rotated` webhook fires so the consumer can fetch the new credential (the webhook payload never carries the password itself). Right for tooling that can refetch on that signal.

The default is `false` deliberately: silent rotation breaks credentials baked into an application, which is what users complained about. So `true` is only the better choice if something is actually listening for that webhook and can refetch. If a password is hardcoded anywhere, `true` will break it silently at the 90-day mark instead of warning first - ASK which situation this user is in rather than guessing.

The instance must be `running` or `provisioned` and the username must be free.

target_database.description: Specific DB to grant on; omit for cluster-wide

connection_limit.description: Max concurrent connections for this user (default unlimited)

password_expiry_days.description: Days until the password expires; omit for no expiry

password_rotation_enabled.description: false (default) = warn by email, then lock the credential at expiry. true = rotate silently at expiry and fire a `database_user.password_rotated` webhook instead. Only pick true if something is listening for that webhook - it will break a hardcoded password with no warning.

tools.name: update_database_user
tools.description:
Update a database user - change role, connection limit, password expiry or the expiry BEHAVIOUR. Username and target database are immutable (delete + recreate to change them). Postgres, MySQL, ClickHouse and OpenSearch (not Redis).

The password itself is not changed here: use `rotate_database_user_password` for that (it reveals the new password once).

Switching `password_rotation_enabled` is the fix for a credential heading for the wrong ending. Set it `true` when an app consumes the credential and can refetch on the `database_user.password_rotated` webhook, so expiry rotates instead of locking. Set it `false` when a person uses the credential and should be warned by email rather than have it change under them.

A user that has ALREADY been locked by an expiry is not recovered by flipping this - it stays locked until `rotate_database_user_password` runs.

password_expiry_days.description: 0 removes expiry; otherwise sets a new countdown from now

password_rotation_enabled.description: true = auto-rotate at expiry and fire the `database_user.password_rotated` webhook. false = email warnings, then lock the credential at expiry.

SECURITY: save it immediately - there is no way to retrieve it later. Existing connections using the old password are terminated. Postgres, MySQL, ClickHouse and OpenSearch (not Redis).
