tools.name: scale_instance
tools.description:
Manual one-off resize of an instance - change instance type, volume type, size, IOPS, throughput. Only fields you pass are sent (PATCH-style). Response includes `scaling_event_id` you can poll on the instance status (`resizing` / `modifying_storage` → terminal state). Storage must grow, not shrink.

STORAGE CASCADES: growing a data node's volume also expands every live data peer in its cluster to match and storage bills per node - so on a multi-node cluster the cost of `new_size_gb` is multiplied by the number of data nodes. Tell the user before scaling a clustered instance. (Unlike an auto-scale rule, a manual scale takes an absolute size and ignores any cluster_max_storage_gb ceiling.)

ONE KIND OF CHANGE PER CALL: an instance-type change and a storage change cannot ride in one request (backend 422 `split_scale_request`). Do the type change, wait for it to finish, then the storage change.

MULTI-AZ POSTGRESQL, MYSQL AND REDIS: after the master resizes, its HA replicas are resized in place one by one. The master can read `running` while that roll continues, so read `active_scale_event.ha_replicas` on `get_instance` (`status` in_progress, completed, partially_resized, refused, stopped or failed, with `done` of `target`) before telling the user the cluster is done. While it rolls, other changes to the group are refused. A group on `required` durability is refused the in-place roll.

new_size_gb.description: New EBS size; must be ≥ current

new_iops.description: Only valid for gp3/io1/io2 volume types

tools.name: list_scaling_policies
tools.description:
List scaling policies, optionally filtered to one instance. Covers start/stop schedules, auto-scaling rules and cluster tier triggers; each row carries `cloud_instance_pid` so you can tell which instance it belongs to.

TELLING THE THREE APART matters, because they behave nothing alike:
- `cloud_instance_pid` set, `group_id` empty - an ordinary single-instance rule.
- `group_id` set with `scaling_action: resize_instance` - a CLUSTER TIER trigger. It moves the whole group along a capacity ladder and its thresholds are the `cpu_*`/`memory_*` pair plus `window_minutes`, not `metric_name`/`threshold`. Its bounds live on the group's capacity config (`get_capacity_config`), so this row alone does not tell you how far the group can move. Tier triggers come in pairs - one `scale_up`, one `scale_down` - and a group with only an up policy will grow and never shrink, which is worth pointing out.
- Filtering by instance will NOT return a group's tier policies, since they have no instance target. Use `get_capacity_config` for those.

An `expand_storage` policy whose `details` still has `new_size_gb` (instead of `cluster_max_storage_gb`) predates the cluster-cascade contract: it is outdated, cannot be edited or disabled (every save 422s) and must be deleted and recreated. Flag those to the user rather than trying to patch them.

organization_id.description: Org PID; defaults to active org. Used as `organization_pid` on the wire.

tools.name: create_scaling_policy
tools.description:
Create a scaling policy. Use this for both auto-start/stop schedules and reactive/scheduled auto-scaling rules. Shape depends on action + trigger:

• start/stop schedules → schedule_type=scheduled + scheduled_start_time OR scheduled_stop_time (HH:MM UTC) + days_of_week. These are the only policies that may target MANY instances (cloud_instance_pids).
• reactive auto-scale  → schedule_type=reactive + metric_name + comparison_operator + threshold + duration_minutes + cooldown_minutes
• scheduled auto-scale → schedule_type=scheduled + cron_expression (5-field) + optional start_time/end_time (ISO 8601). The reactive fields are still required by the backend; neutral defaults are injected for you (manual_trigger / 85 / '>' / 1m / 0 cooldown) and ignored at fire time.

Action-specific `details` (required on every non-start/stop policy):
• resize_instance → { target_instance_type }
• add_replica     → { max_replicas }
• expand_storage  → { cluster_max_storage_gb }

STORAGE AUTO-SCALE (expand_storage) - read before writing one:
- Growth is a DOUBLING on each fire, clamped to cluster_max_storage_gb and the volume type's own max: target = min(current x 2, cluster_max, type_max). There is no absolute-size or step option; details.new_size_gb and details.growth_step_gb are rejected (422). For a one-off absolute resize use `scale_instance`.
- cluster_max_storage_gb must EXCEED the volume's current size.
- threshold must be between 40 and 85 and the operator must be '>' or '>=' (disk metrics: disk_used_percent / disk_usage_percent).
- The rule may only attach to a DATA, non-replica node (ClickHouse keeper-only nodes are not data nodes).
- Expansion CASCADES: when the volume commits, every live data peer in the cluster is expanded to match and storage bills per node. Warn the user about the multiplied cost on a multi-node cluster.

TIER POLICIES (whole-cluster ladder scaling) are a FOURTH shape and none of the above applies to them. A policy is a tier policy when `scaling_action` is `resize_instance` AND `group_id` is set:
- Required: `group_id`, `target_class`, `direction` (`scale_up` or `scale_down`) and `window_minutes`.
- Thresholds are the direction's CPU **and** memory pair - `cpu_up_threshold` + `memory_up_threshold` for up, `cpu_down_threshold` + `memory_down_threshold` for down. NOT `metric_name` / `threshold` / `comparison_operator`, which are ignored.
- `schedule_type` is FORBIDDEN (422). Tier scaling is reactive only.
- `details.target_instance_type` is NOT used - the ladder decides the next size.
- ONE POLICY PER DIRECTION. Scaling up and scaling down are two separate rules against the same group.
- An enabled capacity config for (`group_id`, `target_class`) must ALREADY EXIST or this is refused. Create it with `create_capacity_config` first.
- HYSTERESIS IS ENFORCED across the pair: a scale_down threshold must be strictly below its scale_up sibling, on both CPU and memory. Equal values are rejected, because they would let the cluster oscillate.
- Server defaults if omitted: 80/80 up, 20/20 down, `window_minutes` 10 up and 360 down, cooldown 30. The long scale-down window is intentional - a quiet afternoon should not shrink a production cluster.
- Use this instead of a plain `resize_instance` rule for any clustered engine: a single-node switchover fired at a multi-node cluster desyncs its tier state.

organization_id.description: Org PID; defaults to active org. Wire field: organization_pid

cloud_instance_pid.description: Target instance PID. Required for every action except bulk start/stop schedules, which may use cloud_instance_pids instead.

cloud_instance_pids.description: Multiple target instances - ONLY valid for start_instance / stop_instance schedules. The backend rejects it for expand_storage / resize_instance / add_replica.

metric_name.description: Metric to watch. Disk fill reports as disk_used_percent (also accepted: disk_usage_percent).

threshold.description: 0-100 for percentage metrics. expand_storage is restricted to 40-85.

timezone.description: Default UTC; BE supports UTC | EST | PST | GMT | CET

group_id.description: TIER POLICY: the instance group to scale as a whole. Setting this with scaling_action `resize_instance` makes this a tier policy, not a single-instance resize. Requires an enabled capacity config for (group_id, target_class).

target_class.description: TIER POLICY: which plane this trigger governs. `data` is the normal choice; `non_data` is ClickHouse keepers.

direction.description: TIER POLICY: required. One policy per direction - up and down are separate rules, not one rule with two thresholds.

cpu_up_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_up): CPU percent that must be exceeded. Defaults to 80.

memory_up_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_up): memory percent that must be exceeded. Defaults to 80. Both CPU and memory apply.

cpu_down_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_down): CPU percent to fall below. Defaults to 20. Must be strictly BELOW the sibling scale_up threshold.

memory_down_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_down): memory percent to fall below. Defaults to 20. Must be strictly BELOW the sibling scale_up threshold.

window_minutes.description: TIER POLICY: how long the condition must hold. Defaults to 10 for scale_up, 360 for scale_down - the asymmetry is deliberate, so a lull does not shrink a cluster.

details.description: Action-specific payload: { target_instance_type } | { cluster_max_storage_gb } | { max_replicas }. Required for every action except start_instance / stop_instance.

tools.name: update_scaling_policy
tools.description:
Update an existing scaling policy. Only the fields you pass are changed - but note the backend re-validates the WHOLE policy, so a rule written under the old storage contract cannot be edited.

LEGACY expand_storage RULES: policies still carrying details.new_size_gb are outdated and every save 422s. There is no in-place migration - delete the rule and create a fresh one with details.cluster_max_storage_gb. Disabling one also fails; only `delete_scaling_policy` works.

Pass scaling_action when you know it so the storage-specific rules (40-85 threshold band, '>' / '>=' only, doubling ceiling) can be checked before the request goes out.

direction.description: TIER POLICY only. Changing direction rewrites which threshold pair applies - normally leave alone.

cpu_up_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_up). Must stay above the sibling scale_down value.

memory_up_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_up). Must stay above the sibling scale_down value.

cpu_down_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_down). Must stay below the sibling scale_up value.

memory_down_threshold.description: TIER POLICY (scale_down). Must stay below the sibling scale_up value.

window_minutes.description: TIER POLICY: how long the condition must hold before firing.

scaling_action.description: The policy's action, from `list_scaling_policies`. Not sent as a change - used to validate the fields below against the right rules.

details.description: Replacement action payload: { target_instance_type } | { cluster_max_storage_gb } | { max_replicas }.

tools.name: delete_scaling_policy
tools.description: Delete a scaling policy. The associated instance is unaffected - only the schedule / rule is removed.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed.

tools.name: get_pitr
tools.description: Get PITR config + restore window for an instance. Returns null when PITR has never been configured. Response includes s3_bucket, retention_days, oldest_restore_point, restorable_until (the latest moment a restore can target: about a minute ago while WAL is shipping, never before the last base backup; null when nothing is restorable), latest_restore_point (an alias of restorable_until since backend 4eec1e872; it used to be the last base backup's time), last_base_backup_at and error_message when status=error.

tools.name: enable_pitr
tools.description: Enable PITR on a Postgres or MySQL instance - streams the transaction log to S3 continuously and takes nightly base backups. Postgres archives WAL (via wal-g); MySQL archives binlog with ~1 minute restore granularity. Not available for Redis or ClickHouse. The S3 bucket must exist in the same region; the instance role needs s3:PutObject / GetObject / ListBucket. Status transitions: configuring → enabled (or error).

s3_bucket.description: S3 bucket name (must exist in same region)

retention_days.description: Days of WAL to keep (default 7, range 1-35). Longer = larger S3 bill.

tools.name: configure_pitr
tools.description:
Change the retention window on an existing PITR configuration - how far back the restore window reaches.

THIS ONLY CHANGES RETENTION. It does not start, stop, pause or resume anything: use `enable_pitr` for first-time setup, `pause_pitr` / `resume_pitr` to suspend and restart it. (Until the 2026-09 sync this tool sent a `status` field that the endpoint never read, so pausing through it silently did nothing.)

SHORTENING THE WINDOW DISCARDS ARCHIVES. Pruning is driven by this number, so cutting 14 days to 3 permanently gives up the ability to restore to anything older than 3 days. Confirm that with the user before reducing it; increasing it is safe but only takes effect going forward - it cannot recover already-pruned WAL.

Requires PITR to be `enabled` or `paused` (422 in any other state). Omitting `retention_days` returns the current window unchanged rather than erroring, so it is a safe read-back.

Retention also drives cost: PITR archives are S3 storage, metered and billed for as long as they exist.

retention_days.description: New restore window in days. Omit to read back the current value without changing it. REDUCING this permanently deletes archives older than the new window.

tools.name: pause_pitr
tools.description:
Pause PITR on an instance: scheduled base backups and retention pruning stop.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT SUSPENDED, because the difference matters: WAL ARCHIVING CONTINUES and existing archives are left alone. So pausing does NOT stop the S3 storage bill and it does not break the existing restore window - it stops new base backups being taken and stops old archives being pruned. If the user's goal is "stop paying for PITR", the answer is `disable_pitr`, not this.

The practical use is a maintenance window where you do not want pruning to discard something you may need.

Only an `enabled` configuration can be paused: a 422 says it is already paused or in some other state. Resume with `resume_pitr`.

confirm.description: Must be true. No new base backups are taken while paused, so the restore window stops advancing.

tools.name: resume_pitr
tools.description:
Resume a paused PITR configuration, optionally with a new retention window.

If the last base backup has gone stale, resuming also triggers a CATCH-UP BASE BACKUP so the restore window closes its gap - the response message says whether one was dispatched. That dispatch is best-effort: a failure does not fail the resume, because the daily scheduler picks the configuration up regardless now that it is enabled.

Only a `paused` configuration can be resumed (422 otherwise). Passing `retention_days` changes the window at the same time - and the same warning applies as on `configure_pitr`: a shorter window permanently discards older archives.

retention_days.description: Optionally set a new window while resuming. Omit to keep the recorded one. REDUCING it permanently prunes older archives.

tools.name: retry_pitr
tools.description: Retry PITR setup after an `error` state. Common error causes: missing IAM permissions on the bucket, wrong bucket region or archiver setup failure (wal-g on Postgres, binlog streaming on MySQL). Fix the underlying issue first, then retry.

tools.name: trigger_pitr_base_backup
tools.description: Trigger a one-off base backup now. Runs in the background (Postgres uses `wal-g backup-push`; MySQL takes a full base backup) - your instance keeps serving traffic. Useful before risky migrations or to seed the restore window after a fresh enable. Postgres and MySQL only.

tools.name: list_pitr_base_backups
tools.description: List historical base backups for an instance. Each row carries status (pending | running | completed | failed), started_at, completed_at and error_message when failed.

tools.name: restore_pitr
tools.description: Restore an instance to a point in time. Creates a NEW instance of the same engine (Postgres or MySQL) recovered to `target_time` - the source instance is untouched. `target_time` must fall within the source instance's [oldest_restore_point, restorable_until] window (see `get_pitr`). `name` is the new instance name; must start with a letter and use letters/digits/hyphens only. The new instance copies the source's network access (allowed_cidr_ranges and public_access) unless you pass either and an explicit `[]` / false restores it into a stricter posture. A PostgreSQL 14 or 15 source cannot be restored any more (those versions were dropped). The restored instance is a Duplicate: it cannot turn Multi-AZ on and its TLS starts off.

name.description: Name for the new restored instance

allowed_cidr_ranges.description: Who may connect to the restored instance (CIDR strings or {cidr, port}); defaults to the source's. [] = reachable only inside its VPC.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. A new instance will be provisioned (provider charges apply).

tools.name: get_wallet_balance
tools.description:
Get the organization's prepaid credit-wallet balance. Returns `balance_cents` + `balance_formatted`, currency, `payment_channel_state` (`unlinked` | `linking` | `chargeable`), `hourly_burn_rate_cents` (current spend rate), `estimated_hours_remaining` (runway), `expiring_soon`, the linked card, `current_invoice` (with `past_due` on a postpaid organisation) and `welcome_credit_withheld_reason`. Credit is consumed hourly while resources exist; when it runs out resources are stopped and, after a grace period, deleted (at once on an organisation that has never paid). There are no plans or tiers.

CHECK `expiring_soon` AND SAY SO UNPROMPTED. Some credit has an expiry date, so a healthy-looking balance can be about to shrink without anything being spent. A runway computed from `balance_cents` alone overstates it in that case. If `expiring_soon` is non-empty, tell the user what expires and when alongside the balance - it is the one thing here they cannot infer from the number they already see.

`estimated_hours_remaining` is the wallet POSITION (balance above its floor, so a postpaid organisation below zero can still show hours) divided by the CURRENT burn rate, so it assumes today's resources stay as they are. It is not a forecast: provisioning anything new shortens it immediately. The burn rate COUNTS STOPPED PROJECT SERVERS (they bill until deleted), so stopping a project does not lengthen the runway.

`welcome_credit_withheld_reason` explains a new organisation with no welcome credit: `already_received_by_this_person` (one welcome credit per person, across organisations) or `network_burst` (too many sign-ups from the same network). Say which, plainly; null means none was withheld. A top-up is the way forward either way.

tools.name: list_skus
tools.description: List the priced resource catalog (SKUs) at this organisation's prices. Each SKU has resource_type, the booked labels hourly_rate_cents + hourly_rate_formatted, currency and the figures billing actually charges: `charged_hourly_millicents` (1,000 millicents = 1 cent) and `charged_monthly_millicents`. For a project server (Hetzner) row, `charged_monthly_millicents` is the Monthly price cap, the most that size bills in a UTC month (below hourly x 730) or null when no monthly price is published. Quote the charged figures, not the rounded labels. Use this to estimate how long a top-up will last for a given resource.

tools.name: list_credit_ledger
tools.description: List credit-wallet ledger entries (most recent first). entry_type is `topup` (credit added), `free_credit` (welcome grant - has expires_at) or `usage_charge` (hourly deduction, negative). amount_cents is signed; remaining_cents shows how much of a positive lot is left.

tools.name: list_wallet_transactions
tools.description: List per-resource hourly billing transactions (most recent first). Each has resource_pid / resource_type, amount_cents, period_start / period_end and status: `applied` (charge deducted) or `skipped` (insufficient balance - the resource was stopped).

tools.name: create_topup
tools.description:
Buy wallet credit. Amount is in cents: min $5 = 500, max $500 = 50000.

THREE DIFFERENT FLOWS and which one you get decides whether a browser is needed:
- **Default** (no flags) - returns a `checkout` payload for Razorpay Standard Checkout plus a `payment_url` fallback. The user pays in a browser; the MCP cannot. The wallet is credited when Razorpay's webhook confirms, so poll `get_wallet_balance` afterwards rather than trusting the response.
- **`save_card: true`** - same browser checkout, but the card is stored for later one-tap and auto-recharge. This is the ONLY way to save a card: the old `POST billing/link` endpoint is gone. `billing_contact_phone` becomes REQUIRED (hard gate - a missing phone blocks the whole top-up, it does not silently fall back).
- **`use_saved_card: true`** - charges the already-saved card off-session. No browser, no URL. Returns status `completed` or `pending_confirmation` (HTTP 202) when the bank wants a challenge, in which case the payment finishes by itself and you just poll the balance.

Errors worth relaying verbatim: `use_saved_card` with nothing saved refuses ("No saved card is linked") and a card carries a per-charge mandate limit the top-up may not exceed - the message names the limit. Both are 422, not a reason to retry.

PASS `idempotency_key` ON EVERY RETRY. This spends real money. The key scopes to user + org + key + a fingerprint of the amount and card flags, so re-sending the same key with the same amount replays the first result instead of charging twice; re-using it with a DIFFERENT amount is correctly treated as a new top-up. Without a key, a blind retry after a timeout is a second real charge.

save_card.description: Save this card for one-tap top-ups and auto-recharge. Requires billing_contact_phone.

use_saved_card.description: Charge the already-saved card off-session - no browser. Mutually exclusive with save_card.

billing_contact_phone.description: E.164 preferred (+14155551234). REQUIRED when save_card is true; optional otherwise.

idempotency_key.description: Send the SAME key when retrying a top-up you are unsure landed, so it replays instead of charging twice.

tools.name: unlink_billing_payment_method
tools.description:
Remove the organization's saved payment method. Returns the resulting `payment_channel_state` (`unlinked` | `linking` | `chargeable`) and whether the provider token was deleted.

This DISABLES auto-recharge as a side effect - the setting keeps its numbers but can no longer be enabled without a token, so an org relying on it to stay above zero will start running its balance down instead. Say so before unlinking if auto-recharge is on (`get_auto_recharge`).

There is no matching "link" call: a card is saved by passing `save_card: true` on a real `create_topup`, not by a separate linking step.

confirm.description: Must be true - removes the saved card and disables one-tap top-ups and auto-recharge.

tools.name: update_billing_contact
tools.description: Update billing contact info on an already-linked org. Doesn't re-run Razorpay - only persists DB overrides for invoices.

tools.name: get_auto_recharge
tools.description:
Read the organization's auto-recharge configuration - the standing instruction to top the wallet up from a saved card when the balance falls past a threshold, so resources are not stopped for running out of credit.

Returns four blocks:
- `setting` - **`null` when auto-recharge has never been configured**, which is the normal state for most orgs. Otherwise `enabled`, `threshold_cents`, `amount_cents`, `monthly_cap_cents`, `token_id`, `provider`, `operational_state`, `paused_reason` and `next_retry_at`.
- `per_charge_cap_cents` - the platform maximum for a single automatic charge. Present on EVERY read, including the first, so use this rather than assuming a figure.
- `cards` - the saved cards that can be used, each with a `token_id`, a display `label` and its own `max_amount_cents` mandate ceiling. An empty list means there is nothing to charge and auto-recharge cannot be enabled - the user has to save a card first via `create_topup` with `save_card: true`.
- `burn` - `hourly_burn_cents`, `estimated_days_to_threshold`, `estimated_days_to_zero`, `spent_this_month_cents`. This is what makes the numbers meaningful: a threshold the balance will not reach for 40 days is a very different thing from one it hits tomorrow.

READ `operational_state` AND `paused_reason` BEFORE REPORTING THAT AUTO-RECHARGE IS ON. `enabled: true` with a paused operational state means it is configured but NOT currently protecting the wallet - typically because a charge failed. That combination is the one worth raising unprompted, because the user believes they are covered.

Requires billing-manager permission on the org.

tools.name: configure_auto_recharge
tools.description:
Set or update auto-recharge: when the wallet drops below `threshold_cents`, charge `amount_cents` to a saved card, up to `monthly_cap_cents` of automatic charges per month.

CALL `get_auto_recharge` FIRST, for two reasons: it gives you the `cards` list (you need a `token_id` from it - there is no other way to get one) and the `burn` block, which is what tells you whether the numbers you are about to set are sensible. Setting a $5 threshold on an org burning $8/day means the recharge fires roughly daily.

THIS SPENDS MONEY LATER, WITHOUT ASKING AGAIN. That is the point of it and it is also why the amounts should be the user's explicit choice rather than your defaults. Confirm all three figures with them.

Bounds the backend enforces, all returned at once on failure:
- `amount_cents`: at least 500 ($5), at most the `per_charge_cap_cents` from `get_auto_recharge` ($150 today).
- `monthly_cap_cents`: at least `amount_cents` and at least 100 ($1).
- `threshold_cents`: at least 100 ($1).
- The card's own mandate ceiling also applies: a token whose `max_amount_cents` is below `amount_cents` is refused and the error names the ceiling.

Configuring does NOT enable it. Call `enable_auto_recharge` afterwards or the settings sit there inert.

threshold_cents.description: Charge when the balance falls below this, in cents (min 100 = $1)

amount_cents.description: How much to add each time, in cents (min 500 = $5, max = per_charge_cap_cents from get_auto_recharge)

monthly_cap_cents.description: Ceiling on total automatic charges per month, in cents. Must be >= amount_cents. This is the user's protection against a runaway loop - set it deliberately.

token_id.description: Saved card token from `get_auto_recharge`'s `cards` list. Required before auto-recharge can be ENABLED.

provider.description: Payment provider for the token (defaults to the org's, normally razorpay)

tools.name: enable_auto_recharge
tools.description:
Switch auto-recharge on. From here the platform will charge the saved card by itself whenever the balance falls below the configured threshold.

Requires an existing configuration (`configure_auto_recharge`) WITH a linked `token_id` - a 422 "No auto-recharge configuration exists" or "A linked payment token is required" means that step is missing. The configured amount is re-validated at this point too, so a setting saved before the per-charge cap moved can be refused here with the cap named.

Tell the user this is a standing authorisation to charge their card without further prompting and that `monthly_cap_cents` is the limit on how much it can spend.

confirm.description: Must be true. This authorises future card charges with no further confirmation.

tools.name: disable_auto_recharge
tools.description:
Switch auto-recharge off. The configuration is kept - thresholds and amounts stay - so `enable_auto_recharge` turns it back on without re-entering anything.

SAY WHAT THIS MEANS: nothing will top the wallet up automatically any more, so the balance will run down to zero and resources will be STOPPED unless the user tops up by hand. Use `get_wallet_balance` for `estimated_hours_remaining` and tell them roughly how long they have.

Idempotent - disabling when no configuration exists is a no-op, not an error.

confirm.description: Must be true. The wallet will no longer top itself up, so resources can be stopped when it empties.

tools.name: list_invoices
tools.description: List the organization's invoices, newest month first: `pid`, `serial_number`, `period` (with `period_start` / `period_end`), `issued_on`, `due_on`, `status` and `total_cents` in `currency`. A prepaid organization's invoice is a monthly statement of what its credit paid for (`paid`); a postpaid one's is a demand (`due`) and an unpaid one past its due date stops new resources (see `current_invoice.past_due` on `get_wallet_balance`). `get_invoice_csv` returns one month's line items. Needs billing read access.

tools.name: get_invoice_csv
tools.description: Download one month's invoice as CSV, the console's "Download CSV": every line item the month billed and the total row. `month` is YYYY-MM, a month `list_invoices` shows. Returns the CSV text; offer to save it to a file for the user's accounts rather than pasting a long one into the chat.

tools.name: redeem_coupon
tools.description: Redeem a promo coupon code into the organization's wallet. It only adds credit, so any member with a verified email can do it; the reply gives `amount_cents` and `new_balance_cents`. An invalid, expired or used-up code answers one generic message on purpose (codes cannot be probed) and a code this organization already redeemed says so. At most 10 attempts an hour per person: use the code the user gives you, never guess one.

code.description: The coupon code, exactly as the user has it

tools.name: list_server_types
tools.description:
List the server sizes a PaaS project can be provisioned on, per location, with live availability and pricing. Public reference data - no org needed and it does not count against the rate limit.

Returns all six locations - `fsn1` Falkenstein, Germany, `nbg1` Nuremberg, Germany, `hel1` Helsinki, Finland, `ash` Ashburn, Virginia, USA, `hil` Hillsboro, Oregon, USA, `sin` Singapore - each with the sizes sold there: code, cores, memory_gb, disk_gb, `category`, `cpu_type`, `architecture`, `offered`, `available`, `deprecated` + `deprecation`, `charged_hourly_millicents`, `charged_monthly_millicents`, plus the rounded labels `hourly_price_cents` and `display_price`. Prices are all-in (platform margin already folded in) and billed hourly against wallet credit.

QUOTE THE `charged_*` FIELDS (1,000 millicents = 1 cent). `hourly_price_cents` and `display_price` are whole-cent labels that round both ways. `charged_monthly_millicents` is the MONTHLY PRICE CAP: the most this size can bill in a UTC calendar month, which is below hourly x 730 (cx23 in fsn1 caps at $12.98, not $15.18). It is `null` when Hetzner publishes no monthly price for that size; then quote the hourly figure only. A project server bills by the hour for every hour it exists, RUNNING OR STOPPED, at its running hourly rate and never more than its size's monthly price (`charged_monthly_millicents`, the Monthly price cap) in a UTC calendar month. Stopping it does not stop the charge; only deleting the project does.

PRICES DIFFER PER LOCATION for the same size, so always name the location alongside a price. `cx*` Cost-Optimized and its Arm twin `cax*` (both `cost_optimized`; `cax` is Ampere Arm, `architecture: arm`) are sold in the three European locations only. `cpx*` Regular (`regular_purpose`) comes in two generations that never share a location: the `cpx*2` line sells in Europe + Singapore and the `cpx*1` line is listed everywhere but in practice only carries stock in the two US locations. `ccx*` Dedicated (`general_purpose`) is sold in all six. The two Regular generations are NOT interchangeable: cpx21 is 3 cores / 80 GB where cpx22 is 2 cores / 80 GB and cpx41 is 240 GB where cpx42 is 320 GB.

Because of that geography, the cheapest US or APAC option is several times the cheapest European one. Say so up front rather than letting the user discover it after they pick a region.

Availability is three states, not two. `offered: false` means Hetzner does not sell that size in that location at all - do not offer it there and do not read the `null` `available` beside it as "out of stock". `offered: true, available: false` means it IS sold there but has no stock right now; that is a one-tap correction (name a location that does have it), not a dead end. Only `available: true` can be provisioned.

Stock genuinely flaps - successive reads minutes apart disagree - so treat availability as live, re-read before acting on it and never cache it into advice. Expect the cheap end to be the tightest: it is normal for most of the Cost-Optimized line to be out of stock across all three European locations at once, leaving cx23 as the only cheap size that can actually be provisioned.

`deprecated: true` means Hetzner has announced an end of life for that size but still sells it; `deprecation` carries the detail. Do not put a user's new project on one.

Call this before `create_project` and show the user the options - the project server is the main cost of a project and `create_project` defaults to the smallest (cx23) in Europe if you don't choose.

tools.name: list_projects
tools.description:
List PaaS projects (app containers) in the active organization. Each project is a provisioned server + Coolify install that deployments and project databases attach to.

Returns pid, name, status (`pending` | `provisioning` | `active` | `failed` | `stopped` | `restoring` | `scaling` - `deleting` and `terminated` are filtered out server-side; `scaling` means a scale-up has the server powered off for a few minutes), `public_ip`, `instance_domain`, timestamps and - the fields worth reading that are easy to miss - `server_type` and `location` (which machine and WHERE it runs), `backups_enabled`, plus a server-computed `ready` and `readiness_detail`.

`ready` IS NOT `status == "active"`. A project is ready only when it is active, carries no terminal error, AND every service and database inside it is ready too. So an `active` project can still be not-ready because something in it is mid-provision. `readiness_detail` lists each child service and database with its own status - use that to say what is holding a project up instead of reporting it as broken.

Answer "where does this run?" from `location`, not from the user's guess: a server cannot be moved after creation and its price depends on where it is. A `stopped` project carries `stopped_at`, `billing_stop` with the reason and, for a credit stop, when it is deleted unless the wallet is topped up; one the user stopped also carries `manually_stopped_at`. A stopped project still bills (see `stop_project`).

`paused_for_review: true` (with `paused_for_review_at`) means the Selfhost.dev team paused the server while it reviews the account: it reads `stopped`, it cannot be started, restored or topped up out of it and the user should email team@selfhost.dev from the address on the account. Say that rather than suggesting a start.

tools.name: get_project
tools.description:
Get one project by pid. Use this to POLL provisioning progress after `create_project`: re-call every ~5-10s until `status` becomes `active` (the server and Coolify are up, deployments can be created) or `failed`. A `status` of `deleting` or a 404, means it is being or has been torn down. `public_ip` and `instance_domain` populate during provisioning.

TWO DIFFERENT QUESTIONS, TWO DIFFERENT FIELDS:
- `status == "active"` - the project's own server is up. This is what gates `create_deployment`.
- `ready` - active AND no terminal error AND every service and database inside the project is also ready. This is what gates telling the user "your project is up".
An active-but-not-ready project is normal while a service is still booting; `readiness_detail` names the child that is holding it.

Also here and worth reporting: `location` (where the server actually runs - a server cannot be moved and the price follows the location), `server_type` and `backups_enabled`. A `stopped` project still bills its server. `paused_for_review: true` (with `paused_for_review_at`) means the Selfhost.dev team paused the server while it reviews the account: it reads `stopped`, it cannot be started, restored or topped up out of it and the user should email team@selfhost.dev from the address on the account. Say that rather than suggesting a start.

If a project has been provisioning for more than ~15 minutes, treat it as stuck rather than slow. `list_project_activities` shows what the server and the platform were doing.

tools.name: create_project
tools.description:
Create a new PaaS project and start async server provisioning. Returns immediately (HTTP 202) with the project in status `pending` - actual provisioning (server → Coolify → DNS) takes ~2-5 minutes. Poll `get_project` until status is `active` before creating a deployment in it. Name must be unique within the org (excluding failed/terminated projects). May return 422 if the platform is at capacity for new servers - retry later.

SIZE IT DELIBERATELY: `server_type` decides what the project costs and omitting it silently provisions the smallest size (cx23, 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk (shared CPU)). Call `list_server_types` for live prices/availability and confirm the choice with the user first. Sizes: cx23 (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk (shared CPU)); cx33 (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk (shared CPU)); cx43 (8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 160 GB disk (shared CPU)); cx53 (16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 320 GB disk (shared CPU)); cax11 (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB disk (shared Arm CPU)); cax21 (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk (shared Arm CPU)); cax31 (8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 160 GB disk (shared Arm CPU)); cax41 (16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 320 GB disk (shared Arm CPU)); cpx21 (3 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 80 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx22 (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 80 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx31 (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 160 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx32 (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 160 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx41 (8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 240 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx42 (8 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 320 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx51 (16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 360 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx52 (12 vCPU, 24 GB RAM, 480 GB disk (shared CPU)); cpx62 (16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 640 GB disk (shared CPU)); ccx13 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx23 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 160 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx33 (8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 240 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx43 (16 vCPU, 64 GB RAM, 360 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx53 (32 vCPU, 128 GB RAM, 600 GB disk (dedicated CPU)); ccx63 (48 vCPU, 192 GB RAM, 960 GB disk (dedicated CPU)).

PLACE IT DELIBERATELY: `location` decides where the server runs AND what it costs - the same size is a different price in different locations and the cheap Cost-Optimized line (x86 and Arm) is sold in Europe only. Omitting it lets the platform pick. A server cannot be moved afterwards, so the location is permanent. The size is not: a project's server can later be scaled UP to a bigger size of the same line (`get_project_scale_ladder`, `set_project_scale_bounds`, `scale_up_project`), with a few minutes of downtime, but never down, so start at what the apps need.

ARM (`cax*`) runs most templates and repos, often cheaper per core, but an image with no Arm build cannot run there: Krayin is refused on an Arm host and a repo deployment whose Dockerfile pins an x86-only base image will fail to build.

CHECK STOCK FIRST. A cheap size is frequently out of stock in every location that sells it, so a `server_type` chosen from the list above without reading `available` will often 422. When that happens the 422 names the locations that do have it - use them rather than silently falling back.

SHELL ACCESS IS OPT-IN AND OFF BY DEFAULT. No customer SSH key is installed unless you ask for one, two ways:
- `ssh_key_pids` - install existing library keys (`list_org_ssh_keys`). They show as `queued` until the server finishes provisioning, then install by themselves.
- `generate_ssh_key: true` - the platform mints a keypair. **The 202 response carries `generated_ssh_key.private_key`, ONCE. It is never stored and cannot be re-fetched.** Hand it to the user immediately, tell them to save it to a file and `chmod 600` it and say plainly that losing it means adding a different key later. Do not summarise the response and drop the key.
Either way access is to a NON-ROOT `shell` user (`ssh shell@<ip>`) with no sudo and no docker - it cannot see containers. Keys can also be added later with `add_project_ssh_key`.

BACK IT UP AT CREATE: `backups_requested` turns on automatic daily server backups (7 kept) as soon as the server exists. Backups cost 20% of the server's billed compute (so they too stop at 20% of the monthly cap); say so and recommend them for anything that will hold data. They can also be turned on later with `enable_project_backups`.

COSTS MONEY: the server bills hourly against wallet credit from the moment provisioning starts. A project server bills by the hour for every hour it exists, RUNNING OR STOPPED, at its running hourly rate and never more than its size's monthly price (`charged_monthly_millicents`, the Monthly price cap) in a UTC calendar month. Stopping it does not stop the charge; only deleting the project does. A 402 means the wallet is empty - top up with `create_topup`. A 402 with `error_code: FREE_TIER_SIZE_LIMIT` is the free-credit size cap instead: on an organisation that has never paid, a server above `max_hourly_cents` (8 cents an hour) needs a top-up first. Relay the message as it is; the welcome credit still applies after the top-up and the smaller sizes need none. A 403 `account_held` or `account_restricted` is an account review decision, not a money problem: relay it and do not retry.

tools.name: delete_project
tools.description: Delete a project - tears down its provisioned server, Coolify install, DNS and all attached deployments/databases/services. This is irreversible: a delete the user asks for keeps no copy of the server (only a billing teardown keeps one, restorable with `restore_deleted_project`). It is also the ONLY thing that stops the project's hourly charge (a stopped server keeps billing), with one final charge for the last window. Returns 202 (async tear-down; status moves to `deleting` then `terminated`). tools.name: stop_project
tools.description:
Power a running project's server off: every app, service and database in it goes down with it. Nothing is deleted and `start_project` powers it back on.

IT DOES NOT STOP THE BILL. A project server bills by the hour for every hour it exists, RUNNING OR STOPPED, at its running hourly rate and never more than its size's monthly price (`charged_monthly_millicents`, the Monthly price cap) in a UTC calendar month. Stopping it does not stop the charge; only deleting the project does. The response carries a `notice` saying so: relay it. If the user is stopping the server to save money, tell them before calling that it will not and that deleting the project (`delete_project`, irreversible) is what ends the charge. A stopped server also keeps draining the wallet: on an organisation that has never paid, a stopped project at a zero balance is deleted; on a paying one it becomes a credit stop with 24 hours of grace.

Only an `active` project can be stopped (409 otherwise and 409 while a stop is already in progress). A 422 `stop_failed` means the power-off did not go through; the platform retries it by itself every hour, so do not loop on this tool. A top-up never powers on a server the user stopped.

tools.name: start_project
tools.description:

Outcomes:
- 200: started. 202: the server powered on and its status updates shortly; poll `get_project`.
- 409: the project is deleted, not stopped or busy (a billing teardown holds it); nothing changed.
- 422 `insufficient_credit`: the wallet cannot cover an hour; top up with `create_topup`, then call again.

- 422 `restart_failed`: the power-on failed; try once more, then open a support ticket.

A project server bills by the hour for every hour it exists, RUNNING OR STOPPED, at its running hourly rate and never more than its size's monthly price (`charged_monthly_millicents`, the Monthly price cap) in a UTC calendar month. tools.name: get_project_metrics

Returns `agent_status`, `last_seen_at` and a `batches` array. Each batch has `timestamp_ms` and `metric_sets`; a metric set with no `resource` belongs to the server, otherwise `resource.pid` identifies the database/service/deployment it describes. For a 'current' snapshot use a narrow window and read the newest batch. Heartbeats land ~every 25s, so poll no faster than ~30s.

tools.name: list_deployments
tools.description:
List deployments (apps) in the active organization. Each entry includes repo_full_name, branch, build_pack, port, status (active | paused - the container lifecycle, distinct from a run's status), deploy_url, custom domains and an inline `deployment_runs` array (newest 50). Run status values: `enqueued`/`building`/`deploying` are in-progress (transient); `active` = deployed successfully; `failed`/`aborted`/`removed`/`skipped` are terminal. Poll until the latest run reaches a terminal status. Since backend #4750 a run stays `deploying` after its container starts until the app answers on its platform URL (the proxy stops returning 502), for up to 2 minutes; after 2 minutes it turns `active` anyway and the "is live" email is skipped. So `active` means the app answered or 2 minutes passed. Apps with public TCP ports are not held. `platform_url` (the platform-generated address) sits beside `deploy_url`, which names a verified custom primary domain first.

`last_deploy_status` + `last_deploy_at` are the deployment's own rolled-up state: `building`, `active`, `aborted` or **`crashed`**. `crashed` means the build SUCCEEDED and the container has since died (exited / dead / stopped / error / restarting) - so a deployment can show a newest run of `active` while being `crashed` right now. Read it before telling a user their app is up. The org owners are emailed once if a crash-loop episode lasts past ~10 minutes and the next push or manual deploy resets the field to `building`.

Use this to POLL deploy progress after `trigger_deploy`/`redeploy_run`/`rollback_run`: re-call every ~5s until the latest run reaches a terminal status. Poll until the latest run reaches a terminal status. So `active` means the app answered or 2 minutes passed. Read it before telling a user their app is up. The org owners are emailed once if a crash-loop episode lasts past ~10 minutes and the next push or manual deploy resets the field to `building`.

tools.name: create_deployment
tools.description:
Create a deployment (app) from a GitHub repo inside an existing project. The project (`coolify_project_pid`) MUST already be `active` (provisioned) - check `get_project` first. For private repos you must pass `installation_id` (from `list_github_installations`). If build_pack/port are omitted they are auto-detected (you can pre-run `detect_repo_config`).

THIS IS ASYNCHRONOUS AND THE 201 IS NOT THE FINISHED ARTICLE. The request validates and detects synchronously, then saves the deployment as status `provisioning` and does the app registration (9-11 Coolify calls, more for a private repo) in a background job before triggering the first build. So the response you get back has `coolify_app_uuid: null` and `deploy_url: null`. That is expected, not a failure - DO NOT report a broken deployment or retry the create.

Poll `get_deployment` until status is `active` (the app is registered, the URL is populated, the first build is running) or `failed` (registration failed; the run carries the error). It used to be synchronous and would 504 at the 30s gateway timeout on private repos, which is why it moved.

RAW TCP PORTS: `public_ports` publishes extra TCP ports on the project's public IP (MQTT, a game server, a database the app embeds); the web `port` keeps going through the proxy. Pass `port_sources` in the same call to say who may connect, because a port without one is open to the whole internet. `port_sources` keys are published HOST ports as strings, e.g. { "8883": { source: "custom", cidrs: ["203.0.113.0/24"] } }. `my_ip` is the public IP the request arrives from, captured server-side: for an MCP running on the user's laptop that is the laptop's egress IP, for one running elsewhere it is that machine's, so read `requester_ip` in the reply before relying on it. A `custom` list of only 0.0.0.0/0 and/or ::/0 is saved as anywhere.

A 403 `account_restricted` here means the repository owner's GitHub account is banned on the platform. `NIXPACKS_NODE_VERSION` set to a Node version the build toolchain cannot ship is a 422 naming the supported ones.

tools.name: trigger_deploy

tools.name: abort_deploy
tools.description:
Abort the deployment's in-flight build run. Use it when a build is hung or when the user pushed the wrong thing and wants to stop it before it goes live.

Only the NEWEST run can be aborted and only while it is still in progress - a 422 "No deployment in progress to abort" means the newest run already reached a terminal status, so there is nothing to stop. It does not roll anything back: whatever is currently deployed keeps serving. To go back to a previous version, use `rollback_run`.

The run lands on status `aborted` and the deployment's `last_deploy_status` becomes `aborted`. If the build had already reached Coolify, the platform also asks Coolify to cancel it; when Coolify does not confirm, the response carries a warning and the run is aborted on our side anyway - the next deploy supersedes it. Relay that warning if it appears, because the build container may run on briefly.

confirm.description: Must be true - this stops a build that is currently running.

tools.name: get_deployment_health
tools.description: Get a deployment's health: whether the deploy_url is reachable, when it was last checked, any error and the attached domains.

tools.name: get_run_logs
tools.description:
Get the full build + container logs for one deployment run, plus the run object. This is the ONLY log surface - there is no separate application-log tool, because the backend returns the running container's stdout/stderr here alongside the build output.

Use it for runtime debugging too, not just builds: pass the newest run pid (from `get_deployment`) to see why a deployed app is failing. If the container is crash-looping, the response falls back to the output captured while it was last reachable; if there is nothing at all, the backend synthesizes one line carrying the container's health status instead of returning empty.

The returned log buffer is cumulative and idempotent - each call returns the whole buffer, so REPLACE (don't append) on each poll. To stream a live build, re-call every ~5-10s until `deployment_run.status` is terminal. A 422 "Deployment has not started yet" means the run is still enqueued - back off and retry. Run status values: `enqueued`/`building`/`deploying` are in-progress (transient); `active` = deployed successfully; `failed`/`aborted`/`removed`/`skipped` are terminal. Poll until the latest run reaches a terminal status. Since backend #4750 a run stays `deploying` after its container starts until the app answers on its platform URL (the proxy stops returning 502), for up to 2 minutes; after 2 minutes it turns `active` anyway and the "is live" email is skipped. So `active` means the app answered or 2 minutes passed. Apps with public TCP ports are not held. `platform_url` (the platform-generated address) sits beside `deploy_url`, which names a verified custom primary domain first.

run_pid.description: Run pid, e.g. run_01h... (from a deployment's deployment_runs)

tools.name: redeploy_run
tools.description: Re-run a previous build. When the source run recorded a commit SHA this rebuilds THAT commit; when it did not - manual `trigger_deploy` runs never record one - it deploys the branch HEAD instead, which is what the plain deploy does. A sha-less run is no longer refused (that used to dead-end every failed manual run). Requires the deployment to be `active` and no in-progress run (422 otherwise). Creates a new run; poll `get_deployment`.

run_pid.description: The run to re-run (its commit will be redeployed)

tools.name: rollback_run
tools.description: Roll back by re-deploying the commit from a PRIOR SUCCESSFUL run. Only runs with status `active` (deployed successfully) can be rolled back to - returns 422 otherwise. Requires the deployment to be active and no in-progress run. Creates a new run; poll `get_deployment`.

run_pid.description: A previously-successful run to roll back to (status must be `active`)

tools.name: get_deployment_port_sources

Read who may connect to each public TCP port of a deployment: `port_sources` keyed by host port, each `{source, cidrs, my_ip?, stale}`, plus `requester_ip` (the IP this request came from). Every published port is listed; one never set reads `anywhere`. `stale: true` marks a `my_ip` entry that no longer matches the requester's IP, the usual reason a user suddenly cannot reach their own port.

Only for apps that publish TCP ports (`public_ports` on `get_deployment`); the proxied web port is not governed here.

tools.name: set_deployment_port_sources

Change who may connect to one or more of a deployment's public TCP ports, without a redeploy: the project server's firewall is updated. Each port named is replaced; ports not named keep their source. The keys must be ports the app already publishes (`public_ports`); to add or remove a port use `update_deployment_build_config`.

Sources: `anywhere` (the whole internet), `my_ip` (the requester's public IP, captured server-side), `custom` (1-16 IPs or CIDR ranges). `port_sources` keys are published HOST ports as strings, e.g. { "8883": { source: "custom", cidrs: ["203.0.113.0/24"] } }. `my_ip` is the public IP the request arrives from, captured server-side: for an MCP running on the user's laptop that is the laptop's egress IP, for one running elsewhere it is that machine's, so read `requester_ip` in the reply before relying on it. A `custom` list of only 0.0.0.0/0 and/or ::/0 is saved as anywhere.

Refused (422, nothing saved) unless the project is active, stopped or scaling or when any entry is invalid. `firewall_applied: false` with an `apply_note` means saved but still being applied: the platform retries it.

CAUTION: a domain left out loses its record here but the app's router KEEPS SERVING it until it is removed with `remove_deployment_domain`, so to take a domain off an app use that tool, not this one. For just adding one domain, prefer `add_deployment_domain`. Each domain that's new auto-creates an org verification record; the response/`get_deployment` then carries the DNS records to add. The deployment must be provisioned (422 otherwise).

domains.description: The complete desired domain set; replaces the current set atomically

tools.name: add_deployment_domain
tools.description: Add (append) one custom domain to a deployment as its primary domain, keeping any existing domains. Auto-creates the org verification record and returns the DNS records to configure: a TXT for ownership and for routing a CNAME (a subdomain such as app.example.com) or an A record pointing at the app's server IP (a root domain such as example.com, which cannot hold a CNAME). Relay the records exactly as returned. After adding them at the DNS provider, call `verify_custom_domain`. The deployment must be provisioned (422 otherwise).

tools.description: Remove one custom domain from a deployment: it is taken out of the app's routing and stops being served, the remaining domains are re-synced and primary metadata updated. This is the way to take a domain off an app (`sync_deployment_domains` only drops the record).

tools.name: verify_custom_domain
tools.description: Check a custom domain's DNS records live and advance its verification. The domain must have been added to a deployment first. Routing passes on the CNAME or on an A record to the app's server IP (the way a root domain routes). Outcomes: `verified` (the TXT and the routing record present → domain goes live with HTTPS); `ownership_verified` (TXT only - add the routing record); `routing_configured` (routing only - add the TXT); or 422 `pending_verification` (neither found yet - DNS can take up to 48h). The `checks` object reports the `txt`, `cname` and `a` records, each with its status, the expected value and what DNS actually answered (`found`), so a wrong value can be named rather than guessed. Routing is checked PER APP: an organisation-verified domain that is still `pending` on some app is re-checked for those apps, answering 200 `verified` when one of them now routes or 200 `ownership_verified` when DNS still points elsewhere (fix the CNAME or A record to the app's server named in `checks`).

tools.name: list_custom_domains
tools.description: List all custom-domain verifications for the active organization, with each domain's status (pending_verification | ownership_verified | routing_configured | verified) and when it was verified.

tools.name: list_env_vars
tools.description:
List a deployment's environment variables as { key, value } pairs.

VALUES ARE REVEALED BY DEFAULT and are secrets: handle them as such. The plain list now masks every value as `••••••••` (backend #4100, 2026-10-28), so this tool reads the reveal endpoint, which works for an Owner, Admin or Manager, at most 30 times a minute and records a `credentials_viewed` activity row per read. For another role it falls back to the keys with masked values and says why. Pass `reveal: false` when only the KEYS matter (before a `set_env_vars`, say): nothing is revealed or recorded.

Call this before `set_env_vars` so you know the full current set (since `set_env_vars` replaces everything). A masked value can be sent back unchanged to keep it.

reveal.description: Default true: return the plaintext values (Owner, Admin or Manager; audited). false lists the keys with masked values.

tools.name: detect_env_vars
tools.description:
Scan a deployment's repo/branch for the environment variables it expects and report which are already configured. Read-only - it changes nothing.

Returns `detected_vars` [{ key, hint, source, configured }] and a `sources` summary (.env.example, GitHub workflow secrets, CI files, Dockerfile/compose, framework config). `hint` is the placeholder found in the repo - a hint, NOT a real secret, so never set it as a value; ask the user for each missing one.

Use it right after creating a deployment (or when a build fails on a missing variable) to find out what still needs setting, then apply the answers with `merge_env_vars`. Vars already stored come back with configured=true so you can skip them; their stored values are not echoed here (`list_env_vars` reveals them).

tools.name: set_env_vars
tools.description: REPLACE a deployment's ENTIRE set of environment variables with the provided map. ⚠️ Any existing key NOT included here is DELETED. To add or edit a few variables without removing the rest, use `merge_env_vars` instead - or call `list_env_vars` first and pass the full merged set here. To keep an existing variable whose value you do not know, send it with the mask `••••••••` as its value: the backend keeps the stored value (the mask on a key that does not exist yet is refused). Keys must match ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$; values must be non-empty. The answer lists every value masked. Saving may trigger a rate-limited redeploy.

env_vars.description: The COMPLETE desired set { KEY: value }; replaces all existing vars

tools.name: merge_env_vars
tools.description: Add or update environment variables WITHOUT deleting any existing ones (upsert/merge). This is the safe way to set a few variables. Keys must match ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$; values must be non-empty. To remove a variable use `delete_env_var`. The answer lists every value masked. Saving may trigger a rate-limited redeploy.

env_vars.description: The variables to add/update { KEY: value }; existing keys are preserved

tools.name: delete_env_var
tools.description: Delete a single environment variable by key. Returns 404 if the key doesn't exist. Saving may trigger a rate-limited redeploy.

tools.name: list_github_installations
tools.description: List the GitHub App installations connected to the active organization, each with its accessible repositories embedded (`repos`: name, full_name, url, private, default_branch, description). Use `isActive`/status to pick a usable installation and the repo's `default_branch` when listing branches. If empty, the org hasn't connected GitHub yet - use `get_github_connect_url`.

tools.name: list_repo_branches
tools.description:
List a repository's branches. Each entry carries `name`, `sha` and `protected`.

TWO MODES and the difference is whether `installation_pid` is passed:
- WITH `installation_pid` (ghi_..., from `list_github_installations`) - reads the repo through that GitHub App installation. Required for any PRIVATE repo.
- WITHOUT it - reads a PUBLIC repo directly, no connected account needed. This is the path for "deploy this public repo" when the user has never linked GitHub and it pairs with `create_deployment`'s public-repo path.

A private repo with no installation_pid fails at GitHub rather than here, so pass the installation whenever you have one.

The API does not flag the default branch - cross-reference the repo's `default_branch` from `list_github_installations` or use `detect_repo_config`, which scans the default branch by itself.

installation_pid.description: Installation pid, e.g. ghi_01h.... Omit for a public repo; REQUIRED for a private one.

tools.name: detect_repo_config
tools.description: Scan a GitHub repo and auto-detect how to build/deploy it: visibility (`private`), `build_pack` (nixpacks | dockerfile | dockercompose | static), `port`, `dockerfile_path`, monorepo `base_directories` and detected environment variables (`detected_vars` from .env.example/CI/workflows - these are hints, not secrets). Run this before `create_deployment` to pre-fill build settings. For PRIVATE repos you must pass `installation_pid` (else 422).

installation_pid.description: Installation pid (ghi_...); required for private repos

branch.description: Branch to scan (defaults to the repo's default branch)

tools.name: get_github_connect_url
tools.description: Get a URL for the human to open in their browser to connect/install the Selfhost.dev GitHub App on their account or org. Connecting GitHub is interactive (GitHub requires a logged-in user to approve and pick repos) and CANNOT be done headlessly. After the user completes it in the browser, poll `list_github_installations` to confirm the new installation appears (status `active`). An installation already active in ANOTHER Selfhost.dev organization is not moved over (the browser lands on `installation_owned_by_another_org`): disconnect it there first. A GitHub account banned on the platform lands on `account_restricted`.

redirect_to_frontend.description: Optional URL to return the browser to after install

tools.name: disconnect_github_installation
tools.description: DESTRUCTIVE: disconnect one GitHub App installation from the active organization. Pushes for its repos stop triggering deploys immediately. The backend refuses while deployments are still using the installation - delete or repoint those first. This only detaches it on the Selfhost.dev side; the response includes a GitHub URL the user must open to revoke the app on GitHub itself. Reconnecting later is a browser flow (`get_github_connect_url`).

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed.

tools.name: disconnect_all_github_installations
tools.description: DESTRUCTIVE: disconnect EVERY GitHub App installation from the active organization at once. All auto-deploys stop. Blocked by the backend while any deployment still uses one of them. Returns `disconnected_count` and a `github_revoke_urls` list the user must open to revoke the app on GitHub. Prefer `disconnect_github_installation` when only one account should go.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed.

tools.name: list_project_databases
tools.description:
List the databases attached to a project (Postgres/Redis/MySQL/MongoDB provisioned via Coolify, NOT AWS managed instances). Returns pid, name, db_type, status (`active` | `inactive` | `creating` | `failed` | `unknown`), is_public, public_port, an `extensions` array on Postgres (per-extension `status` / `version` / `error_message`) and a `provisioning` block with per-stage progress.

Each entry carries a `connection` block (username, database, host, port) without the password; `get_project_database` reveals the password. Once the container exists it also carries `internal_connection` (`host`, `port`): the address an app or service IN THE SAME PROJECT uses over the project's Docker network, public or private (backend #4627). A private database (`is_public: false`) is reached only that way. Statuses on this list are the last known values; `get_project_database` re-reads one live from Coolify.

tools.name: get_project_database
tools.description:
Get one project database, with its status re-read LIVE from Coolify rather than served from the last known value. Use this when `list_project_databases` shows `creating` and you need to know whether it has actually finished or when a status looks stale.

Also returns the `extensions` array (Postgres - each with `status`, `version` and `error_message`, so this is where a failed CREATE EXTENSION is visible) and the `provisioning` stage block, so it is the tool to reach for when a user asks why provisioning is taking so long.

Unlike create, this works on a stopped or billing-suspended project. On one of those the live refresh is skipped (the server is powered off and there is nothing to ask) and you get the stored record - so a `creating` status on a stopped project means "we never found out", not "still working".

CONNECTION DETAILS AND THE PASSWORD: the `connection` block carries the username, database name, host and port and the password. The database's own read now masks the password as `••••••••` (backend #4100, 2026-10-28), so this tool then calls the reveal endpoint. The reveal works for an Owner, Admin or Manager, only while the project is running, at most 30 times a minute and is recorded in the activity log as `credentials_viewed`; refused, the masked value comes back with the reason. Pass `include_credentials: false` to skip the reveal.

include_credentials.description: Default true: reveal the real password (Owner, Admin or Manager only; audited). false keeps it masked.

tools.name: create_project_database
tools.description:
Create a database inside a project (provisioned via Coolify; returns 202, status starts `creating` or `pending` while the project is still provisioning - poll `list_project_databases`). The project must be able to take children (409 otherwise; a stopped project names the start). Provide the type-specific credentials (see fields). Passwords must be 8+ chars with no spaces or shell-dangerous chars. `is_public` is REQUIRED and has no default: ASK THE USER whether the database should be publicly reachable on a port (convenient for external clients but exposes it to the internet) or kept private to the project (safer). Do not assume.

POSTGRES EXTENSIONS - pass `extensions: [...]` (catalog names). The old `timescaledb_enabled` / `vector_enabled` booleans were REMOVED backend-side and are now IGNORED, so sending them yields a database with no extensions.
- CREATE-TIME ONLY HERE. Unlike an AWS instance, a project database can never gain an extension later - a forgotten one means recreating the database. Ask the user what they need BEFORE creating.
- CHECK `coolify_supported` FIRST via `list_postgres_extension_catalog`. A project database is a container and can only run what its image ships, so the catalog is narrower here than on a managed instance. Today `pg_partman` is the one entry no image provides and requesting it is a 422 rather than a silent drop.
- The platform picks the cheapest image that covers your WHOLE request, so combinations that used to be impossible now work: pgvector and timescaledb together resolve to the bundled image. You no longer have to choose one.
- PostgreSQL 17 only - that is what the images ship.
- `is_public: false` BREAKS THE EXTENSION STEP. With no external URL the platform cannot connect to run CREATE EXTENSION, so every requested extension settles as `failed` with "database is not public" in its `error_message`. The database itself still works. If the user wants extensions on a private database, they must create them by hand from inside the project.

is_public.description: Required choice (ask the user, do not assume): true = expose on a public port (internet-reachable); false = private to the project.

public_port.description: Public port when is_public (defaults: pg 5432, redis 6379, mysql 3306, mongo 27017)

extensions.description: postgres only, create-time only: PostgreSQL extensions by catalog name, e.g. ["pgvector"]. Only entries whose `coolify_supported` is true can run here - check `list_postgres_extension_catalog`. Pins PostgreSQL 17.

tools.name: delete_project_database
tools.description: Delete a project database. The exact current `name` must be supplied and match (a safety check, 422 otherwise). Returns 202 (async tear-down). Irreversible.

name.description: Exact current database name - must match

confirm.description: Must be true. Permanently destroys the database and its data.

tools.name: list_project_services
tools.description:
List the one-click application templates deployed in a project. Returns pid, name, template_type, status (`pending` | `awaiting_approval` | `creating` | `active` | `inactive` | `failed` | `unknown`), is_public, public_port, external_url, `error_message` when it failed, a `provisioning` block with the per-stage progress and an `update` block with the release it runs and whether a newer one is offered (see `list_project_service_upgrades`).

`awaiting_approval` is a template waiting for a Selfhost.dev platform admin (the OpenSSH server, code-server or a Jupyter template on an organisation that has never paid; on an account held for review also WireGuard and the VPN/DePIN nodes, even on a paying organisation): nothing is deployed yet and that is the expected state, not a fault. `pending` is a service declared while its project is still coming up; it starts by itself.

CREDENTIALS ARE NOT HERE. Use `get_project_service` for those.

`external_url` can be null on an otherwise `active` service when the project has no usable public IP; that is a real state, not a bug and the service simply has no public URL to hand out.

A `template_type` you do not recognise means the backend shipped a template newer than this tool. Report the wire string as-is; delete still works on it.

tools.name: get_project_service
tools.description:
Get one deployed service, INCLUDING ITS CREDENTIALS.

HOW THE CREDENTIALS ARE READ (backend #4100, production 2026-10-28): the service's own read now returns every secret masked as `••••••••`, so this tool reads the service and then calls the reveal endpoint for the real values. The reveal works for an Owner, Admin or Manager of the organization, only while the project is running, at most 30 times a minute and each reveal is recorded in the activity log as `credentials_viewed`. When it is refused (another role, a stopped project) the masked values are returned with the reason; relay that rather than handing the user bullets as a password. Pass `include_credentials: false` to read the service without revealing anything.

The block can be absent or partial until the service reaches `active`; then the right answer is "not ready yet", not an error. What it holds depends on the template:
- Login templates: the username and password plus `public_url`; Supabase adds the anon key, Keycloak and Vaultwarden an `admin_url`.
- Email-login templates (Krayin, Mautic, BookStack): the email as `username`, the password and `public_url`.
- First-visitor templates (n8n, n8n (Postgres), Twenty (CRM), WordPress, Immich, Strapi, Metabase, Chatwoot, Open WebUI + Ollama, Uptime Kuma): `public_url` only, because their first admin is created through the app's own first-run screen rather than from env.
- Password-only templates (code-server and the Jupyter family): `password` and `public_url` and no username.
- API-key templates: Qdrant and Evolution API return `api_key`, `public_url` and a `dashboard_url` / `manager_url`; LiteLLM adds a `master_key`.
- Discourse: `admin_email` and `public_url`; no password exists.
- OpenSSH server: `host`, `port`, `username`, `password` and a ready-made `ssh_command`; no URL.
- WireGuard: the admin `username` and `password`, the HTTPS `public_url` and `wireguard_endpoint` (the project IP, UDP 51820) for VPN clients.
- AdGuard Home: the login, `public_url`, `dns_server`, `dns_allowed_clients` and `doh_url`, the private DNS-over-HTTPS address (a secret).
- Mysterium: `public_url` (its HTTP panel on port 4449), the fixed username `myst`, the password and the `panel_sources` allowed to open it.
- Mysterium VPN Gateway: `proxy_endpoint`, `proxy_sources`, `country` and `service_type`; no login.
- Sentinel dVPN: `node_api_endpoint`, `wireguard_port` and `moniker`; the wallet phrase is never returned.
- Nginx and Caddy: `content_path`, the directory to upload the site to over SSH.
- URnetwork: a `hint` only; the node is managed at ur.io/app.

HAND THE URL OVER WITH THE WARNING ATTACHED for the first-visitor templates: the account is claimed by whoever opens it first, so an unattended public URL is an open door until the user completes setup.

Call this after `create_project_service` reports `active` and give the user the credentials - creating a service and not passing on how to log into it leaves the job half done.

include_credentials.description: Default true: reveal the real secrets (Owner, Admin or Manager only; audited). false reads the service with its secrets masked.
