CREDENTIALS DIFFER PER TEMPLATE AND THE WRONG SHAPE IS REFUSED HERE rather than sent and silently dropped:
- Templates taking a username + password: pass `dashboard_username` and `dashboard_password`. The accepted username FORM varies - a slug for Jenkins, Grafana, EspoCRM and listmonk, a login name (the slug plus the dot) for Langflow, Keycloak and AdGuard Home, an EMAIL for Krayin, Mautic and BookStack, a Linux login name for the OpenSSH server, anything for the rest. Where the catalogue says "optional username" the backend defaults it, so it may be left out.
- Templates taking a password only: pass `dashboard_password` alone. The app owns the username (GitLab is `root`, Elasticsearch `elastic`, Mysterium `myst`), has none (code-server, the Jupyter family) or the "password" is really the API key (Qdrant, Evolution API) or the admin token (Vaultwarden). Passing a username is refused.
- Discourse: pass the admin EMAIL as `dashboard_username`, no password and your SMTP server (`smtp_address`, `smtp_port`, `smtp_username`, `smtp_password`, `smtp_from`), all required, because Discourse cannot confirm any account without mail. The SMTP password is a secret: never repeat it back.
- Templates taking nothing: pass neither. "No login and nothing to claim" (Nginx, Caddy, the Mysterium VPN Gateway, Sentinel dVPN) is NOT the first-visitor case below.
- URnetwork takes an `auth_code` from ur.io/app instead of a login. It is a secret: never repeat it back.
- `$` and control characters are refused in the username and password of most templates: they are delivered through the container's environment, where `$` would change the password the app actually boots with.

TEMPLATE-SPECIFIC FIELDS, each refused on any other template:
- Mysterium: `panel_source`, the IP or CIDR allowed to open its HTTP panel on 4449.
- Mysterium VPN Gateway: `proxy_source`, the IP or CIDR of the apps that will use the proxy on 3128; `country` (two-letter code, optional); `service_type` (wireguard, the default or scraping, data_transfer, quic).
- AdGuard Home: `dns_allowed_clients`, the IPs or CIDRs (up to 32, none broader than a /16 or an IPv6 /48) allowed to use plain DNS on port 53.
  For these three, an omitted source makes the backend use the IP this MCP's requests come from, which is the machine running this server and not necessarily where the user or their devices are. Pass it explicitly; `list_project_ssh_keys` shows the `requester_ip` the backend sees. A world range (`/0`) is refused.
- Sentinel dVPN: `mnemonic`, the 12- or 24-word recovery phrase of an already-funded Sentinel wallet (required, a secret: never repeat it back) and an optional `moniker`, the node's public name.
- GitLab and the OpenSSH server: `public_port`. GitLab binds its SSH (for `git clone git@...`) to it; the OpenSSH server listens on it (default 2222 and a second SSH server in the same project needs another). Every other template publishes no host port and the backend would drop one, so it is refused.
- OpenSSH server: `public_key` (one OpenSSH public key line, optional) and `password_access` (default true; false only with a key and the password still gates sudo).
- Mysterium (VPN node), Mysterium VPN Gateway, URnetwork (bandwidth node), Sentinel dVPN (node) share the server's network with other people or spend money outside the platform, so each needs `acknowledge_network_terms: true`. Explain what they are agreeing to and ask; never set it on the user's behalf.

FIRST-ADMIN SECURITY WARNING, for every template marked "first visitor owns it": these ship with no admin credentials whatsoever. Whoever opens the public URL first gets the owner account. Say this UNPROMPTED, tell the user to finish setup the moment it is up and tell them not to share the URL before then.

SIX TEMPLATES NEED A PLATFORM ADMIN'S APPROVAL ON AN ORGANISATION THAT HAS NEVER PAID: the OpenSSH server, code-server, JupyterLab, Jupyter Data Science, Jupyter + TensorFlow and Jupyter + PyTorch. There a customer's create comes back `awaiting_approval`: nothing deploys, no port opens and no credentials exist until a Selfhost.dev platform admin approves it; the user is emailed either way and a declined request is deleted. Say so up front so the user is not left polling a service that is waiting on a person. On an account the Selfhost.dev team holds for review, those six plus WireGuard, Mysterium, the Mysterium VPN Gateway, URnetwork and Sentinel dVPN wait the same way even on a paying organisation. A 403 `account_restricted` (a banned account or a banned OpenSSH public key) is a decision, not an error to retry.

`is_public` is REQUIRED with no default: ASK THE USER. Most templates are web apps whose first-run setup happens at the public URL, so `true` is usually what they want, but do not assume it. These are refused with `false` because the backend would never open the port they are reached on: Stalwart (mail server), Mysterium (VPN node), Mysterium VPN Gateway, WireGuard (wg-easy), OpenSSH server, AdGuard Home, Sentinel dVPN (node).

CAPACITY: a project is ONE server and these limits are refusals at declare time, not slow degradation. `heavy` templates must leave more headroom (65% memory / 75% disk vs 80% / 85%); some need a minimum TOTAL host RAM whatever is free; at most 5 children per project; Stalwart (mail server), Mysterium (VPN node), Mysterium VPN Gateway, WireGuard (wg-easy), AdGuard Home, Sentinel dVPN (node) are one-per-project (their ports are fixed on the host). Check the recommended RAM against the project's server BEFORE promising a deploy. A full server can be scaled up to a bigger size of its family (`get_project_scale_ladder`, `set_project_scale_bounds`, `scale_up_project`, a few minutes of downtime) or the template goes into a new project.

The project must be able to take children (409 otherwise; a stopped project names the start). Returns 202 with status `creating` (`pending` while the project is still provisioning, `awaiting_approval` for a template waiting on a platform admin); poll `list_project_services`, then call `get_project_service` for the credentials once it is `active`.

EXPECT THESE REFUSALS: a duplicate service name inside the same project; a port already claimed by another database or service (a second OpenSSH server left on 2222 is the common one); the capacity guard refusing the template; a second instance of a one-per-project template; Krayin on an Arm (`cax*`) host, whose image has no Arm build at any tag; a Discourse SMTP host that does not resolve.

tools.name: delete_project_service
tools.description: Delete a project service. The exact current `name` must be supplied and match (a safety check, 422 otherwise). Returns 202 (async tear-down) and removes the service's volumes, configs and networks along with it. Irreversible. Works on any template_type, including one this tool does not recognise.

tools.name: request_project_container_logs
tools.description:
Ask the project's host to capture container logs for one service or database, then read them with `get_project_container_logs`. THIS DOES NOT RETURN LOGS: it dispatches a fetch to the host agent and returns a `pending` record, because the round-trip is too slow to block a request on.

Reach for this when a service or database is `active` but misbehaving. This is the container's own stdout/stderr, which is where a crash loop, a failed migration or a bad env var actually shows up - the platform's own status fields will only tell you it is unhealthy, not why.

Read-only: the backend runs an allow-listed `docker logs` scoped to this resource's containers. There is no start/stop/restart/exec anywhere on this surface.

resource_type.description: `service` for a one-click template, `database` for a project Postgres/Redis/MySQL/MongoDB. Picks which collection the pid is looked up in.

resource_pid.description: The service or database pid, as returned by list_project_services / list_project_databases

tools.name: get_project_container_logs
tools.description: Read container logs previously requested with `request_project_container_logs`. The response is a `fetches` array, newest first (up to 20). Each carries `status` (`pending` | `completed` | `failed`), `output` once completed, `error` when it failed and `lines_requested`. A fetch still `pending` after 3 minutes settles as `failed` - the agent's reply was lost, so request a fresh one rather than polling on. An empty array means nothing has been requested for this resource yet.

resource_type.description: `service` for a one-click template, `database` for a project Postgres/Redis/MySQL/MongoDB. Picks which collection the pid is looked up in.

resource_pid.description: The service or database pid, as returned by list_project_services / list_project_databases

tools.name: request_project_container_stats
tools.description:
Ask the project's host for a live resource snapshot of one service's or database's containers - `docker stats`: CPU, memory, network and block IO. Dispatches a fetch and returns a `pending` record; read it with `get_project_container_stats`.

THIS IS THE TOOL FOR "why is my project server full?". A project is ONE VM shared by every service and database in it and the capacity guard refuses new children once it fills up. Identifying which container is eating the memory is the first actionable answer; the others are scaling the server up a size (`scale_up_project`, a few minutes of downtime) or moving work to a new project.

resource_pid.description: The service or database pid, as returned by list_project_services / list_project_databases

tools.description: Read the resource snapshot previously requested with `request_project_container_stats`. The response is a `fetches` array, newest first (up to 20). Each carries `status` (`pending` | `completed` | `failed`), `output` once completed, `error` when it failed and `lines_requested`. A fetch still `pending` after 3 minutes settles as `failed` - the agent's reply was lost, so request a fresh one rather than polling on. tools.name: set_project_service_custom_domain
tools.description:
Point a custom domain at a project service's web UI. Every template exposes a web component except the ones with no web UI to route: Mysterium (VPN node), Mysterium VPN Gateway, URnetwork (bandwidth node), OpenSSH server, Sentinel dVPN (node). The backend refuses a domain for those, so do not offer one.

DNS MUST ALREADY BE POINTING HERE BEFORE YOU CALL THIS. The backend resolves the domain and refuses if it does not already answer with the project's public IP - deliberately, because applying a domain before DNS lands burns Let's Encrypt rate limits on certificate requests that are guaranteed to fail. The correct order is:
1. `get_project` for the project's `public_ip`.
2. Have the user create a DNS **A record** for the domain pointing at that IP (a CNAME chain resolving to it also passes).
3. Wait for propagation.
4. Call this. A 422 naming the IP means step 2 or 3 is not done - relay it and retry later, do not loop.

Pass a BARE HOSTNAME you own: no scheme, no path and not a platform-generated suffix. The service must already be provisioned (`uuid` present) - a 422 says it is not ready yet.

Templates whose containers bake their own public URL from the domain (Twenty's SERVER_URL, n8n's WEBHOOK_URL) re-derive it on the redeploy this triggers, so there is no env var for you to fix afterwards. The platform hostname keeps answering beside the domain. Routing and TLS are verified after the call returns - re-read `get_project_service` to see the domain's status settle.

Keycloak builds its issuer, login and redirect URLs from this address, so on Keycloak set the domain BEFORE apps are integrated with it. The service redeploys, which is a brief interruption and a 409 means a template upgrade owns the service right now.

domain.description: Bare hostname, e.g. crm.example.com - no https://, no trailing path

tools.name: remove_project_service_custom_domain
tools.description:
Remove a project service's custom domain and re-pin its platform-generated hostname. A 422 means no custom domain is set on that service.

The service redeploys so its containers pick the platform URL back up, which means a brief interruption. Anything referencing the custom domain - bookmarks, webhooks registered with third parties, OAuth callback URLs - stops working, so say so before doing it.

confirm.description: Must be true. The service redeploys and anything pointing at the custom domain - webhooks, OAuth callbacks - breaks.

tools.name: list_project_service_upgrades
tools.description:
Read a one-click service's release and its upgrade history: the `update` block plus the last 50 upgrade runs, newest first. Use it to answer "is there a newer version?" and to POLL an upgrade started with `upgrade_project_service`.

The `update` block: `current` (the release it runs, `unknown` when none was recorded), `available` (the newest the platform ships), `update_available`, `security` with its `cves` when a pending release fixes vulnerabilities, `release_notes_url`, `risk` (`low` | `medium` | `irreversible`) and `upgradeable`, which is exactly when `upgrade_project_service` will be accepted. When it is false, `blocked_reason` says why: `irreversible_upgrade` (a one-way data migration: the console will not apply it, the user contacts support), `template_not_enabled` (upgrades are switched off for this template) or `template_drift` (the service runs a release the platform does not list). A null block means the template is not version-tracked.

A run moves `queued` → `prefetching` → `deploying` → `verifying` → `finalizing` → `succeeded`; a failed deploy goes `rolling_back` → `rolled_back` (the previous release is back) or `failed_needs_attention` (it could not roll back cleanly: tell the user to contact support). `cancelled` means it was stopped before it deployed.

Reads work on any service the caller can see. Pass `upgrade_pid` to read one run instead of the list (cheaper when polling a run you started).

upgrade_pid.description: One upgrade run's pid, from upgrade_project_service or the list

tools.name: upgrade_project_service
tools.description:
Upgrade a one-click service to the newest release the platform ships, the console's Update button. It swaps the service's compose to the new images and redeploys, so the app is briefly unavailable while it restarts; a deploy that fails is rolled back to the previous release automatically.

BEFORE UPGRADING A SERVICE THAT HOLDS DATA, take a whole-server snapshot (`create_project_snapshot`, then wait until `list_project_snapshots` shows it complete). Whether a stateful app's rollback restores its data has not been proven end to end and the snapshot is the undo that is certain.

Call without `confirm` first: it reads `list_project_service_upgrades` and states the move (from, to, risk, security fixes, release notes) for the user to approve. Refused when the service is not deployed yet, is already on the newest release, its template has upgrades switched off, the move crosses a one-way migration (`irreversible_upgrade`: contact support) or an upgrade is already running (409). Needs an Owner, Admin or Manager.

Returns 202 with the run. Poll `list_project_service_upgrades`. A run moves `queued` → `prefetching` → `deploying` → `verifying` → `finalizing` → `succeeded`; a failed deploy goes `rolling_back` → `rolled_back` (the previous release is back) or `failed_needs_attention` (it could not roll back cleanly: tell the user to contact support). `cancelled` means it was stopped before it deployed. While a run is in flight the service refuses restarts, custom-domain changes and deletion with a 409.

confirm.description: Must be true. The service redeploys on the new release (a short outage).

tools.name: cancel_project_service_upgrade
tools.description: Cancel a one-click service upgrade that has not started deploying. Only a run in `queued` or `prefetching` can be cancelled; once the new compose is deploying (409) the run finishes or rolls back on its own and a finished run cannot be cancelled either. Nothing about the running service changes. Needs an Owner, Admin or Manager.

upgrade_pid.description: The run's pid, from `list_project_service_upgrades` or the upgrade response

tools.name: get_project_service_port_sources
tools.description: Read who may reach a source-locked port of a one-click service. Two templates lock a port to chosen sources: the Mysterium node's panel (4449) and the Mysterium VPN Gateway's HTTP proxy (3128). Returns `port_sources` keyed by port, each `{source, cidrs, my_ip?, stale}` and `requester_ip`. `stale: true` on a `my_ip` entry means the saved IP no longer matches the requester's, which is how "the panel stopped loading after my IP changed" shows up. Any other template answers 422.

tools.name: set_project_service_port_sources
tools.description:
Change who may reach a source-locked port of a one-click service (the Mysterium panel on 4449, the Mysterium VPN Gateway's proxy on 3128), without recreating it: the project's firewall is updated. This is the fix when the owner's IP changed and the panel or proxy stopped answering. Recreating the service instead would cost the node its identity.

Each port named is replaced; ports not named keep their source. Sources: `my_ip` (the requester's public IP, captured server-side; for an MCP that is the machine running it, so read `requester_ip` in the reply), `custom` (1-16 IPs or CIDR ranges) or `anywhere`. AVOID `anywhere` on the gateway: an HTTP proxy open to the internet is abused within hours; for the node panel it exposes the login page to everyone. `applied: false` with an `apply_note` means saved and still being applied.

ports.description: Map of port to source, e.g. { "4449": { source: "custom", cidrs: ["203.0.113.7"] } }

confirm_anywhere.description: Required to set any port to `anywhere`, which opens it to the whole internet

tools.name: reauthenticate_urnetwork_service
tools.description:
Give a URnetwork node a new auth code without recreating it, the console's re-authenticate. The node keeps its identity (its data volume) and is redeployed with the new code, which its entrypoint exchanges for a login on boot.

Use it when URnetwork rejected the code (it expired or was used before the node's first boot exchanged it: the container logs a "[selfhost] URnetwork login failed" line and stops) or when the node should move to another URnetwork account. Once a node has logged in, the code expiring changes nothing, so do not re-authenticate a working node.

The code comes from ur.io/app and is short-lived: ask the user for a fresh one right before calling. Whether URnetwork accepted it cannot be seen from here; after a minute or two check `request_project_container_logs` for the login line or the account at ur.io/app.

auth_code.description: A fresh auth code from ur.io/app

tools.name: list_deployment_notification_bindings
tools.description: List the notification channels bound to a deployment (which channels get notified when a deploy succeeds/fails/aborts). Returns binding_pid, notification_channel_pid, channel_type, name and bound_at.

tools.name: bind_deployment_notification_channel
tools.description: Bind an existing org notification channel to a deployment so it's notified on deploy outcomes. The channel pid (nchan_...) comes from `list_notification_channels` (create one with `create_notification_channel` if needed). Returns 422 if already bound, 404 if the channel doesn't exist. Org owner only.

notification_channel_pid.description: Org notification channel pid, e.g. nchan_...

tools.name: unbind_deployment_notification_channel
tools.description: Unbind a notification channel from a deployment (it will no longer be notified on deploy outcomes). Pass the notification_channel_pid (NOT the binding pid). Org owner only.

notification_channel_pid.description: The notification channel pid (nchan_...) to unbind

tools.name: list_project_backups
tools.description:
List the automatic backups of a project's server, read live from Hetzner.

Returns `backups_enabled`, a `backup_schedule` (`cadence`, `retention` and the UTC window) and the `backups` themselves. Each backup carries the image id you pass to `restore_project_backup`.

Backups are daily and seven are kept - both fixed, neither configurable. Hetzner assigns the daily window shortly AFTER backups are switched on, so a just-enabled project can legitimately report the cadence and retention with a null window; that is "window pending", not a fault.

This is a read and works on a stopped or billing-suspended project, so it is safe to call when a project is in trouble and the user is deciding whether they can recover it.

Backups cost 20% of the project server's billed compute while they are on, stopped or running, so in a full month they add at most 20% of the size's monthly price. Quote it as a share of the server price from `list_server_types`, never as a fixed amount.

tools.name: enable_project_backups
tools.description:
Turn on automatic daily backups of a project's server. Seven are kept, on a window Hetzner assigns shortly after this call.

COSTS MONEY: backups cost 20% of the project server's billed compute for as long as they stay on, whether the server is running or stopped (at most 20% of the size's monthly price in a month). Say so before enabling, as a share of the server price the user already pays.

They are still the only automatic restore point a project has, so recommend them for any project holding real data, with the price stated.

The project must be `active`. A 409 means the project is not `active` yet (or its server is not up) - wait, do not retry in a loop. A 502 means Hetzner refused the operation.

Returns 202. Confirm with `list_project_backups`; the first backup appears after the first window passes, not immediately.

tools.name: disable_project_backups
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: turn off automatic backups for a project AND DELETE THE BACKUPS ALREADY TAKEN. Hetzner removes them with the schedule; there is no pause that keeps them and no way to get them back.

So this is not "stop making new backups" - it is "stop and throw away every restore point this project has". Check with the user that they mean both. Turning backups off does save the 20% backup share of the server rate; make sure they weigh that against losing every restore point.

The project must be `active`. A 409 means the project is not `active` yet (or its server is not up) - wait, do not retry in a loop. A 502 means Hetzner refused the operation.

You MUST set confirm=true to proceed.

confirm.description: Must be true. Deletes every existing backup of this project, irreversibly.

tools.name: restore_project_backup
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: rebuild a project's server from one of its backups. The VM's boot disk is overwritten, so EVERYTHING on it goes back to the state it was in when that backup was taken - the Coolify install, every service and every project database, including anything written since.

This is a real rollback, unlike the ClickHouse data restore in `restore_backup` which merges. Data created after the chosen backup is gone and cannot be recovered.

The project goes to status `restoring` and is UNAVAILABLE while the server is rebuilt. Every app and database in it is down for the duration.

Requires `image_id` from `list_project_backups` and `name` must exactly match the project's current name (422 otherwise) - that check exists so a restore cannot be fired at the wrong project. Backups must be enabled.

A 409 means the project is not `active` yet (or its server is not up) - wait, do not retry in a loop. A 502 means Hetzner refused the operation.

Before calling: show the user the backup list with dates, get them to pick and state what they will lose. You MUST set confirm=true.

image_id.description: The backup image to restore, from `list_project_backups`

name.description: The project's exact current name - must match or the backend refuses

confirm.description: Must be true. Overwrites the server's disk; everything written since this backup is lost.

tools.name: list_project_snapshots
tools.description:
List the project's on-demand snapshots - manual point-in-time images of the whole server, distinct from the automatic daily backups `list_project_backups` shows.

Returns each snapshot's `image_id`, description, size and creation time, plus `max_snapshots` (the cap, currently 10). Use `image_id` for restore and delete.

Unlike the automatic backups, these persist until someone deletes them - they are not rotated. A 409 means the project is not `active` yet (or its server is not up) - wait, do not retry in a loop. A 502 means Hetzner refused the operation.

tools.name: create_project_snapshot
tools.description:
Take a snapshot of the project's server right now - "back up before I break something". This is the tool to reach for BEFORE a risky change: upgrading a service, editing env vars that boot an app or restoring a database.

It captures the WHOLE VM, so it covers every service, database and anything installed on the box - which is also why it is the only real undo a project has.

Returns 202: Hetzner creates the image in the background, so it is not usable the instant this returns. Poll `list_project_snapshots` until it appears complete before relying on it.

Capped at 10 per project - a 422 means the cap is reached and an old one has to go first (`delete_project_snapshot`). A 409 means the project is not `active` yet (or its server is not up) - wait, do not retry in a loop. A 502 means Hetzner refused the operation.

No metered charge today: the platform bills no snapshot component for projects and the console states no price for one. Do not quote a price either way.

description.description: A label so the user can tell snapshots apart later, e.g. "before upgrading n8n". Strongly recommended - the list is unreadable without one.

tools.name: restore_project_snapshot
tools.description:
Rebuild the project's server from one of its snapshots. THE MOST DESTRUCTIVE OPERATION ON A PROJECT.

WHAT THIS DOES: the whole VM is rebuilt from the image. Every change made since the snapshot was taken is GONE - not just the thing the user wanted to undo, but every service, database write, config edit and uploaded file across the entire project. There is no partial or per-service restore.

BEFORE CALLING: take a snapshot of the CURRENT state first (`create_project_snapshot`), so the restore itself is reversible. Say out loud what the user will lose - name the age of the snapshot they are restoring, since "restore from the 3rd" means discarding everything since the 3rd.

The project's exact `name` must be supplied and match, as a backend safety check. Returns 202; the rebuild runs in the background and the project is unusable while it does.

A 409 means the project is not `active` yet (or its server is not up) - wait, do not retry in a loop. A 502 means Hetzner refused the operation.

name.description: The project's exact current name - a safety check, must match or the backend refuses

confirm.description: Must be true. Rebuilds the entire server; everything written since the snapshot is destroyed.

tools.name: delete_project_snapshot
tools.description:
Delete one on-demand snapshot. Irreversible - the restore point is gone.

Do this to free a slot when the 10-snapshot cap blocks a new one. Check with `list_project_snapshots` which is genuinely the oldest or least useful rather than guessing and do not delete the only snapshot a project has without saying so.

confirm.description: Must be true. The snapshot is permanently deleted and can no longer be restored from.

tools.name: list_project_activities
tools.description:
The history of what has happened to a project, newest first. This is the tool for "why did my project go down", "when was this restarted", "who deleted that service" - questions no other project tool can answer.

Two sources merged into one chronological, paginated feed, each item tagged with `source`:
- `hetzner` - infrastructure actions on the server itself: create_server, rebuild, enable_backup, assign_primary_ip and so on.
- `platform` - our own events: backups, restores, deployments, provisioning stages, lifecycle changes including credit-driven stops.

Reading them together is the point. A project that stopped answering shows the platform event and the server action side by side, which is usually enough to tell "we stopped it for billing" from "the machine was rebuilt".

If Hetzner is unreachable the feed degrades to platform events only and sets `meta.server_activities_available: false` rather than failing. Check that flag before concluding nothing happened at the infrastructure level - an empty infra history and an unavailable one look identical otherwise.

Works on a stopped or billing-suspended project.

page.description: 1-based page number; omit for the first (newest) page

tools.name: get_proxysql
tools.description: Get the ProxySQL connection-pooling config and status for a MySQL instance. Returns null when pooling has never been configured. ProxySQL status: disabled | enabling | enabled | disabling | error.

tools.name: enable_proxysql
tools.description: Enable ProxySQL connection pooling on a MySQL instance (MySQL-only). Clients connect on port 6033 once status reaches `enabled`; the ProxySQL admin interface listens on port 6032. Status is one of disabled | enabling | enabled | disabling | error. After enabling, poll `get_proxysql` until status is `enabled`.

multiplexing.description: Reuse backend connections across clients when safe

connection_max_age_ms.description: Max age of a backend connection in milliseconds before recycling (>= 0)

tools.name: reconfigure_proxysql
tools.description: Apply new ProxySQL settings on an already-enabled MySQL instance. Only sends the fields you provide (PATCH-style). Status must be `enabled`; will return an error otherwise.

tools.name: disable_proxysql
tools.description: Disable ProxySQL on a MySQL instance. Existing connections drain gracefully. The config row is preserved so you can re-enable later with `enable_proxysql`. Valid from `enabled` or `error` state - use this to recover from `error`.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Disabling will drop pool warmth and force clients back to port 3306.

tools.name: get_mysql_config
tools.description: Get the current MySQL configuration for a running instance, showing calculated defaults, overrides and effective values.

tools.name: update_mysql_config
tools.description: Update MySQL configuration parameters on a running instance. Set a value to null to revert to the calculated default. max_connections and innodb_buffer_pool_size require an instance restart.

max_connections.description: Max concurrent connections (e.g. 151). Set null to revert to default. Requires restart.

innodb_buffer_pool_size.description: InnoDB buffer pool memory (e.g. '256MB'). Set null to revert. Requires restart.

tmp_table_size.description: Max size of in-memory internal temp tables (e.g. '16MB'). Set null to revert.

wait_timeout.description: Seconds an idle connection is kept before it is closed (e.g. 28800). Set null to revert.

tools.name: get_chproxy
tools.description:
Get the CHProxy connection-pooling config for a ClickHouse instance. Returns null when pooling has never been configured. Status: disabled | enabling | enabled | disabling | error (with error_message).

The same payload is embedded as `chproxy_config` on every instance response, so get_instance already tells you the state if you have the instance in hand.

tools.name: enable_chproxy
tools.description:
Enable CHProxy connection pooling on a ClickHouse instance - the ClickHouse counterpart to PgBouncer/ProxySQL. Clients connect over HTTP on port 9090 once status reaches `enabled` (poll via get_chproxy); the native TCP port 9000 is unaffected. Defaults: max_concurrent_queries=100, max_queue_size=200, max_queue_time=30, max_execution_time=0 (unlimited).

ClickHouse instances only. The instance must be running/provisioned with a live agent.

max_concurrent_queries.description: Max simultaneous queries per user (default 100, range 1-2000)

max_queue_size.description: Max queries queued once the concurrency limit is hit (default 200, range 0-10000; 0 = reject immediately)

max_queue_time.description: Seconds a query waits in the queue before rejection (default 30, range 0-3600)

max_execution_time.description: Max query execution time in seconds (default 0 = no limit, range 0-86400)

tools.name: reconfigure_chproxy
tools.description: Apply new CHProxy settings to a ClickHouse instance. Only sends the fields you provide; omitted fields keep their current values. Valid from `enabled`, `enabling` or `error` - use it to retry a failed enable without disabling first.

max_concurrent_queries.description: Max simultaneous queries per user (default 100, range 1-2000)

max_queue_size.description: Max queries queued once the concurrency limit is hit (default 200, range 0-10000; 0 = reject immediately)

max_queue_time.description: Seconds a query waits in the queue before rejection (default 30, range 0-3600)

max_execution_time.description: Max query execution time in seconds (default 0 = no limit, range 0-86400)

tools.name: disable_chproxy
tools.description: Disable CHProxy on a ClickHouse instance. The config row is preserved so you can re-enable later with enable_chproxy. Valid from `enabled` or `error` - use this to clear a stuck error state.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Clients pooling on port 9090 must move back to the direct HTTP port 8123.

tools.name: list_postgres_extension_catalog
tools.description:
List the PostgreSQL extensions the platform can install, with no instance in play. Use this for the two cases where there is nothing to ask about yet: choosing extensions for an instance you are ABOUT to create (pass them to `create_instance` as `extensions`) and choosing them for a project database (`create_project_database`, where they are creation-only).

Pass `db_version` and/or `architecture` to have the server apply the compatibility gate and fill in a `reason` on each rejected entry. With neither, everything comes back under `available` and you must gate yourself on each row's `supported_postgres_versions` / `supported_architectures`. An unsupported value is a 422, not a silent ignore.

Each row carries `name` (the API id - send this exactly, `uuid-ossp` keeps its hyphen), `display_name`, `category`, `description`, `install_source`, `requires_restart`, `dependencies`, `conflicts` and `coolify_supported`.

FILTER ON `coolify_supported` BEFORE OFFERING ANYTHING FOR A PROJECT DATABASE. A managed instance installs binaries on the host so it can run the whole catalog; a project database is a container and can only run what its image ships. Offering a name the create will refuse is the specific mistake this field exists to prevent - today `pg_partman` is the one entry no image provides.

If an instance already exists, `list_instance_extensions` is the better call - it knows that instance's version, architecture and current rows.

Catalog today (orientation - trust the response, not this line): pgvector (vectors), timescaledb (time_series), pgcrypto (security), uuid-ossp (data_types), postgres_fdw (integration), pg_partman (partitioning), pg_stat_statements (observability), pg_trgm (search), pg_cron (scheduling), postgis (geospatial), pg_textsearch (search, PG 17-18 only).

db_version.description: PostgreSQL major, e.g. "17". Filters the catalog and explains each rejection.

architecture.description: CPU architecture of the instance you intend to create.

tools.name: list_instance_extensions
tools.description:
List PostgreSQL extension state for one managed instance, split three ways:

- `enabled` - every row ON this instance, whatever its status. READ THE PER-ROW `status`: `enabled` (done, with the `version` reported by `pg_extension`), `pending` (recorded, no task yet), `installing` (a task is running - `replica_tasks` shows per-node progress on a Multi-AZ group) or `failed` (with `error_message`). A `failed` row is the retry affordance - call `enable_instance_extensions` with the same name again. Nothing is ever marked `enabled` optimistically; only a verified on-host outcome promotes a row, so this is a real answer and not a hopeful one.
- `available` - catalog entries this instance could enable and has no row for.
- `unavailable` - entries this instance CANNOT use, each with a `reason` (its PostgreSQL version or CPU architecture). Do not offer these; the enable would 422.

Also returns the instance's `db_version`, `architecture` and `status`, which is what determines the split.

404 for any non-PostgreSQL instance - extensions are a PostgreSQL feature and `extensions` is `[]` on every other engine.

tools.name: enable_instance_extensions
tools.description:
Enable one or more PostgreSQL extensions on an existing managed instance. Batch them in ONE call - everything is validated together before any state changes, so you get every problem back at once instead of discovering them one failed request at a time.

PERMANENT. There is no disable endpoint on any path, because dropping an extension can break objects that depend on it. Confirm with the user before calling.

SOME EXTENSIONS RESTART POSTGRESQL. A restart happens once, only when a required library is not already loaded and it drops live connections for a few seconds. Called without `confirm`, this tool reads the instance's own extension state first and tells you exactly which of your names need a restart, which are already enabled and which this instance cannot run - so the confirmation you show the user is accurate rather than generic.

What happens on accept (202): each requested row goes to `installing`, the instance and each replica move to `updating` and one `postgres_enable_extensions` task runs per node. Replicas are prepared BEFORE the primary on purpose - a standby replaying `CREATE EXTENSION` for a library it does not have would stall replication - so a replica failure cancels the primary and the error names the node. Poll `list_instance_extensions` until the rows settle to `enabled` or `failed`.

Re-sending names that are already `enabled` or `installing` is safe: the response is a 200 with them under `skipped`, no task, no status change.

Requirements: instance must be `running` or `provisioned` (replicas and instances mid-scale are refused), a registered agent is required (400 without one) and enables are rate-limited to 10/min.

Catalog today (orientation - `list_postgres_extension_catalog` is the authority and a newer platform may offer more): pgvector (vectors), timescaledb (time_series), pgcrypto (security), uuid-ossp (data_types), postgres_fdw (integration), pg_partman (partitioning), pg_stat_statements (observability), pg_trgm (search), pg_cron (scheduling), postgis (geospatial), pg_textsearch (search, PG 17-18 only). Send `name` exactly as the catalog spells it; `vector` is accepted as an alias for `pgvector`.

Once TimescaleDB is enabled these metrics join the instance's `postgresql.database` alert set - a rule on them silently never fires before that: timescaledb_hypertable_count, timescaledb_chunk_count, timescaledb_compressed_chunk_count, timescaledb_compression_ratio, timescaledb_total_size_bytes.

extensions.description: Catalog names, e.g. ["pgvector", "pg_stat_statements"]. Free-form on purpose: the server validates against the live catalog, so an extension newer than this release still works.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Omit it first to get the per-extension restart / already-enabled / unavailable breakdown for this specific instance.

tools.name: set_instance_tls
tools.description:
Turn client TLS on or off for a managed PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse or Redis instance group: encryption in transit between clients and the database. (OpenSearch is always HTTPS; Kafka's TLS is chosen at create.) This tool was `set_postgres_tls` up to 0.12.1.

WHOLE GROUP, ONE CALL. TLS is group state, so this covers the primary and every replica together; there is no per-replica setting.

EACH ENGINE SERVES IT DIFFERENTLY and the reply says what clients must change:
- PostgreSQL: same port; clients opt in with `sslmode=require`.
- MySQL: same port and once enabled it is ENFORCED: plaintext clients are refused. Warn the user before enabling on a database with live clients.
- ClickHouse: secure ports 9440 (native) and 8443 (HTTPS) beside the plain 9000/8123.
- Redis: TLS on 6380 beside the plain 6379.

Enabling is the right default for anything a client reaches over a network the user does not control. TURNING IT OFF is a downgrade: confirm the user means it.

The instance must be `running` or `provisioned` and have a registered agent. Enabling can be refused when the extra TLS ports would push the instance's security group past its rule limit: trim allowed_cidr_ranges first. A reply saying TLS is "already" in that state is a no-op, not a failure.

AFTER A RESTORE OR A FORK, TLS IS OFF even if the source had it on. Re-enable it explicitly and tell the user.

tls_enabled.description: true = serve TLS for client connections across the group; false = back to plaintext only

confirm.description: Required when turning TLS OFF and when turning it ON for MySQL (which then refuses plaintext clients).

tools.name: get_tls_notice_preferences
tools.description:
Read who hears about a managed database's TLS certificate: `announcements_enabled` (the routine notices before and after a certificate rotation: announcement, reminder, rotated) and `extra_recipients` (addresses that get every TLS notice besides the organization's owners), with `max_extra_recipients`. Failure alerts and expiry reminders always go out and cannot be muted. The setting belongs to the instance's group, so every member reads the same one.

Worth reading for a user whose clients pin the server certificate or its CA: a rotation then needs action on their side and the announcement is the warning.

tools.name: set_tls_notice_preferences
tools.description:
Change who hears about a managed database's TLS certificate rotations. Only the fields passed change. `announcements_enabled: false` mutes the routine rotation notices (failure alerts and expiry reminders still go out); `extra_recipients` REPLACES the list of extra addresses that get every TLS notice (`[]` clears it; the reply states the maximum). Applies to the whole instance group. Needs update rights on the instance.

Do not mute announcements for a user whose clients pin the certificate or its CA: the announcement is their only warning before a rotation breaks those clients.

announcements_enabled.description: Routine rotation notices on or off

extra_recipients.description: REPLACES the extra recipient list; [] clears it

tools.name: list_log_sources
tools.description:
List the log sources available on a managed database instance. Call this before `fetch_instance_logs` - the valid `log_source` values are per engine and per instance.

Log sources differ per engine and `list_log_sources` is the only authority - do not guess a name, an unknown one is a 422. Every engine has `engine` (the server's own log) and a `replication` view; Postgres and MySQL add backup/restore logs and ClickHouse adds separate backup, native-restore, fork and upgrade logs. `replication` is a server-side FILTERED view of the engine log rather than a separate file on Postgres and MySQL, so it is the right source for a replication question and will look like a subset of `engine`.

Returns `{sources: [{key, label}]}`. An EMPTY list means the engine does not support log tailing at all (only Postgres, MySQL and ClickHouse do) - it does not mean something went wrong.

A 422 saying to top up means the organization's wallet is empty. This endpoint is behind the same balance gate as the fetch itself, so an empty source list and a billing block are different answers: read the message.

tools.name: fetch_instance_logs
tools.description:
Ask the instance for the tail of one of its logs. This is how you actually look at a database that is misbehaving - no SSH needed.

TWO STEPS. This POST creates a PENDING fetch and returns immediately; the agent on the box collects the output and posts it back a moment later. Read it with `list_instance_log_fetches`. The response here almost never contains the log text.

Log sources differ per engine and `list_log_sources` is the only authority - do not guess a name, an unknown one is a 422. Every engine has `engine` (the server's own log) and a `replication` view; Postgres and MySQL add backup/restore logs and ClickHouse adds separate backup, native-restore, fork and upgrade logs. `replication` is a server-side FILTERED view of the engine log rather than a separate file on Postgres and MySQL, so it is the right source for a replication question and will look like a subset of `engine`.

`lines` defaults to 200 and is clamped to 2000. Output is capped at 1 MB per fetch, so a very chatty log is truncated rather than refused - ask for fewer lines and a specific source if you are hunting something particular.

DEDUP AND COOLDOWN, both worth understanding before you loop:
- A pending fetch for the same source is returned as-is instead of a second one being started. So an immediate repeat call is a no-op, not progress.
- After a fetch completes or fails there is a ~10s cooldown per (instance, source) and a further request is rate-limited.
So: request once, wait, then read. Do not poll this endpoint.

Requires the instance to be `running` or `provisioned`, with a registered agent and `cloud_instances:update` (a 403 means the caller's role is too low - reading the result needs only view access). Replicas are fine.

log_source.description: A `key` from `list_log_sources` for this instance. Guessing gets a 422.

lines.description: Tail length; defaults to 200, clamped to 2000

tools.name: list_instance_log_fetches
tools.description:
Read the results of log fetches on an instance - the last 20, newest first, WITH their output. This is where the log text you asked for with `fetch_instance_logs` actually shows up.

Each row: `pid`, `log_source`, `lines_requested`, `status`, `output`, `error` and timestamps.

`status` is `pending` until the agent reports back, then `completed` (read `output`) or `failed` (read `error`). A fetch whose agent result was lost is flipped to `failed` when you read this endpoint rather than sitting pending forever - so reading is also how a stuck fetch gets cleared.

Because the backend keeps the last 20 per instance, previous fetches are already here: check them before requesting a new one, since a recent fetch of the same source may answer the question and avoid the cooldown entirely.

Output can be up to 1 MB. Summarise what matters to the user rather than replaying the whole tail.

tools.name: capture_db_stats
tools.description:
Take a query-workload snapshot of a database: what it is actually doing right now. Use this for "why is my database slow" before reaching for metrics - metrics say the CPU is busy, this says which queries are making it busy.

SAMPLES OVER TIME. The agent reads the engine's cumulative counters twice, `sample_seconds` apart and reports the difference - so the result describes that window, not a single instant. Default 10s, allowed 5 to 60. A longer sample smooths out a spiky workload; a short one catches a burst.

Same two-step shape as the logs: this POST returns a PENDING sample and you read the result with `list_db_stats`. Do not poll this endpoint - a pending sample is returned as-is instead of starting a second one and there is a per-instance cooldown after one finishes.

Postgres, MySQL, ClickHouse and OpenSearch - but THE OPENSEARCH PAYLOAD IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE. The relational engines return a ranked list of slow queries; OpenSearch returns a search-shaped cluster snapshot (indices, shards, search and indexing rates) rather than "the top N queries". Read the fields you get back instead of looking for a query list that is not there and do not describe it to the user as slow-query analysis. NOT available on a ClickHouse keeper-only node (a keeper runs clickhouse-keeper, not clickhouse-server, so there is no query log to sample) - that is a 422 and the answer is to target a data node instead. Instance must be `running` or `provisioned` with a registered agent and this needs `cloud_instances:update`.

sample_seconds.description: Sampling window in seconds; default 10, clamped to 5-60

tools.name: list_db_stats
tools.description:
Read query-workload samples for an instance - the last 20, newest first, with their results. This is where a `capture_db_stats` sample lands.

Each row: `pid`, `sample_seconds`, `status`, `stats`, `error` and timestamps. `status` is `pending` until the agent reports, then `completed` (read `stats`) or `failed` (read `error`).

Check here first: a recent sample may already answer the question and reusing it avoids both the sampling wait and the cooldown.

Remember what the numbers are - a delta over the sample window, not lifetime totals - so "queries per second" figures are for that window only and a quiet moment will understate a workload the user is complaining about. If the numbers look implausibly calm, take a longer sample while the problem is happening rather than concluding the database is fine.

tools.name: list_capacity_ladders
tools.description:
List the machine-size ladders a database engine can be scaled along. A ladder is an ordered list of instance types and every tier bound elsewhere in this module is an INDEX into it - so read this before setting or interpreting `min_tier_index` / `max_tier_index`.

Returns `profiles` keyed by profile name, each an array of `{index, instance_type, vcpu, memory_gib}`:
- `default` - the data plane's ladder.
- `auxiliary` - the ladder for non-data nodes (ClickHouse keepers).

A 404 means no ladder is configured for that engine and provider, which means tier scaling is not available for it - not that something failed. Ladders exist for AWS; Hetzner has definitions but no execution in this version.

Cheap and stable: fetch it once and reuse it while you reason about tiers, rather than per question.

cloud_provider.description: Defaults to `aws`, which is the only provider that executes tier moves today

tools.name: get_capacity_config
tools.description:
Read a group's tier-scaling guardrails, where it currently sits on the ladder and any scale plan in flight. This is the tool for "is my cluster scaling?" and "why is it stuck?".

Returns `config` (bounds, profile, enabled), `current_tier_index` and `current_instance_type`, the `resolved_ladder` and every instance in scope with its own tier index.

Plus, when the data plane is involved:
- `active_scale_plan` - a move in progress, with `ordered_node_replacements` so you can say which node is being replaced and how many remain. This is what makes the zero-downtime claim checkable rather than a promise.
- `last_failed_scale_plan` - READ THIS WHENEVER SCALING SEEMS DEAD. A failed plan BLOCKS all further automatic scaling for the group until it is retried or deleted and nothing else surfaces it. Its `error_message` says why and `retry_cluster_scale_plan` / `delete_cluster_scale_plan` are how you clear it.
- `active_tier_event` / `last_tier_event` - the equivalent for a SINGLE-NODE group, which moves tier via an in-place resize and produces no plan object at all. On a single-node cluster these are the only progress you get, so do not conclude "nothing is happening" from an absent plan.

A 404 means no config exists for that group (or you own no instances in it) - the group simply is not set up for tier scaling, which is a normal state and the answer to give.

group_id.description: The instance group id (from an instance's `group_id`)

tools.name: create_capacity_config
tools.description:
Set up tier-scaling guardrails for an instance group: the floor and ceiling it may move between on the machine-size ladder.

Guardrails and triggers are separate. This config only says HOW FAR the group may move; nothing moves until a tier policy says WHEN. Create the config first (a policy against a missing or disabled config is refused), then `create_scaling_policy` with `scaling_action: "resize_instance"`, `group_id`, `target_class` and a `direction` of `scale_up` or `scale_down`.

`min_tier_index` and `max_tier_index` are indexes into the ladder from `list_capacity_ladders` - fetch that first and show the user the actual machine types the bounds correspond to. A ceiling is a spend ceiling: state what the top tier costs before setting it, because automatic scaling will use it.

`profile` is normally left out and defaulted server-side from `target_class` (`data` to `default`, `non_data` to `auxiliary`). Only set it if you specifically mean to use a different ladder.

`deprecation_window_minutes` is how long a replaced node is kept before teardown - a rollback window. Too short and a bad move cannot be undone; it also means paying for both nodes for that long.

`enabled: false` creates the guardrails without arming anything, which is a reasonable way to stage a setup for review.

AWS and the data plane are what actually execute today.

target_class.description: `data` for the data plane, `non_data` for ClickHouse keepers (v1 executes data only)

min_tier_index.description: Lowest ladder index the group may scale down to

max_tier_index.description: Highest ladder index it may scale up to - this is a spend ceiling, quote its cost to the user

deprecation_window_minutes.description: How long a replaced node is retained before teardown (rollback window; both nodes bill during it)

enabled.description: Arm the guardrails. false stages the config without allowing any move.

profile.description: Ladder profile. Omit - it is derived from target_class.

tools.name: update_capacity_config
tools.description:
Change a group's tier bounds, rollback window or whether tier scaling is armed at all.

DO NOT SEND `target_class` FOR A BOUNDS-ONLY CHANGE. Passing it makes the backend re-derive `profile`, which can swap the group onto a different ladder and silently reinterpret every tier index. Send only the fields you are actually changing.

`enabled: false` is the pause: it stops automatic tier moves while keeping the config and its policies intact. Prefer it over deleting.

Raising `max_tier_index` raises the spend ceiling - say what the new top tier costs. Lowering bounds below where the group currently sits does not move it back on its own; a scale-down policy has to fire.

enabled.description: false pauses automatic tier scaling without deleting anything

target_class.description: Leave this OUT unless you intend to change the ladder - sending it re-derives `profile`.

tools.name: delete_capacity_config
tools.description:
Remove a group's tier-scaling guardrails entirely. The group stays on whatever machine size it is on now - nothing is resized - but it loses the ability to move tier automatically.

A 422 means enabled tier policies still reference this config. Delete or disable those policies first (`list_scaling_policies` then `delete_scaling_policy`); the backend refuses rather than leaving triggers pointing at bounds that no longer exist.

If the intent is only to stop automatic scaling, `update_capacity_config` with `enabled: false` does that and keeps the setup. Offer that first.

You MUST set confirm=true.

confirm.description: Must be true. Removes the guardrails; the group's current size is unchanged.

tools.name: retry_cluster_scale_plan
tools.description:
Retry a FAILED cluster scale plan, picking up from where it stopped rather than starting over.

WHY THIS MATTERS: a failed plan blocks every further automatic tier move for its group. A cluster whose scaling has quietly stopped working usually has one of these sitting in `last_failed_scale_plan` on `get_capacity_config`. Retrying or deleting it is what unblocks the group.

Read the plan's `error_message` first and decide whether the cause is likely gone. Retrying into an unchanged cause just fails again; if the underlying problem is permanent, `delete_cluster_scale_plan` is the way to clear the block.

Returns the plan with status `in_progress`. A 422 means it is not in a retryable state - typically already running or not failed.

tools.name: delete_cluster_scale_plan
tools.description:
Discard a FAILED cluster scale plan, giving up on that move and unblocking automatic tier scaling for the group.

Use this when the plan's failure cause is not going away and `retry_cluster_scale_plan` would just fail again. The group stays on the size it currently has; the abandoned move is simply forgotten.

A 422 means the plan is not failed - only a failed plan may be discarded, so a running one has to finish or fail first. A 404 means it is already gone, which is the outcome you wanted anyway.

You MUST set confirm=true.

confirm.description: Must be true. Abandons the scale attempt; the group keeps its current size.

tools.name: list_webhook_endpoints
tools.description:
List the organization's outgoing webhook endpoints - the HTTPS URLs the platform calls when subscribed events happen.

Each row carries its `pid`, `url` and `subscribed_events`.

Not to be confused with deployment notification channels (`list_deployment_notification_bindings`), which push a specific deployment's outcome to Slack or email. These are org-wide, event-typed HTTP callbacks for a receiver you run.

tools.name: get_webhook_endpoint
tools.description: Get one webhook endpoint - its URL and the events it is subscribed to. Use it to check what a receiver will actually be told before changing anything.

tools.name: create_webhook_endpoint
tools.description:
Register an HTTPS URL to receive platform events for this organization.

The URL MUST be HTTPS - plain HTTP is rejected. At least one event is required.

Available events:
- `instance.scaling_failed` - an auto-scale or resize did not complete. The one worth subscribing to for anything production: a failed scale is silent otherwise and a failed cluster scale plan also blocks all further scaling for that group.
- `deploy_run.succeeded` / `deploy_run.failed` / `deploy_run.aborted` - a build run reached a terminal state. Fires for every deployment in the org, not one app.
- `preview_deployment.created` / `preview_deployment.destroyed` - a per-branch preview environment appeared or went away.
- `database_user.password_rotated` - a database user's password was rotated. THIS IS THE SIGNAL a credential consumer needs when `password_rotation_enabled` is true on that user: the payload never carries the password, so the receiver must refetch with `rotate_database_user_password`. Subscribing to it is what makes automatic rotation safe rather than breaking.

Subscribe deliberately: every event fires for the WHOLE organization, so `deploy_run.*` on a busy org is a lot of traffic to a receiver that only cares about one app.

A signing `secret` is generated server-side at create and is NOT settable. The receiver should verify it - tell the user to grab it from the create response, because that is how they authenticate the calls.

Requires `webhook_endpoints:create` (owner or admin).

url.description: HTTPS URL to POST events to. Plain HTTP is rejected.

subscribed_events.description: Events to send. An unknown event name is rejected with the offending value named.

tools.name: update_webhook_endpoint
tools.description:
Change a webhook endpoint's URL or which events it receives.

`subscribed_events` REPLACES the list, it does not add to it. Read the current set with `get_webhook_endpoint` and send the full intended list or you will silently unsubscribe the receiver from everything you left out.

Available events:
- `instance.scaling_failed` - an auto-scale or resize did not complete. The one worth subscribing to for anything production: a failed scale is silent otherwise and a failed cluster scale plan also blocks all further scaling for that group.
- `deploy_run.succeeded` / `deploy_run.failed` / `deploy_run.aborted` - a build run reached a terminal state. Fires for every deployment in the org, not one app.
- `preview_deployment.created` / `preview_deployment.destroyed` - a per-branch preview environment appeared or went away.
- `database_user.password_rotated` - a database user's password was rotated. THIS IS THE SIGNAL a credential consumer needs when `password_rotation_enabled` is true on that user: the payload never carries the password, so the receiver must refetch with `rotate_database_user_password`. Subscribing to it is what makes automatic rotation safe rather than breaking.

Requires `webhook_endpoints:update` (owner or admin).

subscribed_events.description: REPLACES the whole subscription list - include everything the endpoint should keep receiving

tools.name: delete_webhook_endpoint
tools.description:
DESTRUCTIVE: delete a webhook endpoint. Its delivery history goes with it and the receiver stops being told anything.

Check what it was subscribed to first (`get_webhook_endpoint`). If it carried `database_user.password_rotated` for a user with automatic rotation on, deleting this silently removes the only signal that credential's consumer gets - that consumer will break at the next rotation with nothing to explain why. Say so before proceeding.

If the goal is to receive less rather than nothing, `update_webhook_endpoint` can narrow the event list instead.

Requires `webhook_endpoints:destroy` (owner or admin). You MUST set confirm=true.

confirm.description: Must be true. The receiver stops getting events and the delivery history is removed.

tools.name: list_org_ssh_keys
tools.description:
List the organization's SSH public-key library. Each entry has `pid`, `name`, `public_key`, `fingerprint`, who added it and when.

This is a LIBRARY, not access: a key here grants nothing until it is installed on a specific project with `add_project_ssh_key` (or selected at `create_project`). Any org member can read it.

tools.name: add_org_ssh_key
tools.description:
Save an SSH PUBLIC key to the organization's library so it can be installed on projects.

PUBLIC HALF ONLY - the string starting `ssh-ed25519 ` or `ssh-rsa `, normally from `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`. Never ask for, accept or forward a private key. The backend refuses one with a specific warning; if you see it, relay it verbatim and tell the user to rotate that key, because they have just pasted a secret somewhere it did not belong.

If the user has no key yet, have them run `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "<their email>"` and paste the `.pub` file. Alternatively `create_project` can mint a keypair for them with `generate_ssh_key` - that returns the private key ONCE and never stores it.

Saving a key does NOT grant access anywhere. Install it per project with `add_project_ssh_key`.

Owner/admin only. Keys are unique by SHA256 fingerprint within an org, so re-adding the same key 422s and names the collision - that means it is already there, not that something is wrong.

name.description: A label the user will recognise later, e.g. "mac-laptop"

public_key.description: The full public key line, e.g. `ssh-ed25519 AAAA... user@host`. NEVER a private key.

tools.name: delete_org_ssh_key
tools.description:
Remove a key from the organization's library.

THIS DOES NOT REVOKE ACCESS. It is the single most important thing to say before doing it: the key material stays in `authorized_keys` on every server it was already installed on, so anyone holding the private half keeps their shell. To actually revoke, call `remove_project_ssh_key` on each project the key is installed on FIRST, then delete it here.

If the user's intent is "stop this person getting in", deleting the library entry alone does not achieve it. Check `list_project_ssh_keys` on their projects and say which ones still carry it.

Owner/admin only.

confirm.description: Must be true. Removes the library entry only - it does NOT remove the key from servers it is already installed on.

tools.name: list_project_ssh_keys
tools.description:
Show shell access for one project: the ready-to-copy `ssh_command`, the server's `public_ip`, every installed or pending key and the SSH source firewall rule.

`ssh_command` is `ssh shell@<public_ip>` - a NON-ROOT user, deliberately. Do not tell a user to `ssh root@`; it will be refused.

IF THE PLAIN COMMAND FAILS WITH "Permission denied (publickey)", the cause is almost always that their key is not one of SSH's default identities, not that the install is broken. The fix is `ssh -i ~/.ssh/<their key> shell@<public_ip>`. Offer that before investigating anything else.

Per-key `status`: `installed` (live on the box), `queued` (added while the project was still provisioning - it installs by itself once provisioning finishes), `pending_approval` (a `write` request waiting on a platform admin or ANY key added while the account is held for review by the Selfhost.dev team) or `rejected` (a request an admin declined). `access_level` and `approval_status` are on each key too.

`source` / `cidrs` / `requester_ip` ride this payload as well, so one call answers both 'who has a key' and 'which IPs can even reach port 22'. `requester_ip` is the address the backend would store for `my_ip` - useful to show the user and it reveals whether they are on IPv4 or IPv6 right now.

Cap: 10 keys per project.

tools.name: add_project_ssh_key
tools.description:
Install an SSH key on one project's server, giving its holder a shell on the non-root `shell` user.

TWO WAYS TO NAME THE KEY:
- `org_ssh_key_pid` - an existing library key (`list_org_ssh_keys`). Preferred.
- `name` + `public_key` - an inline key, which is ALSO saved to the library (or silently reused if a key with the same fingerprint is already there).

ACCESS LEVEL and the difference is who signs off, not what the key can do:
- `read_only` (default) - auto-approves and installs immediately, except on an account held for review, where it waits for a platform admin like `write` (the reply then says "SSH key submitted for review"). A 403 `account_restricted` means the key's fingerprint is banned.
- `write` - NOT INSTALLED. It files a request that a SELFHOST PLATFORM ADMIN must approve; admins are emailed and the requester is emailed on the decision. The call still returns 201, with the key at `pending_approval`. Tell the user plainly that they are waiting on us and cannot self-serve it, so they do not sit refreshing.
Both levels land on the SAME non-root user with the same on-box powers - `access_level` is a governance and audit label plus the approval gate, not a capability.

You can set the SSH source firewall in the same call with `source` (+ `cidrs`). KEY AND SOURCE SAVE AS A UNIT: if the key install fails, the source change is discarded with it.

Cap 10 keys per project. Owner/admin only. A key added while the project is still provisioning comes back `queued` and installs automatically once provisioning completes - that is normal, not a failure. A failed on-box apply rolls the record back and 422s, so the list never claims a key is installed when it is not.

org_ssh_key_pid.description: Existing library key pid (orgkey_...). Use this OR name+public_key.

name.description: Label, when supplying an inline public_key

public_key.description: Inline PUBLIC key line. Also saved to the org library. NEVER a private key.

access_level.description: read_only (default, installs at once) or write (queued for Selfhost.dev platform-admin approval, NOT installed)

source.description: Optionally set the SSH source firewall in the same save: anywhere | my_ip | custom

cidrs.description: Only with source="custom": 1-10 entries. Ignored for my_ip.

tools.name: remove_project_ssh_key
tools.description:
Revoke one key's shell access on one project. Unlike deleting a library entry, THIS is what actually removes the key from the server's `authorized_keys`.

Scope is this project only: the same key stays installed on any other project it was added to. To revoke someone everywhere, do this for each project that lists the key.

Owner/admin only. If the on-box removal fails the call 422s and the record is left alone, so the list never claims a key is gone while it still works.

project_ssh_key_pid.description: The PROJECT key pid (prjkey_...) from `list_project_ssh_keys` - not the library pid

confirm.description: Must be true. Whoever holds this key loses their shell on this server.

tools.name: set_project_ssh_access
tools.description:
Set which source IPs may reach the project server's SSH port (22). This is the firewall, separate from which keys are installed - both have to allow you in.

THREE MODES:
- `anywhere` (default) - port 22 open to all IPs, protected by key auth alone. Clears any stored list.
- `my_ip` - only the address the REQUEST came from. CAPTURED SERVER-SIDE: any `cidrs` you pass are ignored and because the MCP server makes the request, the address stored is the MACHINE RUNNING THIS MCP SERVER, not the user's laptop. If those differ - and with a remote or containerised MCP they do - you will lock the user out. Read `requester_ip` from `list_project_ssh_keys` first and confirm it is really the address they SSH from; if not, use `custom`.
- `custom` - 1-10 CIDRs you supply. Bare IPs are normalised (`203.0.113.25` becomes `/32`, IPv6 `/128`) and HOST BITS ARE ZEROED, so `10.1.2.3/8` is stored as `10.0.0.0/8`. Show the stored value back rather than what was typed.

LOCKOUT IS ALWAYS RECOVERABLE. This API does not travel over SSH, so a user whose address changed just sets it again. Say so if they hesitate. The platform's own egress is always unioned in, so a user cannot cut us off from the server we manage - do not list those addresses, only the customer's choice.

READ `applied` IN THE RESPONSE. `true` means the firewall was rewritten (or already matched). `false` with an `apply_note` means the setting was SAVED BUT NOT YET IN FORCE - usually the project is still provisioning - and a retrying job applies it later. The setting is never lost, but do not tell the user the port is locked down until it is.

A restricted mode can 422 with "try again shortly": the backend could not verify its own address and saving then would compose a rule locking the platform out. Retrying is the right answer, not an escalation.

IPv4 vs IPv6 catch: `my_ip` stores whichever family the API call used. Someone who reaches the API over IPv6 but SSHes over IPv4 needs `custom` with both.

confirm.description: Required for my_ip and custom - both can lock the user out of their own server if the address is wrong.

tools.name: get_project_scale_ladder
tools.description:
The sizes a project's server can grow into: the ladder that holds its current type, priced at its location. Read this before setting bounds or scaling up.

Returns `family`, `ladder`, `location`, `current_server_type` and `rungs`, smallest first, each with `server_type`, `vcpu`, `memory_gb`, `disk_gb`, `architecture`, `charged_hourly_millicents` (the metered hourly price at this location; 1000 millicents = 1 cent, so 2,080 per hour is $0.0208) / `charged_monthly_millicents` (the Monthly price cap: the most that size bills in a UTC calendar month, below hourly x 730; `null` when no monthly price is published), `current` and `available` (Hetzner stock: false means out of stock right now, null means unknown, so let the move check live).

A server only moves UP its own ladder: never to another family or generation, never down. A 422 means the server's type is on no ladder, so it cannot be scaled.

tools.name: get_project_scale_bounds
tools.description:
A project's scale bounds and where its server stands: `scale_bounds` (`min_server_type`, `max_server_type`, `enabled` or null when none are set), `current_server_type`, `current_rung` (specs and today's metered price), `ladder`, `autoscale_enabled` and `autoscale_held_by_upscale_pid`.

No bounds means the server never moves on its own AND cannot be scaled up by hand: `set_project_scale_bounds` comes first. `autoscale_enabled: false` with bounds set means automatic moves are paused or the server left the ladder the bounds were set on (set them again). A held upscale pid means a failed automatic move is holding automatic scaling off until the owner scales up by hand or changes the bounds.

tools.name: set_project_scale_bounds
tools.description:
Set or change a project's scale bounds: the smallest and largest sizes its server may run on, both rungs of its own ladder (`get_project_scale_ladder`), with the current size inside them. The ceiling is a cost cap: nothing, manual or automatic, moves the server past it.

`automatic` decides whether the platform may also move the server up BY ITSELF inside the bounds when it runs hot (it checks every 2 minutes; each move is a few minutes of downtime, announced to the owners first). It is REQUIRED when the project has no bounds yet: ASK THE USER. A user who wants one bigger server now wants `automatic: false`, which still allows `scale_up_project`. On a project that already has bounds, pass only what changes.

Creates the bounds when the project has none (POST) and updates them otherwise (PUT). Needs an Owner, Admin or Manager. A 422 names the rule broken: a size not on the ladder, min above max or the current size outside the pair.

min_server_type.description: The smallest size; usually the size it runs on now. Required when creating bounds.

max_server_type.description: The largest size, the cost ceiling. Required when creating bounds.

automatic.description: true: the platform may move the server up by itself inside the bounds (each move is downtime). false: manual scale-ups only. Required when the project has no bounds yet; ask the user.

tools.name: remove_project_scale_bounds
tools.description: Remove a project's scale bounds. The server stays on the size it runs now; it simply stops moving on its own and `scale_up_project` is refused until bounds are set again. To stop only the AUTOMATIC moves and keep manual scale-ups, use `set_project_scale_bounds` with `automatic: false` instead. Needs an Owner, Admin or Manager.

confirm.description: Must be true. Removes the bounds; the server keeps its current size.

tools.name: scale_up_project
tools.description:
Move a project's server UP to a bigger size now: the console's Scale up now. The answer to a full server ("the capacity guard refused my template", "the box is out of memory") other than a new project.

A move powers the server off for a few minutes: every service, database and app in the project is unavailable meanwhile. The disk grows to the new size and can never shrink back, the new size's price applies from the first hour and the organization's owners are emailed before and after.

PRECONDITIONS: scale bounds must exist (`set_project_scale_bounds`; `automatic: false` is enough), the target must be on the server's ladder, above its current size and within the bounds and offered at its location. The project must be `active` with its agent reporting and nothing else running on the host (409 otherwise: retry once that finishes). The wallet must carry the price difference (a top-up refusal names the gate). On an organisation that has never paid, a target above 8 cents an hour is refused with 402 `FREE_TIER_SIZE_LIMIT`: a top-up comes first.

Call without `confirm` first: it reads the ladder and states the move (new size, both prices, downtime, disk) for the user to approve. Needs an Owner, Admin or Manager.

Returns 202 with the upscale event; the project goes `scaling` and returns to `active` on the new size (or on the old one when Hetzner refused the type). Poll `get_project` or `list_project_upscales`. An out-of-stock refusal is recorded as a failed event before anything stops, so it can be retried later or tried with another size.

server_type.description: The size to move to: a rung of this project's ladder above its current size, within its bounds

confirm.description: Must be true. Powers the server off for a few minutes and grows its disk for good.

tools.name: list_project_upscales
tools.description:
A project's scale-up history, newest first, with what it runs on now (`current`) and `project_status`. Pass `upscale_pid` to read one move.

Each event carries `trigger` (`manual` | `auto`), `from_server_type` / `to_server_type` with the rungs and prices frozen when it was requested, `status` (`pending` | `in_progress` | `completed` | `failed` | `cancelled`), the `phase` it reached and a `failure_code` when it failed (`out_of_stock` before any stop means nothing went down). Use it to answer "why did my server restart?" and "did the move finish?".

upscale_pid.description: One event's pid (pue_...) to read just that move

tools.name: list_deleted_projects
tools.description:
List the organization's deleted projects that can still be restored, newest first: `pid`, `name`, `server_type`, `location`, `deleted_at`, `retained_until` (the last moment a restore is possible), `image_count`, `restorable`, `deleted_reason` and `last_revive_failure` when an earlier restore failed.

Only a project the PLATFORM removed keeps a copy: one whose credit ran out (14 days for a paying organization, 3 for a free one whose project had gone live) or, with `deleted_reason: "account_review"`, one removed after an account review (its restore answers 403 `account_held` or `account_restricted` while the review stands). A project the user deleted themselves is gone for good and never appears here, so an empty list is the usual answer. Any member can read it.

tools.name: get_deleted_project
tools.description:
One deleted project, with its kept images read LIVE from Hetzner: each with `image_id`, `source` (a converted daily backup or a manual snapshot), `retained_until`, `status` (`available` can be restored; `creating`, `unavailable`, `missing` or `unknown` cannot right now), `size_gb` and `created_at`. Also `hourly_cost_cents`, what the restored server will bill per hour (with backups when they were on before) and `restorable`, true only when at least one image is `available`.

Read this right before `restore_deleted_project` and pick an `available` image, usually the newest.

project_pid.description: The deleted project's pid, from list_deleted_projects

tools.name: restore_deleted_project
tools.description:
Bring a deleted project back from one of its kept images. The server is rebuilt from that image, on the same server type and location and under the same name, with everything that was on its disk when the image was taken; anything written after it is not there.

IT BILLS FROM THE MOMENT IT STARTS, like a new project: `hourly_cost_cents` from `get_deleted_project`, plus backups when they were on. The wallet must carry it for the runway a create needs (a refusal with `insufficient_credit` means top up first; `invoice_unpaid` means a past-due invoice must be paid; `free_tier_size_limit` means the box is above the free-credit size cap of 8 cents an hour and an organisation that has never paid tops up before it comes back).

Refused when: the image is not one of this project's, has passed `retained_until` (`image_expired`) or is not `available` yet (`image_not_ready`); a live project already has the same name (`name_taken`: rename or delete that one first); the project cannot be revived any more (`not_restorable`). Needs an Owner or Admin.

Returns 202; the project reappears in `list_projects` as `restoring`. Poll `get_project` until it is `active`, then check its services and databases.

confirm.description: Must be true. Rebuilds the server and starts billing for it.

tools.name: list_database_tables
tools.description:
