List the tables of a managed PostgreSQL or ClickHouse database, with their columns (name, type, nullable), kind and estimated row count: what the console's SQL tab shows beside the editor. Read this before writing a query against an unfamiliar database.

The backend keeps the latest look at the schema and answers from it; when there is none (or `refresh: true`), it starts a new look on the database and this tool waits up to 30 seconds for it. A look still running after that comes back with its pid: call again shortly. A look that failed lately is answered as failed for 10 minutes unless refreshed. The response also lists the instance's `databases`, for the `database` parameter.

Needs an Owner, Admin or Data Viewer (403 `data_access_required` otherwise), a running database and a wallet above its minimum. At most 10 new looks a minute per person. Reads names, types and estimates only, never a row.

database.description: Which database to look at. Default: the engine's own default database.

refresh.description: Start a fresh look instead of answering from the last one (after a schema change).

tools.name: run_sql_query
tools.description:
Run ONE read-only SQL statement on a managed PostgreSQL or ClickHouse database and return the rows: the console's SQL tab.

READ ONLY, ONE STATEMENT: SELECT and EXPLAIN on both engines, plus SHOW, DESCRIBE and EXISTS on ClickHouse. Anything that writes, changes the schema, chains a second statement or reads a catalog of secrets is refused before it runs, with the character position when the backend gives one. It runs as a read-only account on the group's PRIMARY, so a heavy query loads production: add a LIMIT and prefer an EXPLAIN first on a big table.

Limits: 30 seconds per statement, at most 1,000 rows and 4 MB (`truncated: true` says the cap hit). This tool waits up to 40 seconds for the answer; the very first run on a database also sets up the read-only account, which can take about 90 seconds and a run still going then comes back with its pid for `get_sql_run`.

THE ROWS COME BACK ONCE. The backend hands a finished run's answer over a single time and keeps no copy, so present the result from this response; to see it again, run the query again.

Needs an Owner, Admin or Data Viewer (403 `data_access_required` otherwise), a running database and a wallet above its minimum. One run of yours per database at a time; one run per person every 2 seconds and 60 every 10 minutes.

instance_id.description: The managed database instance pid (awsinst_...); any node of the group, the run goes to the primary

database.description: The database to run in. Default: the engine's own default database.

tools.name: get_sql_run
tools.description:
Read a SQL run started by `run_sql_query` that was still going when that tool stopped waiting. Waits up to 40 seconds more for it to finish.

The finished run's rows come back ONCE: the read that sees it `completed` takes them and later reads return the run without rows (`delivered: true`). An answer nobody collects within 15 minutes is dropped (`expired`). Only the person who started a run can read it (404 otherwise).

instance_id.description: The instance pid the run was started on

tools.name: get_index_advisor
tools.description:
Index Advisor's state on a managed PostgreSQL database: whether it is on and why not, what it has seen and how much that is worth.

Returns `setting` (`status`, `enabled`, the `database` it watches, `source` (`default` when the platform turned it on for a new database), `off_reason` when off: `never_enabled` | `turned_off` | `enable_failed` | `rolled_back` | `database_deleted` | `database_failed`), the `prerequisites` (pg_stat_statements and whether turning it on would restart PostgreSQL), `summary` (last collection and analysis, snapshots, `open_recommendations`), `overview` (the cards, null until the first collection), `observation` (how long each kind of finding needs to have been watched and how long it has been), `coverage` (how much of the workload the findings rest on) and `details_visible` (whether this caller may read the findings at all).

Read this before quoting a finding: a recommendation resting on a few hours of a quiet workload is weak and `observation` / `coverage` say so. Turning Index Advisor on or off is done in the console (it can restart PostgreSQL once).

instance_id.description: The managed PostgreSQL instance pid (awsinst_...); any node of the group

tools.name: list_index_advisor_recommendations
tools.description:
Index Advisor's findings for a managed PostgreSQL database, proposals first by impact. Each has `pid`, `kind`, `status`, `confidence` (`low` | `medium` | `high`), `source` (`static` analysis or `ai`), the table it concerns, `impact` (score and level, on proposals), `first_seen_at` / `last_seen_at` and how long the kind needs observing (`required_observation_days`).

Kinds: `missing_index` (a proposal to create one), `unused_index`, `redundant_index`, `duplicate_index`, `invalid_index`, `no_index_needed`, `other_cause` (the slowness is not an index problem) and `insufficient_evidence`.

By default only `open` and `acknowledged` findings are listed; pass `status` for the others or `all`. Each also carries `definition_sql` (the suggested DDL, where there is one) and `explanation`; read one with `get_index_advisor_recommendation` for the statements and the evidence behind it. These are recommendations: nothing here creates or drops an index and a `low` confidence or a short observation is worth saying out loud. Needs an Owner, Admin or Data Viewer.

status.description: Default: open and acknowledged. `all` for every status.

kind.description: Only this kind, e.g. missing_index or unused_index

tools.name: get_index_advisor_recommendation
tools.description: One Index Advisor finding in detail: the statements behind it (`supporting_queries`), the `evidence` and `validation`, the suggested DDL (`definition_sql`) where it proposes one, its `explanation`, `expected_benefit`, `tradeoffs` and `size_estimate` and its impact and confidence. Present the DDL as a suggestion for the user's own migration (run it at a quiet time; building an index on a large table takes locks and time), never as something already done. Needs an Owner, Admin or Data Viewer.

tools.name: get_query_statistics
tools.description:
The raw query statistics behind Index Advisor on a managed PostgreSQL database: its latest collection from pg_stat_statements and the catalog. Useful for "what is slow?" before any finding exists.

`statistics` carries `database`, `collected_at`, `period`, `statements` (each with its normalised `query` shape, never values, plus `calls`, `total_exec_time`, `mean_exec_time`, `max_exec_time` in ms, `rows` and block counts), `tables` (sequential vs index scans, live and dead tuples, size, columns), `indexes` (definition, scans, size, validity) and `activity` (sessions by state and wait and long-running ones with their transaction age). `statistics: null` means nothing was collected yet: the first collection runs within a few minutes of Index Advisor being on (`get_index_advisor`).

Rank by `total_exec_time` for where time goes and by `mean_exec_time` for slow single statements; a table with many `seq_scan` and large `seq_tup_read` is the usual index candidate, but suggest DDL only as the user's own migration. Needs an Owner, Admin or Data Viewer (it names the schema and statements).

instance_id.description: The managed PostgreSQL instance pid (any node of the group)

tools.name: list_support_tickets
tools.description:
List the signed-in user's support tickets, newest first: `pid`, `subject`, `state` (`active` | `pending_user_confirmation` | `closed`), `about` (what it concerns: a project with its name, billing, the account or other), `last_message` (who wrote last and a 160-character excerpt), `has_unread_replies` (support answered and the thread has not been opened since), `closed_by` (`you` or `team`), timestamps and `reopen_until` on a closed one. Also `open_count` against `open_limit` (2), `closed_count`, `unread_count` and `has_more`.

Tickets belong to the person, not the organization: teammates' tickets are not listed. `state: "open"` lists the two open states together. `q` searches subjects and every message body (case-insensitive, within the newest 500 tickets of that state) or matches a ticket reference such as #1a2b3c4d exactly; the counts stay the user's totals either way.

state.description: Filter: `open` (active and pending_user_confirmation) or one state

q.description: Search text (subject, messages or a #reference), up to 100 characters

tools.name: create_support_ticket
tools.description:
Open a support ticket with the Selfhost.dev team, as the signed-in user. The reply arrives in the console's Support page and by email; read it later with `get_support_ticket`.

Write it as the user would: what they tried, the resource pids involved (project, service, instance), what happened and when. Never put a password, token, private key or recovery phrase in a ticket.

Say what it is about with `about_kind` (`project` with `about_project_pid`, `billing`, `account` or `other`): naming the project puts it in front of the team with the ticket, so prefer it whenever one is involved.

Show the user the subject and message and get their go-ahead before sending: it goes to people. A user has at most two open tickets (`open_ticket_limit`), so check `list_support_tickets` first (`q` searches them) and reply on an existing ticket about the same problem. Text only. Pass the `request_id` of an earlier attempt to retry it without filing twice.

about_kind.description: What it is about; `project` needs about_project_pid

about_project_pid.description: With about_kind `project`: the project's pid (one of the user's live projects)

request_id.description: Idempotency key; omit for a new ticket, reuse to retry one

tools.name: get_support_ticket
tools.description:
Read one support ticket and its thread: the ticket (`state`, `has_unread_replies`, `reopen_until`) and its messages oldest first, each with `body`, `author_role` (`user` or `representative`), `author_name` (a representative's first name or Selfhost.dev), `created_at` and any attachments' names. Reading the thread marks support's replies as read, as opening it in the console does.

`pending_user_confirmation` means support asked whether the problem is solved: tell the user, then reply with their answer or, if it is solved, `close_support_ticket`.

page.description: Messages page (50 a page, oldest first)

tools.name: reply_to_support_ticket
tools.description:
Reply on one of the user's support tickets, as the user. Replying to a ticket support marked `pending_user_confirmation` puts it back with the team (`active`). A closed ticket takes no reply (`ticket_closed`): reopen it with `reopen_support_ticket` within 48 hours of its closing or file a new one.

Write it as the user would: what they tried, the resource pids involved (project, service, instance), what happened and when. Never put a password, token, private key or recovery phrase in a ticket. Show the user the reply and get their go-ahead before sending. Text only. Pass the `request_id` of an earlier attempt to retry it without posting twice.

request_id.description: Idempotency key; omit for a new reply, reuse to retry one

tools.name: close_support_ticket
tools.description: Mark one of the user's support tickets as solved, the console's "Mark as solved". Works whether the ticket is `active` or `pending_user_confirmation` and on an already closed ticket it changes nothing. A closed ticket can be reopened with `reopen_support_ticket` for 48 hours. Only on the user's say-so: closing tells the team the problem is fixed.

tools.name: reopen_support_ticket
tools.description: Reopen a closed support ticket, within 48 hours of its closing (`reopen_until` on the ticket). Refused after that (`reopen_window_expired`: file a new ticket) and when the user already has two open tickets (`open_ticket_limit`). After reopening, add what changed with `reply_to_support_ticket`.

tools.name: list_registry_logins
tools.description:
List the container registry logins saved on a project's server: `pid`, `host`, `username` and timestamps, sorted by host. The password or token is write-only and never listed.

Use it to check which private registries a project can pull from and after a `save_registry_login` that answered `pending` (the host appears here once the server confirms the login, about two minutes later at most).

tools.name: save_registry_login
tools.description:
Log a project's server in to a private container registry, so images from it can be pulled there (a template or Compose service whose image is private, for example). One login per registry host; saving a host that already has one replaces it.

The platform runs `docker login` on the server BEFORE saving, so a refused login is never stored: a 422 `registry_login_refused` carries the registry's own reason. The project must be `active`.

`host` is the registry host, optionally with a port: `ghcr.io`, `registry.gitlab.com`, `123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com`, `registry.example.com:5000`. A scheme, a trailing `/v2` and the Docker Hub aliases are normalised (`index.docker.io` and `registry-1.docker.io` become `docker.io`); any other path is refused.

`password` should be a token scoped to READ/PULL only (a GitHub PAT with `read:packages`, a GitLab deploy token, a Docker Hub access token), not an account password. It is write-only: stored encrypted, never returned by any call. Ask the user for it; never invent or reuse one from elsewhere. Note that an AWS ECR password expires after 12 hours, so ECR needs a fresh save before pulls once it lapses.

Answers:
- 201 saved, 200 replaced (`replaced: true`).
- 202 `pending: true`: the server took the login but did not confirm within the gateway's 30 s. Check `list_registry_logins` in a couple of minutes instead of saving again.
- 409 `server_not_ready` / `registry_login_busy`, 422 `registry_login_refused` / `agent_out_of_date`: explained in the reply. Nothing was saved.

The call can take up to about 25 seconds.

host.description: Registry host, optionally :port (ghcr.io, registry.gitlab.com, docker.io, registry.example.com:5000)

password.description: Token or password. Write-only: never returned. Prefer a pull-only token.

tools.name: delete_registry_login
tools.description: Remove a registry login from a project's server: the server is logged out of that registry first and the login is deleted only if that worked (409 `logout_failed` keeps it). Images already pulled stay on the server; new pulls of private images from that host will fail.

confirm.description: Must be true. Later pulls of private images from this registry will fail on this server.

tools.name: get_duplicate_sync
tools.description:
Read a PostgreSQL Duplicate's sync state: `sync` (the latest run or null), `last_skip` (the latest scheduled run that was skipped after it, with its code) and `auto_sync` (`enabled`, `interval_days`, `run_at`, `timezone`, `next_sync_at`, `last_synced_at`, `last_status`, `consecutive_skips`, `disabled_reason`).

A run has `status`, `overall_status`, nine `stages` each with its own status, `current_stage_name`, `elapsed_seconds`, `explanation` and on failure `failed_stage_name`, `failure_reason`, `recovery_required` and `retry_eligible`. Poll every 10 to 20 seconds while the Duplicate reads `duplicate_syncing`; quote `explanation` to the user rather than paraphrasing a stage key. 422 `not_duplicate` on a database that is not a Duplicate.

tools.name: start_duplicate_sync
tools.description:
Sync a PostgreSQL Duplicate from its Source now: the Duplicate's data is REPLACED, in place, with a fresh copy of the Source's. Its machine, connection address and its own login stay the same, so apps keep their connection strings; everything that exists only on the Duplicate (rows, schema changes, roles) is lost.

Typically 15 to 30 minutes, longer for a large volume. The Duplicate reads `duplicate_syncing` throughout and is UNREACHABLE for a few of those minutes while its machine stops and starts; stop, start, update, resize and fork are refused until it finishes. Poll `get_duplicate_sync`.

Single-node PostgreSQL Duplicates only, with a running Duplicate, a Source that still exists and the same PostgreSQL major on both. Needs a funded wallet. Refusals carry a code the reply explains. Confirm with the user first: this destroys the Duplicate's own data.

confirm.description: Must be true. Replaces every row, schema change and role that exists only on the Duplicate.

tools.name: set_duplicate_auto_sync
tools.description:
Turn a PostgreSQL Duplicate's Auto sync on or off or change its schedule. Auto sync runs the same sync as `start_duplicate_sync` every `interval_days` days at `run_at` in `timezone`, each run REPLACING the Duplicate's data with its Source's. Fields left out keep their value.

Enabling needs all three schedule fields (the first time), a Source that still exists and `confirm_overwrite: true`; it starts nothing at once: the first run is the next occurrence of `run_at`. Turning it off keeps the schedule for next time. A Multi-AZ Duplicate cannot have Auto sync on (it can only be turned off) and while Auto sync is on Multi-AZ cannot be enabled. Refusals carry a code the reply explains.

enabled.description: true turns Auto sync on (needs confirm_overwrite), false turns it off

timezone.description: IANA timezone, e.g. Asia/Kolkata or Europe/Berlin

confirm_overwrite.description: Required (true) to turn Auto sync on: the user accepts that every run replaces the Duplicate's data
